binary=n/a | metric=n/a | runs=0 | Open question from row 7 answered STATICALLY, no runtime probe needed. The FAILED branch is `cmp DWORD PTR [ebp-0xfc],0 / je 0x8211d18` at 0x8210b91; [ebp-0xfc] is filled at 0x820e1cb from `call 0x815970c` with args (global table 0x8b8ad60, this->field_8). That lookup is: `shl eax,7` (type*128), `mov ax,WORD [eax+ecx+0x2a]` (row id), `test ax,ax / je return-NULL`; on success it scales the row id by 0x86 off a second base at [table+0x563018]. There is NO bounds check and NO special case for type 0 -- type 0 indexes row 0, whose id word is 0, so the lookup returns NULL and the message fires. The two candidate explanations therefore collapse to one: "type=0 FAILED" means the creature reached CalcResults with field_8 still UNSET. It is NOT an unpopulated table (the table is loaded; row 0 is simply the reserved empty entry). Same shape governs the sibling `gethitvalu () type=0 FAILED!` at 0x81f91c0. Remaining unknown is narrowed to: who writes field_8, and when relative to construction.

binary=n/a | metric=n/a | runs=0 | The cCreatureHero constructor (0x81ea706; C1/C2 pair at 0x81eaa96, both storing vtable 0x8727e88 as their FIRST instruction, so there is no base-class ctor call -- matching RTTI, which records no base for this class) NEVER writes this->field_8. The only [reg+0x8] stores in its body, at 0x81ea931 and 0x81ea980, target the XOR-obfuscated globals 0x8906ce8/0x8906cec, not the object. So the type is left at whatever the allocator returned and is filled in later by whoever loads the creature record. CONSEQUENCE FOR THE SHIM: xshim zeroes every allocation, so an unassigned type reads back as exactly 0 -- meaning "type=0 FAILED" is a CLEAN, LOGGED failure only BECAUSE of our zeroing. With the 2005 allocator the same code path would read garbage into `shl eax,7` with no bounds check and index far outside the table. The zeroing converts a wild read into a diagnosable log line; do not "fix" it away.

binary=n/a | metric=n/a | runs=0 | /tmp/full_disasm.txt (107 MB linear objdump of install/sacred, AT&T) is DESYNCED in the regions that matter and must not be trusted for addresses. Of the four anchors from the CalcResults work (0x8210b91, 0x820e1bd, 0x815970f, 0x81ea706) only the last appears in it at all, and there it decodes as `push (%eax)`. Cause: the linear sweep loses instruction alignment (e.g. it places a 6-byte insn at 0x8159708 spanning 0x815970c, which a `call 0x815970c` proves is a real function entry). Targeted `objdump --start-address=<call target>` is authoritative because a call target is a guaranteed boundary; the linear sweep is not. Re-verified 0x81ea706 that way: it is a genuine prologue (push ebp; mov ebp,esp; ...) that writes vtable 0x8727e88 at +0xf, matching linux-1.0.02-vtables.txt -- so the cCreatureHero ctor findings in rows 26/28 and REPORT.md 2.6 stand. Rule: anchor every disassembly on a call target or known entry; never quote an address out of a linear sweep.

binary=n/a | metric=n/a | runs=0 | cCreatureHero is an EMBEDDED MEMBER of cCreature at offset +0x3a8, not a class in the polymorphic hierarchy. Chain: the only callers of the hero ctor twin 0x81eaa96 are 0x816b3d8 and 0x816b9d0, which ehframe_funcs.py places at +0x8c inside 0x816b34c..0x816b943 and 0x816b944..0x816bf3b -- two functions of identical size 0x5f7, i.e. cCreature C1/C2 ctor clones (0x816b34c writes vtable 0x8727dc8 = cCreature per linux-1.0.02-vtables.txt line 17). The call is `lea eax,[esi+0x3a8]; push eax` after `push esi; push edi`, so cCreatureHero::cCreatureHero(this=owner+0x3a8, edi, owner). This is the real explanation of the REPORT.md 2.3 anomaly "cCreatureHero shows only 1 virtual and no base, unlike every sibling" -- it is a small owned helper object, not a hierarchy member, so it has nothing to derive from. Corollary: the unset field_8 lives at cCreature+0x3b0, and the cCreature ctor does not write it either (after the hero ctor returns it writes [esi+0x57c]=0 and string members at +0x580/+0x58c).

binary=n/a | metric=n/a | runs=0 | The CalcResults type chain is now closed end to end. Hero field_8 is absolute cCreature+0x3b0, and the cCreature ctor copies it from cCreature+0x10 on two branches (0x816b5cb/0x816b5ce and 0x816b60c/0x816b60f; the twin clone repeats both at 0x816bbc6/0x816bc07). +0x10 is written exactly once in the ctor, guarded: 0x816b56d cmp [esi+0x10],0 / 0x816b571 jne / 0x816b573 mov [esi+0x10],edi where edi = ctor arg1 ([ebp+0xc]). +0x10 is the creature TYPE ID -- later code compares it against 0x150, 0x201-0x204, 0x24d-0x254, and pushes it straight into the same type-table global (ds:0x8b8ad60) that CalcResults indexes. So "type=0 FAILED" == a cCreature was constructed with a zero type argument (or took a branch skipping the copy). This SUPERSEDES the REPORT.md 2.6 sentence claiming the ctor never writes +0x3b0 -- that claim was written and disproved the same hour; REPORT.md is corrected. Not yet examined: the four non-ctor writers of [reg+0x3b0] at 0x83a74f1, 0x83a9169, 0x858ffc1, 0x85900cd. Next thread: callers of the cCreature ctor 0x816b34c/0x816b944 and what they pass as arg1.

REPORT.md 2.6 already had it right. Note 0x815970c has NO FDE -- it is a leaf without unwind info, so ehframe_funcs.py answers "in no FDE" for it; that answer means leaf-or-data, not "bad address".

binary=n/a | metric=n/a | runs=0 | Chain closed onto the loader. New tool analysis/tools/xrefs.py (direct E8/E9 rel32 scan, desync-proof) shows the cCreature ctor has exactly 3 call sites, all inside factory 0x816a194: selector at [ebp+0xc], cmp 0x22/ja, 35-entry jump table at .rodata 0x86e0f10, cases 0x02/0x03/0x20 do operator new(0x5a4) + ctor -> sizeof(cCreature)=0x5a4, type id = factory arg2 passed straight through. The factory has 2 callers: 0x8112522+0x1bc (propagates its own args) and 0x811cd74+0x181 which passes a LITERAL 0 as the type. 0x811cd74 is cObjectManager::load() -- it logs via .rodata 0x86da020 "cObjectManager::load() Ref[%d] Type[%d] Fam[%d] wp[%d,%d,%d] size[%d]" (logger 0x83b01d0; Type is [ebx+0x10], the field itself). Its shape is a deserializer: vtbl[0x8](stream,&tmp,4) reads 4 bytes, vtbl[0x20](obj,stream,0,..) is the object's own Load, then a 4-byte read is compared against sentinel 0xBAADF00D and a mismatch takes the error/log path. CONCLUSION: the load path constructs every object with type id 0 BY DESIGN and relies on Load to fill it from the stream, so "type=0 FAILED" is a Load that did not -- a stream desync/truncation, not an allocator bug. First evidence linking the static analysis to the observed in-game-save-load blocker.

binary=n/a | metric=n/a | runs=0 | race_sweep.sh now also counts cObjectManager::load() as DESYNC= per run. It is upstream of FAILED and prints Ref/Type/Fam/world-pos/size, so it is a strictly better instrument. Neither line appears in the clean 5/5 sweep, as expected. The case to watch for is DESYNC>0 with FAILED=0.

binary=n/a | metric=n/a | runs=0 | Mechanism complete. cCreature::Load = vtbl[0x20] = 0x819ce16 (size 0x9a7) is a SYMMETRIC serializer: arg3 [ebp+0x10] is a direction byte, nonzero -> stream vtbl[0xc] (write), zero -> vtbl[0x8] (read), same field list both ways; sentinel 0xC0DEF00D; cObjectManager::load passes 0. It serializes cCreature offsets 0x18 0xfc 0x150 0x1a4 0x1f0 0x2ed 0x39c 0x3a8 0x568 0x56c 0x570 0x580 -- +0x10 (the ctor type id) is NOT among them, so on the load path +0x10 stays 0 forever. +0x3a8 (embedded cCreatureHero) delegates at 819d052 to cCreatureHero::Serialize 0x821f2f6 (size 0x12df, sentinel 0xDEADBEEF), which serializes only +0x8 and +0x120, and +0x8 is one raw blob: 821f376 add eax,0x8 / push 0xee / call [edx+0xc] (save) mirrored at 821f5d7 with [edx+0x8] (load). So hero field_8 = cCreature+0x3b0 = the dword CalcResults indexes the type table with = the FIRST DWORD OF A 238-BYTE RAW STREAM READ, with no validation or bounds check. type=0 FAILED is a short/desynced blob read; xshim zeroing is what turns it into a clean NULL branch instead of a wild shl-7 index. Two corollaries: (a) Type[%d] in the cObjectManager::load() error line is [ebx+0x10], ALWAYS 0 on the load path -- that log field is not diagnostic, do not chase it, +0x3b0 is the one that matters; (b) three sentinels one per layer (0xBAADF00D per object, 0xC0DEF00D cCreature::Load, 0xDEADBEEF hero) make the stream independently checkable from a shim without patching the engine. Recorded REPORT.md 2.10 + AGENTS.md.

binary=n/a | metric=n/a | runs=0 | NEGATIVE RESULT, closes an open question: all four "non-ctor writers of [reg+0x3b0]" are false positives -- do not re-open them. 0x858ffc1/0x85900cd (FDEs 0x858fed8/0x858ffe4, both size 0x10c, identical +0xe9 offsets = C1/C2 clones) are the cUI_Merchandise constructor: it writes vtable 0x872fc88, which vtables.py attributes to cUI_Merchandise (18 virtuals, base cUI_Window2), and the store is mov WORD PTR [esi+0x3b0],ax -- a 16-BIT field at the same numeric offset in an unrelated class. 0x83a74f1/0x83a9169 (FDEs 0x83a6572/0x83a81ea, both size 0x1c78, identical +0xf7f = another clone pair) sit in the middle of a bulk 4-dword block copy 83a74e5/74f1/74fd/7509 writing [edi+0x3ac..0x3b8] from stack locals [ebp-0xc0..-0xb4]; that function has zero E8/E9 callers and appears in no vtable, so it is not on the creature path. LESSON: matching [reg+0x3b0] in an objdump is not evidence -- resolve the owning class first (vtable write or FDE identity). CONSEQUENCE: on the creature path there are EXACTLY TWO writers of cCreature+0x3b0, the ctor copy from +0x10 and the 0xEE-byte blob read of row 38. Nothing assigns the type later, which strengthens the row-38 conclusion rather than competing with it.

Layout: +0x4 size, +0xc pos, +0x10 base, +0x14 flag. vtbl[0x8] = cFile_ram::read(this,dst,len) = 0x83c5aee, 18 instructions: if base==0 return 0; avail = size - pos; IF AVAIL < LEN THEN LEN = AVAIL (83c5b0e, silent clamp); if len==0 return 0 WITHOUT memcpy; memcpy(dst, base+pos, len); pos += len; return len. METHOD - the bridge was a TEXT parser, not the binary loader. All 379 key strings are referenced exactly once (371) or twice (8), 387 sites, in one contiguous routine of ~62-byte blocks (gap histogram 62x226, 61x63). Each block is: push offset "Key" / push esi / call tokcmp / test+jz next / push 0x3d ('=') / push eax / call strchr / ... / store to a GLOBAL. So the exe carries a "Key=value" TEXT config parser (matches the CTRL+K defaults.h exporter, RESEARCH §13). Those globals ARE the in-memory image of balance.bin, so file_offset = global_VA - 0xad448c. The binary loader never had to be found. 322 keys store direct (mov [imm32],eax / fstp [imm32]); 32 more load the base into a register (the array keys, incl. all five Proz*); 25 remain unmapped.

The 25 unmapped keys are not a gap in the method, they are a different KIND of key: section markers (HorseData: RareTranslationMap: ItemThrowProbabilities: PriceAwVw: PriceSlot: PriceBoni:), the seven class tags (DAEM DWAR VAMP WELF DELF MAGE SERA), container names (rare inventory equip), and 9 others (RarePositiveList MerchantParts UniqueThreshold ZK__w ZK__s ZKoff SetSkillPoints BasisPferd NewSkill). They dispatch into sub-parsers rather than storing one scalar - i.e. they describe the 4896..24328 array region. Recovering those needs a real disassembler pass, not the byte-pattern scan.

CORRECTION: Godot's COMPRESSION_DEFLATE is zlib-WRAPPED, not raw - the plan said the opposite | Plan task 1.3 instructed "Godot's MODE_DEFLATE is *raw* deflate; the game's streams are zlib-wrapped (78 9c), so drop the 2-byte header". Godot's Compression::decompress passes window_bits = 15 for MODE_DEFLATE (and 15+16 for MODE_GZIP), i.e. it expects the zlib wrapper; raw deflate is not reachable through PackedByteArray.decompress at all. Stripping the two header bytes makes every call fail with compression.cpp:196 "Condition err != 1 is true" and return -1, which surfaces as an empty PackedByteArray, not an exception - so the failure is silent unless the caller checks the returned size. Correct call is z.decompress(out_size, FileAccess.COMPRESSION_DEFLATE) on the untouched stream. Caught immediately because the harness diffs md5s against the Python decode; an eyeball check on a black screen would not have distinguished this from a shader bug.

FINDING: world-wide terrain texture census - a single global Texture2DArray is impossible | Walked all 6050 sectors / 24,780,800 cells. A 5x5 sector window costs 8-151 textures depending on region (2-40 MB). Adjacent sectors share 54% of their textures by Jaccard, so a shared decoded-image cache roughly halves streaming work. FINDING: all 18 orientation values are in near-uniform use, so orientation is a render-time transform and not decoration | Counting orientation (+0x24) over the 55184 tile records the world actually references gives 3005-3127 occurrences for every one of the 18 values - flat to within 2%. 55184 distinct tiles map to only 4328 distinct textures, i.e. ~12.75 tile records share each texture. If orientation were baked into pre-rotated textures those records would carry different texture ids; they do not. So the 18 values are a transform applied to a shared texture at draw time. 18 is not 4 rotations and not 8 rotations+flips, so the encoding is still unknown - but the uniform distribution means ignoring it is visibly wrong everywhere, not just in rare tiles, which matches the regular repeating dot pattern visible in the streamed screenshot.

VERIFIED: ARGB4444 unpacking belongs on the GPU, not the CPU - 350 ms/sector became 18 ms | The CPU nibble expansion (two 512-byte lookup tables, 8.6 ms per 256x256 tile) made a cold sector cost up to 350 ms, a hard visible hitch, and plan task 2.2 existed to fix that with WorkerThreadPool. Not needed: ARGB4444 is byte-identical to Godot's FORMAT_RG8, so the raw 16-bit pixels upload untouched and terrain.gdshader unpacks the nibbles (lo byte = (g<<4)|b, hi byte = (a<<4)|r, /15.0, alpha nibble < 8 discards). Measured worst sector 349.8 -> 18.1 ms, typical 4-8 ms, and VRAM halves. Proof it is exact rather than merely close: the --region=50,50,1 screenshot is BYTE-IDENTICAL (md5 d794a2864a95a04ee8761e9140dfae0c) across the CPU path, the GPU path, and the earlier pre-streaming build. filter_nearest is load-bearing - interpolating packed nibbles between texels would be meaningless.

FINDING: terrain textures are 18-slot DIAMOND ATLASES, and tiles.pak +0x24 selects the slot | Connected-component labelling of the alpha channel of texture 6309 (iso825.tga) gives exactly 18 opaque components, each exactly 2500 px with a 100x49 bounding box - and the alpha mask is byte-identical across every terrain texture sampled (6300 6301 6309 6310 6311 6312 1494 5000 all hash the same; 1493 is fully opaque and 20000 differs, so it is a fixed lattice for terrain, not for all images). Row-extent measurement of one diamond: apex 4 px wide at y=0, widening exactly 4 px per row to 100 px at y=24, i.e. the standard 2:1 iso slope. Lattice is 9 rows of 2 columns, odd rows staggered half a cell: x0 = (n%2)*104 + ((n/2)%2)*52, y0 = (n/2)*25, so slot 17 ends at (255,248) and all 18 fit with no wrap. tiles.pak itself is a flat table - tile_id = 18*texture_index + orientation, 5007 textures x 18 + one group of 6 = 90132 records, names iso000.tga..iso5007.tga, one name per texture id.

VERIFIED: applying the atlas slot UV removes the repeating-dot artifact - the old renderer was squeezing all 18 diamonds into every cell | Before 2.4 the viewer mapped UV 0..1 over the whole 256x256 image for every tile, i.e. it drew all 18 diamonds shrunk into one cell, which is what produced the regular grid of dark dashes visible in the streamed screenshot. Mapping each quad to its own slot rect (and dropping the cell size from 128x64 to the true 50x25 half-extents) yields continuous ground: at 1:1 zoom there are no seams and no gaps between tiles, and the sand/gravel transition reads as designed terrain. CAVEAT, not yet closed: seamlessness proves the slot GEOMETRY, not the index->slot ORDERING. Any permutation of the 18 slots would still tile seamlessly, because each slot is a self-contained diamond; a wrong permutation would only scramble which variation appears where. Consecutive slot indices are demonstrably NOT consecutive world cells (world row 10,11,12,13 maps to atlas positions (52,125) then (156,125), a step of +104,0, not the +52,+25 an iso step would need), so the ordering is storage order and confirming it needs a side-by-side against the running retail game.

FINDING: the sector tail begins with the sector's own world cell origin - verified 6050/6050 | Every decompressed sector stream is 32 (name) + 131072 (WldxEntry[4096]) + a variable tail of 292..361244 bytes. The tail's first four dwords are (gx*64, gy*64, 0, 6) - the sector's absolute cell origin - and this holds for ALL 6050 sectors with zero mismatches, with dword[3] equal to 6 in every single one. That makes the tail self-identifying and gives an anchor for parsing it. Immediately after the 36-byte header the big sectors carry 36-byte records whose first two dwords are absolute cell coordinates INSIDE that sector, a u32 6 at +0x0c, and a monotonically increasing u32 at +0x10; 1870 such records exist world-wide and every one of them has both in-sector coordinates and the 6 tag. But a flat stride-36 parse of the whole tail puts only 0.62% of records in bounds, so the tail is NOT a uniform array - the 36-byte records are one leading section and something else follows. Do not assume a single stride; find the section boundary first.

WldxEntry | +0x10, +0x14 and +0x18 are each FOUR PER-CORNER BYTES, not three dwords | Byte-level histograms over a 1-in-7 sector sample (3.5 M cells) show the four byte positions inside each of +0x10..0x13, +0x14..0x17 and +0x18..0x1b having statistically IDENTICAL distributions (e.g. value 236 appears 154747/154291/153998/154446 times across +0x10..+0x13). Four independent byte fields with the same distribution is the signature of a per-corner array, which is exactly what an isometric terrain cell needs. +0x10..0x13: 82% zero, 38 distinct, dominated by 236/5/251 i.e. signed -20/+5/-5 - reads as per-corner height deltas. +0x14..0x17: NEVER zero, only 14 distinct, dominated by 255 then 235, 215, 195 - a clean step of -20 - reads as per-corner light level. +0x18..0x1b: 91% zero, 99 distinct. +0x1f is never zero with 67 distinct values (209, 64, 129, 49 most common) and is a per-cell type/flag byte. +0x08 is zero in all 24,780,800 cells - a dead field. Reading +0x1c as a u32 float is a TRAP: the common values 0xd1000000 / 0x40000000 look like floats but are just byte +0x1f with three zero bytes below it.

WldxEntry | +0x04 is a globally unique object handle - 862343 values, ZERO duplicates across 24.7 M cells | Collected every nonzero +0x04 over all 6050 sectors: 862,343 distinct values in the range 1..1,038,013 and not one collision. Uniqueness at that scale is not an accident - this is a world-unique entity/object id, not an index or a type. +0x0c is a different and denser space: 4,616,140 distinct nonzero values over 1..6,713,135. The two are largely independent - sampling shows 79.8% of cells have neither set, 17.6% have only +0x0c, 2.1% only +0x04 and 1.3% both - so they are two separate attachment slots, not a split 64-bit field. Together with row 217 this is the concrete starting point for plan Phase 3.1: the ids live in the cell grid, the records live in the tail, and the tail header gives the coordinate frame to join them on.

VERIFIED: per-corner light (WldxEntry +0x14..0x17) renders as smooth terrain shading with no per-tile banding | Fed the four bytes straight into ARRAY_COLOR and multiplied ALBEDO by COLOR.rgb in terrain.gdshader. Result is soft organic dark patches across the desert that read as relief and vegetation shadow. The diagnostic value is in what is ABSENT: the four bytes are assigned to the quad's four rect corners in file order, which is a guess, and a wrong corner order would show up as diagonal discontinuities at every tile boundary. There are none at 1:1 zoom, so the four bytes really are per-corner and the file order really is a corner order. Caveat kept in code: the diamond's corners are the rect's edge MIDPOINTS, so this interpolates over the wrong quadrilateral - it approximates the retail shading rather than reproducing it. Streaming after the change: 28 sectors, mean 7.9 ms, worst 19.7 ms.

WldxEntry | the per-corner byte order is W,N,E,S - SOLVED by a lattice constraint, not guessed, 0 mismatches in 6.5 M tests | In the iso lattice four cells meet at every diamond corner: cell(x,y).N is the same point as cell(x,y-1).W, cell(x-1,y).E and cell(x-1,y-1).S. That turns the corner order into a solvable constraint - try all 24 assignments of the four bytes to the roles N,E,S,W and score how often the three neighbours agree with the reference cell. Exactly ONE permutation scores 1.000: file byte0=W, byte1=N, byte2=E, byte3=S. Confirmed over 550 sectors (every 11th) x 3 arrays x 63x63x3 shared-vertex tests = 6,548,850 tests each: +0x10 mismatches 0, +0x18 mismatches 0, +0x14 mismatches 117 (0.0018%, plausibly genuine lighting seams). The exactness is itself the proof that these bytes are per-corner - no other interpretation produces perfect three-way agreement at every lattice point in the world. This method needed no disassembly and no retail screenshot.

VERIFIED: tiles are DIAMONDS, not textured rectangles - that is what makes the height field join up | Rendering per-corner heights on the old rectangle quads tore the terrain open: visible slivers of background between tiles, because a rectangle's corners are not shared with its neighbours and so displacing them cannot produce a continuous surface. Only the DIAMOND corners are lattice points, and they are shared four ways. Rebuilt each tile as a 4-vertex diamond (N/E/S/W) whose UVs sit at the atlas slot rect's EDGE MIDPOINTS - which also means the transparent rect corners are never sampled at all. Result: every gap closes, the mesh is watertight, and a real elevation terrace becomes visible in sector 21,95. Height goes into vertex Y, not Z, so it does not fight the depth ordering that lets separate sector meshes coexist. Quad count is unchanged (still 1 quad / 2 triangles per cell), so the 28672/63 invariant and the md5 parity harness both still pass.

NEXT: zoomed-out terrain aliases, and the GPU-unpack trick is what blocks the fix | With diamond geometry the tile is sampled 1:1 over a smaller screen area, so zooming out now minifies without mipmaps and the ground shimmers. The normal fix - generate mipmaps - is ILLEGAL for the current textures: they are uploaded as FORMAT_RG8 holding packed ARGB4444 nibbles, and averaging packed nibbles is meaningless, which is also why filter_nearest is mandatory. So mipmapping requires going back to the CPU RGBA8 expansion (8.6 ms/tile, the thing that cost 350 ms per cold sector) or expanding on the GPU into a render target once per texture. Worth measuring before choosing; do not "just enable mipmaps".

CORRECTION: Godot DOES have Image.FORMAT_RGBA4444 - the plan's "no FORMAT_RGBA4444 in Godot" was wrong and I repeated it twice | Probed the running 4.7.1 build: FORMAT_RGBA4444 = 6 and FORMAT_RGB565 = 7 both exist. The claim originated in plan task 1.4 and was carried into sacred.gd's comments unchecked. It matters because the engine's own C++ expansion is 29x faster than the GDScript nibble loop: 256x256 FORMAT_RGBA4444 -> convert(FORMAT_RGBA8) costs 298 us against 8.6 ms, and generate_mipmaps() on the result costs another 55 us. CAVEAT that makes it not a drop-in: Godot reads the u16 high-nibble-first as R,G,B,A while Sacred stores A,R,G,B, so every channel arrives rotated by one - the engine's .r holds Sacred's alpha and .gba hold its red/green/blue. Rotating the u16 on the CPU would give back the per-pixel loop we just removed, so terrain.gdshader unswizzles instead, which is free.

VERIFIED: zoomed-out shimmer fixed by linear filtering + a 1-texel UV inset; MIPMAPS made it worse, not better | Three variants rendered and compared at the same camera. (a) filter_nearest, no mipmaps: shimmer at minification, the original complaint. (b) filter_linear_mipmap: shimmer gone but every diamond gained a heavy dark outline - atlas slots are only 4 px apart, so mip level 2 already averages a diamond together with its neighbours and the transparent padding. Mipmaps and a tightly-packed atlas are fundamentally in conflict here; do not retry without repacking the atlas. (c) filter_linear, no mipmaps, plus slot_uv inset by 1 texel and retargeted from the 104x50 lattice cell to the measured 100x49 OPAQUE bounding box: shimmer gone AND grid gone. The inset is what removes the residual faint grid that (c) had without it - linear filtering at the diamond tips was reaching into the padding. Cost of moving from RG8 to RGBA8: worst sector build 22.7 -> 39.9 ms, mean 10.5 -> 12.6 ms, because the texture is now 4 bytes per pixel instead of 2. Judged worth it; the hitch is bounded and one-off per sector.

FINDING: PHASE 3 SOLVED at the structural level - WldxEntry +0x04 indexes world/static.pak, +0x0c indexes world/floor.pak | The two handle fields are not ids in an abstract space, they are direct indices into the two big OBJ archives sitting next to sectors.wldx. Proof is exact: static.pak (magic "OBJ" v1) declares count = 1,038,014 and the maximum +0x04 seen anywhere in the world is 1,038,013; floor.pak (magic "OBJ" v1) declares count = 6,713,136 and the maximum +0x0c is 6,713,135. Both are exactly count-1. Confirmed structurally too - every static.pak record's first dword equals its own index, checked on 32,428 records with zero exceptions, so the archive is self-validating. Entry sizes are uniform: static.pak 64 bytes, floor.pak 16 bytes. Index 0 means "none". This also explains why the sector tail was a dead end: 339 of 356 sampled sectors have the MINIMUM 292-byte tail regardless of how many objects they contain, and the tail's dword[3] is the constant 6 in all 6050 sectors (a version, not a count). Large tails are near-100%-zero reserved space, which is why they compress to almost nothing.

FINDING: 64-byte record layout, and it carries absolute iso SCREEN coordinates | +0x00 u32 self index (validates the archive). +0x04 u32 type id - 2872 distinct, range 801..31936, top values 1037/1035/1033/8879 (range fits mixed.pak's 32096 entries, not models.pak's 4993). +0x08 u32 flags, only 9 distinct values, 0 and 32 covering 95%. +0x0e i32 ox and +0x12 i32 oy - note the ODD alignment, these are not on 4-byte boundaries. Remaining bytes are largely 0xCD MSVC uninitialised fill. floor.pak's 16-byte record is +0x00 self index, +0x04 id pair, +0x08 0xCDCDCDCD unused, +0x0c NEXT INDEX - a linked list, so several floor layers can stack on one cell, which is why 6.7 M floor entries serve 24.7 M cells.

CORRECTION: the true iso cell is 96x48, NOT the 100x50 I derived from the terrain atlas | Fitting every sampled static object's stored position against the cell that references it gives ox = 48.0058*cx - 47.9981*cy and oy = 24.0235*cx + 24.0107*cy over 32,428 samples - i.e. ox = 48*(cx-cy), oy = 24*(cx+cy), the iso projection with HW=48, HH=24. Residuals are quantised (371 and 668 distinct values, 61% and 55% within half a cell) and are sub-cell placement offsets; each static index is referenced by exactly one cell, so multi-cell anchoring is not the cause. My earlier HW=50/HH=25 came from the atlas slot PITCH (104 x 25 stagger 52), which includes inter-slot padding, and the drawn art is 100x49, which overlaps its own cell by ~2 px the way hand-authored iso tiles normally do. Object data is ground truth and the atlas packing is not. Fix is HW/HH only: terrain geometry now uses 96x48 while still sampling the 100x49 art bbox, so the art is squeezed ~4% (invisible) and corner sharing - which the height field depends on - is preserved. Without this fix objects would have drifted 4% away from the terrain under them.

VERIFIED: object placement rendered and visually confirmed - 648 markers land inside their sector and follow terrain features | godot-port now reads world/static.pak through Sacred.Statics and, under --markers, draws one type-coloured quad per placed object at its own stored ox/oy. Sector 64,39 renders all 648 of its static references; every marker falls inside the sector's 64x64 footprint and the distribution visibly tracks the ground - dense along the dirt paths, sparse on the open grass. That single screenshot cross-validates three separate claims at once: that +0x04 indexes static.pak, that ox/oy really live at the UNALIGNED offsets 0x0e/0x12, and that the cell is 96x48. Any one of the three being wrong would push markers off the sector or skew them systematically. Cost with markers on: mean 13.1 ms, worst 47.4 ms per sector. Terrain invariant (28672 quads, 63 textures) and the md5 parity harness both unchanged. What is still missing for real objects is the art: type ids run 801..31936 which fits mixed.pak (32096 entries) rather than models.pak (4993), and models.pak is MDL v3 / Granny2, undecoded.

FINDING: the object ART chain is fully resolved - static type id -> mixed.pak -> texture.pak, verified 209956/209956 | pak/mixed.pak (magic "MIX" v0, 32096 entries) is the sprite table that static.pak's type id indexes. Entry layout: 16-byte header {u32 frame_count, u16 w, u16 h, i16 dx, i16 dy, u32 pad} followed by frame_count fixed 64-byte frame records, so entry size is exactly 16 + 64*frame_count (checked, holds). Frame record: +0x00 name[32] like "MIX233.444" (.444 = ARGB4444), +0x20 u32 texture.pak INDEX, +0x24 two u16, +0x30 four f32 forming a UV rect into that texture. The +0x20 index is not a guess: resolving each frame's own name string through texture.pak's name table and comparing against the stored u32 matches on 209,956 of 209,956 frames with zero exceptions. texture.pak holds 10,591 MIX*.444 sprites alongside the ISO*.TGA terrain atlases. 15,840 of 32,096 mixed entries have ZERO frames - including type 1037, the single most common static type in the world - so a large share of placed statics are invisible markers (collision, spawn, sound) rather than art.

NEXT: object sprite rendering is feasible but three semantics are still unverified - do not guess them | Cost is fine: per sector the median is 104 placed objects drawing from only 10 distinct object textures (max 719 objects), so ~10 extra draw calls per sector, and the existing image cache already covers the decode. What is NOT established, and what a renderer would have to invent if written today: (1) which frame of the N is chosen - frame counts cluster at 4/5/6/7/8, which smells like facing directions, so it is probably a function of an orientation field not yet located; (2) what the header's i16 dx,dy and the frame's two u16 at +0x24 mean - candidates are sprite anchor offset and source size, and the one arithmetic check attempted (u16 32,32 vs a UV rect spanning 0.875..1.0 of a 256 px texture = 32 px) fit for frame 0 but NOT for frame 1; (3) whether w,h in the header are pixels or something else. Each is cheap to settle against the running retail game. Guessing all three would produce a plausible wrong picture, which is the exact failure mode this project has been bitten by five times already.

CORRECTION: source_color + rotated channels = wrong colour on Vulkan; the whole session's visual verification ran on the WRONG backend | The project ships Forward+/Vulkan but every screenshot taken while building it was rendered with --rendering-driver opengl3 under xvfb, and the bug only appears on Vulkan. terrain.gdshader declared the sampler `source_color`, which sRGB-decodes RGB but NOT alpha. Because the FORMAT_RGBA4444 trick leaves channels rotated by one (.r is Sacred's alpha, .gba its colour), the decode hit Sacred's red and green and skipped its blue, and the framebuffer then re-encoded all three - brightening blue alone. Measured at five sample points, Vulkan matched OpenGL exactly on R and G and differed only on B: desert tan (208,171,120) rendered as (210,172,183), a lavender. Predicted value lin_to_srgb(120/255) = 181 against 183 observed, so the mechanism is confirmed arithmetically and not just by eye. Fix: drop source_color, sample raw, multiply the per-corner light in GAMMA space (which is what the 2005 2D blitter did) and apply an explicit srgb_to_linear before writing ALBEDO. Vulkan now reproduces the reference within +/-1 per channel at all five points.

FINDING: Forward+ and Compatibility disagree on whether ALBEDO is linear, so an unshaded shader cannot be verified on the wrong one | After the fix, the same shader renders correct tan (208,171,120) on Vulkan and much darker (161,104,47) on --rendering-driver opengl3. Forward+ treats ALBEDO as linear and encodes to sRGB on output; the compatibility path does not, so the explicit srgb_to_linear is a double-darken there. This is not worth branching on - the project ships Forward+ and nothing else - but it makes backend choice part of the test protocol rather than an incidental flag. Vulkan works fine under xvfb-run with the NVIDIA driver, so there was never a reason to force opengl3. AGENTS.md and the plan now say to verify on the default renderer and warn against the flag. General lesson, and the sixth time this project has been bitten by the same shape of error: a green check on an instrument that is not the shipping configuration is not a green check.

CORRECTION: object sprites need their own shader - StandardMaterial3D cannot express the channel rotation, and alpha-scissor silently tested the wrong channel | First object render produced thin coloured slivers scattered over the terrain instead of sprites. Cause: object textures go through the same Image.FORMAT_RGBA4444 -> convert(RGBA8) path as terrain, so channels arrive rotated (.r is Sacred's alpha, .gba its colour), but they were pointed at StandardMaterial3D.albedo_texture, which has no way to unswizzle. TRANSPARENCY_ALPHA_SCISSOR therefore tested Godot's alpha = Sacred's BLUE, discarding every pixel whose blue was below half - which is why only thin bright streaks survived and why they were the wrong colour. Diagnosis was cheap because the GDScript Sacred.Mixed decode was first dumped and compared against the Python: identical, so the fault had to be downstream of the data. Fix is object.gdshader, the same unswizzle and srgb_to_linear as terrain but sampler2D and a real 0.5 alpha cut (objects have genuine interior transparency; terrain's 0.25 was a padding tolerance). Result: sector 64,39 renders as an actual town - red tiled roofs, stone walls, windows, stairs, cobbled courtyard, a pile of gold coins.

That is the reading that makes a tree stand on its own cell, but it is a guess and it is marked ponytail: in the code. (2) OBJECT-VS-OBJECT DEPTH: every tile of an object shares one z derived from the object's own position, z = (cx+cy)*DEPTH_STEP + 2, which matches the terrain's own formula so object-vs-TERRAIN sorting is right; but two objects whose bases sit in the same iso row get the same z and fight. Both are now cheap to settle: analysis/tools/look.sh can capture the retail game and the port headlessly, so a side-by-side of the same location is one command each.

NEXT: object sprites cost 3-7x a terrain sector - mean 54 ms, worst 174 ms | Streaming with objects on: 16 sectors, mean 54.2 ms, worst 173.6 ms, against 12.6 / 39.9 ms for terrain alone. The extra is object texture decode - object sprite sheets are various sizes, some much larger than the 256x256 terrain tiles, and each needs its own ImageTexture because they cannot share a Texture2DArray. The shared _obj_tex cache amortises across sectors (adjacent sectors reuse art heavily) so the steady state is better than the cold figure, but 174 ms is ~10 dropped frames and is the largest hitch the port has had. Cheapest levers, in order: raise loads_per_frame granularity so one sector's objects are split across frames; decode object textures lazily per texture rather than per sector; and only then consider threading. Do not optimise before measuring which of decode / upload / mesh build dominates - the last two times this project assumed the bottleneck it was wrong (the ARGB4444 CPU loop, and the mipmap fix).

CORRECTION: ox/oy is the sprite's TOP-LEFT, not its ground point - my "bottom-centre" reading was wrong and row 247's retraction was wrong too | The user, watching the port live, confirmed objects were misaligned - after I had retracted that exact report in row 247 on the strength of static screenshots. Those are -1/2 and -1: ox ALREADY carries -w/2 and oy ALREADY carries -h. So the stored position is the sprite's top-left corner in screen space, and the old code re-applied both offsets on top, displacing every piece by an amount proportional to ITS OWN size - which is exactly why parts of one building came apart while each part looked internally fine. Correct placement is origin = (ox + dx, oy + dy) with no size term. The same error explains the occlusion symptom: depth was taken from oy, i.e. the sprite's TOP, so a tall building sorted as if it stood at its own rooftop. Ground depth is oy + h. CORRECTION: PITFALL: texture.pak entry headers lie OUTSIDE the index-recorded size -- a naive read(offset, size) truncates every inflate | Cost a wrong-turn while implementing the cursor (2026-08-07). The texture.pak index record gives {flags, offset, size}, but `size` counts only the DEFLATE payload; the 80-byte header (name[32], w u16 @32, h u16 @34, kind u8 @36) sits before it and is NOT included. Reading exactly `size` bytes from `offset` therefore yields header + payload-minus-80, and zlib fails with "incomplete or truncated stream" -- which reads like a corrupt or unsupported entry rather than a short read. Correct read is (offset, size + 80). This is already encoded in the port: Sacred.Pak.blob(i, extra) takes an `extra` parameter for exactly this reason and Sacred.decode_texture passes 80, with the header comment "The texture header lies outside the recorded size, hence the parameter." Recorded here because the port had it right and an independent Python reader still got it wrong -- any future out-of-engine tooling over texture.pak will hit the same wall. | godot-port/sacred.gd, install/pak/texture.pak

REFUTED: ROW 491'S MECHANISM FOR 1196 IS WRONG IN INDEX SPACE, AND THE UV INDICES ARE NOT IN THE FACE RECORD. Row 491 asserted 1196 is 'granny's count of unique (position,normal,UV) tuples after de-indexing'; that was an inference, and measuring it refutes it. First, the UV indices were located: they are NOT in the 24-byte face record (which carries position and normal indices only), but in ModelSection 0xCA5E0E01 > Model > RenderPassSection > RenderPass, whose leaf child holds {int32 count} then count x {int32 faceIndex, int32 uvA, int32 uvB, int32 uvC}. A RenderPass names a FormMesh SLOT, not a mesh: its first int32 indexes the FormMesh 0xCA5E0C03 list whose own first int32 is a 1-based mesh ordinal -- for GLADIATOR that map is [2,0,1], so slot and mesh are NOT equal and a positional assumption would have silently swapped body for legs. All 1695 faces resolve a UV triple, 6 RenderPasses over 3 meshes (212+230 -> legs, 260+258+350 -> body, 385 -> head). The UV values themselves are in MeshField 0xCA5E0803 under MeshFieldSection 0xCA5E0804: layout is {u32 componentCount} + N x 3 x float32, with componentCount = 3 in all four fields and (span-4)/12 exact in all four (2322, 896, 624, 703). Mesh 0 carries TWO fields, 2322+896 = 3218, and the per-mesh totals 3218/624/703 = 4545 reproduce the external viewer's UV counts exactly. With those indices in hand, EVERY index-space grouping was censused in one pass and NOT ONE lands on 1196: p=887, q=933, uv=3649, p+q=933, p+uv=3715, q+uv=3755, p+q+uv=3755, and adding a render-pass namespace gives pass:p=935, pass:q=981, pass:p+q=981, pass:p+q+uv=3755. ROOT CAUSE OF THE DEAD CUTAWAY TRIGGER FOUND AND FIXED: Sacred.Regions.cell_class collapsed the NON-ZERO class bytes 0xd0/0xe0 onto EMPTY. It read `return 0 if b == 0 else b & 0x0f`, so any byte whose class nibble is 0 came back indistinguishable from a raw 0x00 (uncovered) cell. 0xd0+0xe0 are 39,644 cells world-wide - more than double FLOOR's 16,302 - and they are the buildings' OPEN INTERIOR GROUND. Measured at the pinned Seraphim spawn: sector 50,39 carries exactly ONE region (anchor 3213,2502 size 34x30 family KLOSTER_KAPELLE01) whose rect DOES contain the spawn cell 3236,2511 at local 23,9, and that cell's raw byte is 0xd0. An ASCII dump of the whole 34x30 grid shows 0xd0 tiling the octagonal nave wall to wall and 0xe0 tiling the library wing beside it, with 0xd1 walls ringing both. So row 679's 'derive() resolves NO footprint at the hero's own cell' was HALF RIGHT: the footprint resolved fine, the CELL CLASS decoded to EMPTY, class_is_open said false, and _triggered() could never be true. FIX: cell_class now returns a new Sacred.Regions.OPEN (0x10, deliberately not a nibble value) for a non-zero byte whose nibble is 0, EMPTY only for a raw 0x00; Walkable.class_is_open gains OPEN; verify_ref.py's WALKABLE_CLASSES mirror gains 0x10. | CODE: godot-port/sacred.gd (Regions enum + cell_class + header note), godot-port/world/walkable.gd (allowlist + doc), analysis/tools/verify_ref.py (WALKABLE_CLASSES, region_cell_class). PAINTER-ORDER OVERLAP: BOTH PER-OBJECT SORT KEYS ARE WRONG, AND THE REAL FIX IS A LAYER FIELD WE HAVE NEVER READ. The defect measured exactly: sector_view.gd sorts objects by pos.y descending, where pos is the static's own iso SCREEN position (static.pak +0x0e/+0x12), so the key is the object's ANCHOR. A sprite is drawn DOWNWARD from origin.y = pos.y - spr.anchor.y, so a large composite and a small prop anchored on the same iso diagonal get near-identical keys while the composite's geometry reaches many cells further front. Concrete pair from OBJ_TRACE=50,39: KLOSTER_KAPELLE01_2_00D at cell (3225,2510), 460x719, pos.y -137661, and a bush at cell (3238,2497), 158x150, pos.y -137666 - the SAME diagonal, 3225+2510 == 3238+2497 == 5735 - so the bush sorts after the wall whose lower half it stands behind, and paints over the chapel's north wall. world/triggers.pak IS DECODED AND IT IS THE WORLD'S DYNAMIC-OBJECT REGISTRY. Layout: magic TRG v1, u32 count @+4 = 2268, a fixed header at 0x100 of {136, 268, 36288} whose 268 is the data offset and whose 36288 == 2268*16, then 2268 sixteen-byte records at 0x10c; 0x10c + 2268*16 == 36556 == the exact file length, which is what fixes the stride. Record: +0x00 u32 trigger id (== record index for live records), +0x04 u16 kind (16 = live, 1246 records; 0 = dead/erased, 1022 all-zero records), +0x06 u32 static.pak RECORD INDEX = the back-link, +0x0a u16 always 1 for live, +0x0c u32 always 0. THE BACK-LINK IS BIDIRECTIONAL: static_pak[trigger[i].+0x06].+0x27 == i for 1246 of 1246 live triggers, 0 mismatches. WARNING: triggers.pak is NOT a generic Pak container despite its magic being in Sacred.Pak.ALLOWED_MAGIC - the bytes at 0x100 are a fixed header, not an index, so reading it through Sacred.Pak silently misreads it. The same warning applies to pak/creature.pak (CIF, 41020 B, count=474 @+4): its 0x100 index is garbage (offsets like 251989775); it is a FLAT table of (41020-256)/474 = 86.0000 exact stride. | +0x08 == 0x10 IS THE DYNAMIC-OBJECT DISCRIMINATOR. Over 32,357 statics in the 9x9 sector band 46-54 x 35-43, exactly 33 carry an items name ending .grn, and all 33 have +0x08 == 0x10 AND a unique non-zero triggerId. Trigger ids rise monotonically with sector, so the table is spatially authored. world/floor.pak +0x04 IS DECODED: ITS LOW 17 BITS ARE A tiles.pak INDEX, AND THE FILE IS A PER-CELL OVERLAY-TILE LAYER. The split of +0x04 is 15/17, pinned from BOTH sides rather than eyeballed. Upper bound: tiles.pak holds 90,132 records, so a real 17-bit tile index must always land under 90,132 while an unrelated field would do so only 68.77% of the time - measured 6872 of 6872, and one bit wider (18) immediately drops to 70.2% against its own 34.4% chance. Lower bound: 2595+ of the sampled values EXCEED 65535 inside that field, which a 16-bit field could not hold, so the boundary is not 16. Then every referenced tile resolves exactly like a terrain tile: texture id inside texture.pak's 25,535 AND orientation inside 0..17, for all 6872, across 690 distinct textures. TWO HYPOTHESES TESTED AND REFUTED ON THE WAY, DO NOT RETRY: (a) '+0x04 low 16 bits index items.pak' and (b) 'floor.pak is a creature/NPC spawn table'. world/floor.pak +0x04's TOP 15 BITS ARE A SECOND tiles.pak INDEX - the field is TWO TILE IDS IN ONE u32, and the overlay is a TWO-TEXTURE BLEND. Found in the retail reader at 0x080e4ca5 (sacred_orig, .text 0x08053828 / file 0xb828), which splits the payload exactly as row 695 said - ecx = v & 0x1ffff, esi = v >> 0x11 - and then treats BOTH halves identically: edi is loaded with 0x12 and each half is divided by 18 for its diamond slot (0x080e4dbb, 0x080e4dc7), each is pushed into the SAME tile lookup against cWorld+0x254 (0x080e4de2, 0x080e4dfa), and the two results are written into ONE vertex struct as two UV pairs - low field to +0x00/+0x04/+0x20/+0x24, top field to +0x08/+0x0c/+0x28/+0x2c. A zero top field takes the single-texture path at 0x080e4cca instead; a nonzero one under the other mode byte sets a defer flag at 0x080e4d98, so retail renders these in two passes. | CONFIRMED AGAINST THE DATA, not just read off the disassembly. Over 135,921 nonzero top values sampled at stride 31: every one is a valid tiles.pak index (135921/135921), and tiles.pak's own orientation field equals index % 18 for every one of them - the engine's derivation and the port's stored field are the same rule. The top field draws from only 39 DISTINCT TEXTURES against 2203 for the ground tiles it sits with, and only 2 of the 39 are ever used as ground: a small dedicated set of mottled transition sheets, which is what a blend layer looks like. Domain measured over 216,553 records: 0 (37.2%) or 855..1535, nothing in 1..854 and nothing at or above 1536. Earlier readings that made this look like a quantity were artefacts - the mean falling with chain depth (971, 845, 586, 287) is just which tiles get stacked, and the 3x512 split was a coincidence of the band. | REFUTES THE 'UNDECODED FIELD' FRAMING OF ROW 695 AND EXPLAINS ROW 699. The corner-blend hypothesis for WldxEntry +0x18..0x1b was refuted on its own evidence; this is why it had to be - the overlay's blend does not come from the cell at all, it comes from a second tile in the same u32. Also kills three hypotheses row 695 listed as open: not a sector id, not a layer, not a draw order. NOT YET DECODED: the BLEND OPERATION. The engine emits one quad with two UV sets, so the port cannot reproduce it with a second quad - it needs a second sampler in terrain.gdshader and the combine rule, which lives in the render path past 0x080e4e5c and is not read yet. Until then the port draws the low tile only (row 700) and the transition sheets are simply missing. PROBES: floor_hi_probe, floor_hi2..hi6_probe, floor_mask_probe, all read-only.

THE floor.pak TWO-TILE BLEND IS AN ALPHA MASK: the second tile contributes NO COLOUR, only per-pixel alpha. Retail is not a software blitter here - it is fixed-function OpenGL multitexturing through SDL_GL_GetProcAddress pointers, which is why nothing shows up in the ELF relocations. The draw is cWorld::drawFloor at 0x080e4bf2 (size 0x3a1, FDE), the only consumer of the queued-quad list at cWorld+0x37674 besides its builder at 0x080e2706. Per quad it resolves both tile records, reads each one's texture id at record +0x20 (exactly the port's Tiles.texture_id), caches the pair and calls 0x080e111a to set the batch's TWO texture slots at batch+0x4fc0 and +0x4fc4, then submits the quad via 0x080e0fd0. The flush at 0x080e1160 binds +0x4fc0 to TEXTURE UNIT 0 and +0x4fc4 to UNIT 1 (call 0x08055236 with unit 0 then unit 1, the second guarded by a zero check). So unit 0 = the low-17-bit tile, the art; unit 1 = the top-15-bit tile, the transition sheet. | THE COMBINE, read from the render-state setter 0x083b509a (a change-only wrapper over 0x083b50da, dispatching on a state token). Token 0x2000, value 0, at 0x083b590e: glActiveTexture(GL_TEXTURE1); glTexEnvi(GL_TEXTURE_ENV, GL_COMBINE_RGB, GL_REPLACE); glTexEnvi(.., GL_SOURCE0_RGB, GL_PREVIOUS); glTexEnvi(.., GL_COMBINE_ALPHA, GL_REPLACE); glTexEnvi(.., GL_SOURCE0_ALPHA, GL_TEXTURE); glEnable(GL_TEXTURE_2D); glActiveTexture(GL_TEXTURE0); glTexEnvi(.., GL_SOURCE0_ALPHA, GL_PREVIOUS). Unit 1 therefore REPLACES rgb with PREVIOUS - the mask sheet's own colour is thrown away - and REPLACES alpha with its own texel. Value 1, at 0x083b534c, is the single-texture mode: glDisable(GL_TEXTURE_2D) on unit 1 and unit 0 back to COMBINE_ALPHA = MODULATE(TEXTURE, PREVIOUS). POLARITY WAS THE TRAP: ds:0x9553bc0 and ds:0x9553b90 are both one-argument calls on GL_TEXTURE_2D and reading them the wrong way round inverts the whole conclusion. They are pinned by the strings passed to SDL_GL_GetProcAddress at 0x0862b35d and 0x0862b3e5 - 0x9553bc0 is glDISABLE, 0x9553b90 is glENABLE. | THE PASS STRUCTURE, which the port does not need but which explains the state toggling: one loop, flag at [ebp-0x21] starting 0, drawing only the quads matching the current mode and setting a deferred flag for the others, then flushing, XOR-ing the flag, re-setting state 0x2000 to it, and repeating while anything was deferred. Drawn quads are consumed off a per-slot chain (list[i] = quad->next at 0x080e4f02), which is what makes it terminate. NOT VERIFIED, and it matters before implementing: the framebuffer blend function itself. This trace establishes what alpha the fragment ends up with, not what the fixed-function blender then does with it, and GL_BLEND is enabled or disabled by some other state token. PORT IMPLICATION: terrain.gdshader needs a second sampler and must switch from its alpha-test discard to real alpha for these quads, with the mask's alpha read as Sacred's ALPHA channel - which after the RGBA4444 rotation the shader documents is the .r component, not .a.

ROW 702 IS CONFIRMED BY LIVE CAPTURE, WITH ONE ENUM CORRECTED. apitrace 14 (installed this session; the 32-bit wrapper is required, the game is ELF32) traced a full retail run to the pinned chapel spawn under Xvfb via play.sh's SACRED_RUNNER hook - 12 GB, 7.78 M GL calls, screenshot at 100 s shows the Seraphim, the priestess and the blue chest, i.e. the oracle plate itself. The floor draw appears exactly as the disassembly predicted: glActiveTexture(GL_TEXTURE0)+glBindTexture, glActiveTexture(GL_TEXTURE1)+glBindTexture, two GL_TEXTURE_COORD_ARRAYs via glClientActiveTexture, glColorPointer + glVertexPointer at STRIDE 32, and glDrawRangeElements(GL_TRIANGLES, start 0, end 4, count 6) - one quad, four 32-byte vertices = the 128 bytes the builder memcpy's at 0x080e2eb1. 47,365 GL_TEXTURE1 activations in the in-world portion. Textures upload as GL_BGRA / GL_UNSIGNED_SHORT_4_4_4_4_REV, which is the channel rotation the port's terrain.gdshader already documents. | THE FULL VERIFIED EQUATION. Unit 1 (the top-field transition sheet): COMBINE_RGB = GL_REPLACE, SRC0_RGB = GL_PREVIOUS, COMBINE_ALPHA = GL_REPLACE, SRC0_ALPHA = GL_TEXTURE, then glEnable(GL_TEXTURE_2D). Unit 0 (the low-field tile): ENV_MODE = GL_COMBINE, COMBINE_RGB = GL_MODULATE, SRC0_ALPHA = GL_PRIMARY_COLOR, SRC1_ALPHA alternating GL_PREVIOUS / GL_PRIMARY_COLOR. Framebuffer: GL_BLEND enabled, glBlendFunc(GL_SRC_ALPHA, GL_ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA). So the fragment is RGB = low tile x per-corner vertex colour (exactly what the port already computes), ALPHA = the mask sheet's texel alpha and nothing else, composited straight over the ground. THE CORRECTION: row 702 read unit 0's SRC0_ALPHA operand 0x8577 as GL_PREVIOUS. 0x8577 is GL_PRIMARY_COLOR; GL_PREVIOUS is 0x8578. The conclusion is unchanged - unit 1 REPLACEs alpha regardless - but the enum name in row 702 is wrong and should not be copied forward. | THE OPEN ITEM OF ROW 702 IS NOW CLOSED: the framebuffer blend function was the one thing that trace could not settle statically, and it is ordinary src-alpha over. IMPLEMENTATION IS UNBLOCKED and is now fully specified: terrain.gdshader needs a second sampler for the mask sheet at its own UV, and must replace its alpha-test discard with real alpha for these quads, reading the mask's alpha as the .r component after the RGBA4444 rotation. METHOD NOTE worth reusing: SACRED_RUNNER="apitrace trace --api gl --output <path>" composes cleanly with shot.sh's autopilot and Xvfb, timings hold under tracing overhead (the 20 s menu shot landed on the menu), and the output path must contain NO SPACES because play.sh leaves SACRED_RUNNER unquoted. Artifacts: ~/sacredtrace/world.trace (12 GB, delete when done) and state.log, a 562k-line pre-filtered index of every glActiveTexture/glTexEnvi/glBlendFunc/GL_BLEND call in the run.

THE MASK BLEND IS IMPLEMENTED AND VISIBLE. SectorView._tile_stack now returns the floor.pak chain as PAIRS (art, mask) rather than single ids, and _build_sector splits the sector into TWO SURFACES of one ArrayMesh, mirroring retail's own two passes: surface 0 is the existing alpha-tested terrain (ground tiles plus overlays whose mask is 0, appearance unchanged), surface 1 is the masked overlays under a new terrain_mask.gdshader. The mask's slot UV and array layer ride in ARRAY_CUSTOM0 (RGBA float) because UV2 is already spent on the art tile's layer, and CUSTOM0 is vertex-stage only so it crosses to the fragment as a varying. Both surfaces share one Texture2DArray - the 39 mask sheets simply take further layers. The shader is retail's combine exactly: ALBEDO = art.gba * per-corner light, ALPHA = mask.r, where .r is Sacred's ALPHA after the RGBA4444 rotation terrain.gdshader documents. render_mode blend_mix, depth_draw_never - these are decals and must not occlude what is drawn later, though depth TESTING stays on. | ONE REAL BUG FOUND BY LOOKING, WHICH IS THE ONLY REASON IT WAS CAUGHT. Blended quads join the same transparent queue the object sprites sort in (they carry sorting_offset), and on the first render every prop standing on a masked cell - the chapel's carpet, benches, cabinet, candles, blue chest - was washed out or erased, because the floor painted over them. Fixed by giving the masked material render_priority = -1, which Godot sorts BEFORE depth, so the whole floor pass precedes every sprite exactly as retail's does. The mesh also had to move from material_override to set_surface_override_material, since an override applies one material to both surfaces; nothing else reads the terrain mesh's material (the cutaway's _apply_swap walks the object band meshes, which are children with their own overrides). If a mask texture fails to decode the quad falls back to the art-only surface rather than being dropped. | EVIDENCE AND GATES. Before/after at the chapel: /tmp/look/port-202150.png (overlays opaque, hard-edged tan road rectangles) vs port-212022.png (same view, soft transitions, scrub fading into dirt, every prop present). Second site sector 7,7 via --region=7,7,0 renders coherently. Region load-path invariant UNCHANGED at 35340 quads (the split moves quads between surfaces, it does not add or lose any) and floor_check passes. NOTE the 63-textures figure in that line counts GROUND tiles via _world.tile_ids and has never counted the overlay or mask layers - do not read it as evidence about this change either way. PRE-EXISTING GATE FAILURE, NOT CAUSED HERE: verify_ref.py emits a 'pak tiles.pak count=90132' line that verify.gd does not, because verify.gd uses Sacred.Tiles and tiles.pak no longer opens through Sacred.Pak at all (row 695). The Python reference is stale on that one line; nothing in this change touches verify.gd, sacred.gd or either reader. ALSO WORTH KNOWING for anyone driving look.sh: --zoom= takes a zoom INDEX 0..2, not a size, and --sector= is overridden every frame by the camera following the player, so use --region=gx,gy,r to look anywhere else.

WldxEntry +0x18..0x1b IS A SECOND PER-CORNER SIGNED HEIGHT, SAMPLED CONTINUOUSLY - and row 699 was right to say the statistics had gone as far as they could. Found by scanning .text for the FOUR-CORNER read pattern (movsx/movzx of a base+disp8 at four consecutive displacements within one 64-byte window): +0x10 has exactly two such sites (0x080e29e7, 0x080e5232, the two terrain quad builders), +0x18 has exactly ONE (0x080ef81a, inside the function at 0x080ef688, size 0x2bc), and +0x14 the light field has NONE, so the lights are read some other way. The single +0x18 reader sign-extends all four bytes, fild's each, multiplies each by 2.5 (.rodata 0x086de620), averages them with x0.25 (0x086de624) and compares that against zero, then BILINEARLY INTERPOLATES the four - indexing them as an array via [ebp+ebx*4-0x38] / [ebp+ecx*4-0x38] - and returns a single float. Its neighbour constant at 0x086de61c is 53.66563, the world SCALE this project already uses in save_patch.py, so the function works in world units. The caller at 0x080ef5e6 adds the returned float to a per-object term (byte [obj+0x33] x 28) and returns the sum: a HEIGHT AT A POSITION. Roughly a dozen call sites. | MEASURED RELATIONSHIP TO THE KNOWN +0x10 HEIGHT, over 221,184 cells (every 11th sector). P(+0x10 non-zero) = 0.1766, P(+0x18 non-zero) = 0.0979, P(both) = 0.0904 against 0.0173 if independent - a lift of 5.23, and note P(both) is 92% of P(+0x18), so a cell carrying this field almost always carries a visual height too. Over the 53,142 corner pairs where both are non-zero the SIGNS AGREE 99.51% of the time. Magnitudes are related but NOT a mechanical rescale: +0x10 is always a multiple of 5 (row 218) and h == f*5 exactly for 49.3% of pairs, with the h/f ratio spreading 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 10, 15 beyond its mode of 5 - and 10:1 and 10:2 both occur, as do 15:1, 15:2 and 15:3. So the two are authored independently, not derived from one another. Observed +0x18 values span -7..+14, concentrated on +1 (19,595) and +2 (11,598). | WHAT IS PROVEN VS WHAT IS INFERRED, stated separately because the difference matters. PROVEN: it is four signed per-corner values, scaled x2.5, bilinearly interpolated to a continuous value across the cell, summed into a height total, and NEVER read by either terrain quad builder - those read +0x00, +0x04, +0x08, +0x0c, +0x10..0x13 and +0x1c..0x1f and skip both +0x14 and +0x18. INFERRED, and NOT yet traced to its call sites: that this is the height things STAND on while +0x10 is the height the ground is DRAWN at. That reading fits every measurement above but the caller semantics have not been read, so do not write it up as settled. THIS DOES NOT CLOSE THE ENTRY - +0x04, +0x08 and +0x1e remain undecoded. No port change: OpenHeilig's movement is 2D over a walkable grid and has no ground height to feed this into yet. PROBE: godot-port/corner3_height_probe.gd, read-only. Row 699's refutation of the overlay-blend reading stands and is now positively explained - the overlay's blend comes from a second tile (row 701), never from the cell.

WldxEntry +0x04 WAS ALREADY DECODED, AND +0x08 IS NOT AUTHORED DATA AT ALL. +0x04 heads the static.pak chain and the port has been reading it all along at sacred.gd:549 via _statics.chain() (row 686) - a full-grid census confirms it: 862,343 of 24,780,800 cells carry a non-zero handle (3.48%), maximum 1,038,013, which is exactly static.pak's count-1 as printed at startup (1,038,014 statics). Nothing to do there. +0x08 is the interesting one and the answer is that it is a RUNTIME SLOT. Retail's terrain builder loads it at 0x080e296c and walks it at 0x080e4455 as a CIRCULAR LINKED LIST: the id is resolved to a record by the lookup at 0x08118560 against the global at ds:0x8b8d0c0, the next id is read from record+0x30, and the walk stops when the next comes back to the head it started from. Each record's +0x1c/+0x20 are turned into screen coordinates - view origin subtracted, then +0x200 and +0x180 added, i.e. half of 1024x768. That is a per-cell list of objects being drawn at positions that move. | MEASURED EXHAUSTIVELY, not sampled: +0x08 IS ZERO IN ALL 24,780,800 CELLS OF THE WORLD - every cell of every one of the 6050 present sectors, not a stride sample. The +0x04 census above ran in the same pass as a control, so a reading bug that zeroed the field would have zeroed that too, and it did not. Two independent lines therefore agree: the disassembly says the field is the head of a list of things that MOVE, which an engine builds at load time rather than ships, and the data says the shipped value is empty everywhere. CONCLUSION: there is nothing in the file to decode here. The slot exists so the loader has somewhere to hang the cell's mobile-object list once creatures and dropped items are spawned into it. | THIS CLOSES THE WldxEntry except for +0x1e. Full 32-byte map as it now stands: +0x00 tile id, +0x04 static.pak chain head (row 686), +0x08 runtime mobile-object list head (empty on disk, this row), +0x0c floor.pak overlay chain head (rows 695/701), +0x10..0x13 signed per-corner render heights (row 218), +0x14..0x17 per-corner light bytes, +0x18..0x1b signed per-corner second height, bilinearly sampled (row 705), +0x1c/+0x1d signed parent-object deltas (rows 670-672), +0x1e UNDECODED, +0x1f cell class nibble. GUARD ADDED: floor_check.gd now asserts +0x08 is zero across sector 50,39 and names this row, so the claim cannot quietly rot - it passes. PROBE: godot-port/cell08_probe.gd, read-only, full-grid. A NEGATIVE RESULT IS STILL A RESULT: the value of this row is that it stops the next person spending a session looking for meaning in a field that has none on disk.

WldxEntry +0x1e IS A SPARSE BITFIELD AND ONLY THREE OF ITS EIGHT BITS ARE EVER SET. Full-grid census of all 24,780,800 cells: 98.8% are 0x00, and the only values that occur at all are 0x00..0x07 - 0x02 x189,851, 0x01 x77,814, 0x03 x29,531, 0x04 x1,050, 0x05 x349, 0x06 x210, 0x07 x152. Bits 3 through 7 are NEVER SET anywhere in the world. Retail reads the byte UNSIGNED at 0x080e2983 and treats it as flags. BIT 0 IS THE ONE WITH A TRACED MEANING: at 0x080e350f the terrain builder tests it and, when set, computes the cell's OWN WORLD POSITION (cell index >> 6 as the row, index & 0x3f as the column, plus the sector origin at +0x44/+0x48) and uses it as the key for a lookup, 0x080eede0 then 0x080ef1ac. That second call is the SAME lookup the +0x18 height sampler's caller uses at 0x080ef642 (row 705), where the returned record's byte +0x33 is multiplied by 28 and ADDED to the interpolated corner height. So bit 0 marks cells that have an entry in a per-position table whose records carry a height LEVEL, and 28 is the per-level step. A second consumer of the same bit sits at 0x0811772c. | BIT 4'S BRANCH IS DEAD IN SHIPPED CONTENT, which is worth knowing before anyone chases it. At 0x080e3402 the builder tests 0x10 and only then reads the +0x1f class, masking &0xF0 and accepting 0x10/0x20/0x90/0xA0 - WALL/FLOOR/DOOR/STEP in the HIGH nibble. The branch is real code, but bit 4 is set in ZERO of 24,780,800 cells, so retail data never reaches it. Two further testers of this byte at 0x08231bea and 0x0826aeb6 check bit 3, which is likewise never set, and are most likely reading a different structure that merely shares the offset - 0x1e is a common displacement and a raw scan turns up 140 sites, of which only six survive the filter of having a +0x1f read within 48 bytes. CORRELATION for bit 0, measured: P(cell has a static chain | bit 0) = 0.360 against a base rate of 0.035, a 10x lift but nowhere near equality, so bit 0 is NOT simply 'this cell has a static'. | HONEST SCOPE: BITS 1 AND 2 ARE NOT DECODED. Bit 1 is the COMMONEST of the three (0.89% of cells, 219,382 counting 0x02, 0x03, 0x06 and 0x07) and bit 2 is rare (1,761 cells), and no reader for either was found among the six cell-like sites - so their consumers are reached through a base register the adjacency filter missed, and finding them needs a different scan than the one used here. Do not write +0x1e up as decoded; it is one bit of three. THIS ALSO CORRECTS ROW 706's closing line, which called +0x1e 'the only byte left' as though it were a single unknown - it is a byte with three independent flags in it, one of which is now understood. The WldxEntry is therefore fully mapped at FIELD level with bits 1 and 2 of +0x1e the only content still unexplained. PROBE: godot-port/cell1e_probe.gd, read-only, full-grid.

BIT 2 OF WldxEntry +0x1e IS SOLVED AND BIT 0 IS CORROBORATED; BIT 1 IS NOT, AND THIS ROW SAYS SO PLAINLY. Bit 2 (0x04, 1,761 cells world-wide): its reader is 0x080eeec4, a small accessor that fetches the cell, requires bit 2, then reads the cell's +0x04 STATIC CHAIN HEAD, requires it non-zero, and passes it to the object lookup 0x080ef1ac - the same lookup whose record byte +0x33 is multiplied by 28 and added to the interpolated corner height in row 705's wrapper. The data confirms the guard exactly: P(cell has a static chain | bit 2) = 1.0000 over all 1,761 cells, against a base rate of 0.0348. Not 0.99 - every single one. Bit 2 is enriched 23x for class high-nibble 0xe0 (0.163 vs a 0.007 base). Bit 0 (0x01, 107,846 cells) gains an independent corroboration too: P(the cell has non-zero +0x1c/+0x1d PARENT-OBJECT deltas | bit 0) = 0.9887 against a base of 0.0043, a 230x lift, which ties row 707's traced position-lookup directly to the parent-object link of rows 670-672. Its class skew is 0xd0 at 0.857 vs a 0.244 base. | BIT 1 REMAINS OPEN, and what is known about it is mostly negative. It is the commonest of the three - 219,744 cells, 0.89% - but it occurs in only 161 of the 6050 present sectors, and inside those it forms NEAR-SOLID BLOBS: the mean number of a bit-1 cell's four neighbours that are also bit 1 is 3.91. Those 161 sectors are scattered across the whole 100x100 grid rather than forming one zone. Every correlation measured is weak-to-moderate and none is a rule: P(static) 0.130 vs 0.035 base, P(floor overlay) 0.449 vs 0.186, P(second height) 0.229 vs 0.118, P(parent deltas) 0.134 vs 0.0043, class high-nibble 0x40 at 0.323 vs 0.165 and 0xb0 at 0.215 vs 0.081. HYPOTHESIS REFUTED, DO NOT RETRY: bit 1 is NOT the marker for 'this cell is covered by a region sub-grid'. Measured P(inside a region rect | bit 1) = 0.199 and P(bit 1 | inside a region rect) = 0.260, and the sector sets barely agree - 161 sectors carry bit 1, 361 carry regions, only 91 carry both. A visual look at sector 18,5 (1792 bit-1 cells) was INCONCLUSIVE and is not evidence either way: the port has no overlay for this flag, so which cells were which could not be seen. It is a dark camp with tents and trees, not open water, but that only weakly disfavours a water reading. | WHY IT IS HARD, AND THE TWO NEXT MOVES. No reader for bit 1 exists anywhere I can currently see. A scan of all 32 'test byte [reg+0x1e], imm' sites in .text finds immediates 0x01, 0x02, 0x04 and 0x08, but every 0x02 site sits in a function with no cell-pointer idiom and outside the world/cell accessor family at 0x080eea62..0x080eff00, whose members test only bits 0, 2 and 3. The terrain builder itself tests exactly three bits: 0 (live), 4 (at 0x080e3402, gated on the +0x1f class high nibble being WALL/FLOOR/DOOR/STEP) and 7 (at 0x080e47af, via shr 7) - AND BITS 4 AND 7 ARE SET IN ZERO OF 24,780,800 CELLS, so both are dead branches for retail content. NEXT: (a) bit 1's consumer most likely loads the byte into a register or stack slot first, exactly as the builder does at 0x080e2983 before testing [ebp-0xe4] - so the scan that finds it must follow the copy, not match on [reg+0x1e]; (b) cheaper and probably decisive - add a debug overlay to SectorView that paints bit-1 cells and render two or three of the 161 sectors, which is how height and light were each settled. PROBES: cell1e_bits_probe, cell1e_map_probe, cell1e_region_probe, all read-only, all full-grid.

+0x1e IS A PER-CELL ROOM-TOPOLOGY BYTE: bit 0 = STRUCTURE, bit 1 = ROOM INTERIOR, bit 2 = DOOR. Settled the way height and light were settled - by drawing it and looking. New --flags1e overlay in SectorView._build_flags1e paints the three live bits red/green/blue above the terrain. The decisive picture is sector 71,12 (1303 bit-1 cells, and one of the 70 bit-1 sectors that contain NO region sub-grids at all): a stone dungeon of four walled rooms joined by corridors, where GREEN covers the ROOM FLOORS EXACTLY and stops at the corridors, and BLUE sits precisely on the four DOORWAYS where each room opens onto the corridor. Sector 50,39, the cathedral, shows the same grammar: an L-shaped green interior floor EDGED IN RED along the wall line. Sector 18,5 is a camp whose green blob covers the camp ground under the tents. | THE NUMBERS AGREE WITH THE PICTURE, measured over all 24,780,800 cells against the +0x1f class low nibble (WALL=1, FLOOR=2, DOOR=9, STEP=0xa; base rates 0.6417, 0.1066, 0.00005, 0.0001, with 0.2516 at nibble 0 = the OPEN interior-ground family). BIT 2 IS DOORS: 27.20% of its 1,761 cells are class DOOR against a base of 0.005%, a lift of roughly 5,000x, and P(cell has a static chain | bit 2) = 1.0000 exactly - the door OBJECT, which is precisely why its reader at 0x080eeec4 requires bit 2 and then dereferences +0x04 through the object lookup 0x080ef1ac. BIT 0 IS STRUCTURE: class WALL 0.8804 vs 0.6417 base, STEP 0.0236 vs 0.0001, and P(non-zero +0x1c/+0x1d parent-object deltas | bit 0) = 0.9887 vs a 0.0043 base. BIT 1 IS ROOM INTERIOR: class nibble 0 at 0.5909 vs a 0.2516 base - and nibble 0 with a 0xd0/0xe0 high nibble is exactly what sacred.gd already documents as a building's open interior ground. | HONEST LIMITS. Bit 1's class-0 share is 59%, not 100%, so 'room interior' is the shape of the field rather than a rule, and the camp at sector 18,5 reads as outdoor ground under a strict room reading - the flag is better described as ENCLOSED/INTERIOR AREA than as a four-walled room. Row 708's refutation of 'bit 1 = covered by a region sub-grid' STANDS and is now explained: the region rect includes walls and courtyard while bit 1 is only the interior-floor subset, and most bit-1 areas (70 of 161 sectors) are dungeons with no region sub-grid at all. Bits 3..7 remain set in ZERO cells world-wide, and the builder's tests of bit 4 (0x080e3402) and bit 7 (0x080e47af) are dead branches for retail content. THIS COMPLETES THE WldxEntry: every one of its 32 bytes now has a meaning. TOOLING: --flags1e added to main.gd and SectorView; gates re-run clean, headless has no errors and the region invariant is unchanged at 35340 quads. Plates: /tmp/look/port-220449.png (dungeon, the decisive one), port-220350.png (cathedral), port-220321.png (camp).

THE +0x1f HIGH NIBBLE IS A 16-CLASS GROUND-TYPE TAG, AND sacred.gd's DESCRIPTION OF IT WAS WRONG. The in-repo comment called it 'an undecoded family split (0xd/0xe)'. Measured over all 24,780,800 cells, ALL SIXTEEN values occur: 0xd 0.2437, 0x4 0.1653, 0x8 0.1325, 0x3 0.1309, 0xb 0.0810, 0x9 0.0769, 0x1 0.0428, 0xc 0.0420, 0xf 0.0317, 0x0 0.0250, 0x2 0.0178, 0xe 0.0069, 0x6 0.0025, 0xa 0.0008, 0x5 0.0001, 0x7 0.0000 - while the LOW nibble is essentially only {0, 1, 2} (0.2516 / 0.6417 / 0.1066, with DOOR and STEP together under 0.02%). 76 distinct whole-byte values. So the byte is a small class in the low nibble and a much richer field in the high one, not one enum with a family prefix. | WHAT IT IS, from drawing it and from the engine. New --classhi overlay (SectorView._build_classhi) paints the high nibble one hue per value; at the cathedral sector 50,39 it segments the ground into contiguous areas that track the VISIBLE SURFACE - the lawn is one value, the cobbled courtyard another, the building floor another, the hedged garden another, with small isolated patches where props stand. It is not derived from the art: over 987,136 cells and 738 textures, a cell takes its texture's modal high nibble only 0.6470 of the time and just 99 of 738 textures are single-valued, so the tag is authored alongside the tiles rather than computed from them. Retail queries it BY EQUALITY OVER A RECT: 0x080f1d2a walks a cell range, masks each cell's +0x1f with 0xF0, compares against a target passed in on the stack, and accumulates a float where it matches - an area measurement over cells of a given type. Twelve such high-nibble consumers exist in .text. | HONEST LIMIT: WHICH VALUE MEANS WHICH SURFACE IS NOT ESTABLISHED. Naming them needs either the table the engine indexes with the tag or a per-value render survey across biomes, and neither was done - do not write 'grass = 3' anywhere on this evidence. Two guesses were checked and are NOT supported: it is not an index into sndprofiles.pak (8192 records, not 16), and it is not a second copy of the class enum despite the builder at 0x080e3415 comparing &0xF0 against 0x10/0x20/0x90/0xA0, since the high nibble's distribution looks nothing like the low one's. NO PORT BEHAVIOUR CHANGED: walkable.gd and interior.gd read the LOW nibble and are untouched; this row only corrects a false comment and adds a debug overlay. Gates clean, region invariant unchanged at 35340 quads. PROBES: class_nibble_probe, class_hi_probe, read-only, full-grid. Plate: /tmp/look/port-221354.png.

startcode.bin IS OPENED FOR THE FIRST TIME AND ITS RECORD FRAMING IS SOLVED. The file is a flat record stream: u16 OPCODE, u16 RECORD LENGTH (counting those four bytes), then a tagged argument list. Walking by the length field crosses all 15,422 records of type_npc_seraphim/startcode.bin without a single desync, which is the proof the framing is right, and yields 33 distinct opcodes - the busiest being op 50 x2463, op 8 x2003, op 48 x1942, op 108 x1595, op 23 x1427, op 94 x1267, op 40 x1021 (always 80 bytes) and op 114 x906 (always 10 bytes). All eight class files are within 3 KB of each other in size (575,477..578,356), so they are the same script with per-class edits and DIFFING THEM is an obvious lever nobody has pulled yet. Tool: analysis/tools/startcode.py. | THE ARGUMENT GRAMMAR IS ONLY PARTLY SOLVED, and the row says so rather than dressing it up. Three tags are certain because the fixed-length opcodes close on them exactly - opcode 114's 10-byte body is precisely `0b <u32> 02 <u32>`: 0x01 = NUL-terminated string, 0x02 = u32, 0x0b = u32. 8,450 of 15,422 records parse under that partial table. The rest need tags not yet identified, and a size-solver that maximised clean parses DRIFTED INTO NONSENSE, assigning ASCII letters (0x42 'B', 0x4d 'M', 0x52 'R') as tags - the signature of landing inside a string, so at least one string-bearing tag is still mis-sized. Do not trust a parse that reports letter-valued tags. NEXT METHOD, and it is the one that worked for the fixed opcodes: group records by (opcode, length) and find the byte positions that are constant across the group; that reads a schema off the data instead of guessing sizes. | WHAT IS ALREADY VISIBLE, and it bears directly on the blocked threads. 17,490 embedded strings, 10,202 distinct: chestTrigger x2273, GRABSTEINMOUSEOVER x1022, BRUNNENMOUSEOVER, PanelTrigger, WWTrigger, Versteck_1..111 (hiding places), Abuecherstaender, plus 170 NPC-related names including NPC_Dialog_Farmer / _Citizen / _Noble / _Soldier / _Magician - so DIALOGUE ROUTING BY NPC TYPE is authored here. AND THE TEXT CHAIN RESOLVES: the scripts carry 335 references of the form res:N and cres:N (135 distinct, range 17,085..22,008), and install/scripts/us/global.res is the English string table they point into - magic 'SZ', a 16-byte-per-slot index ending at the first data offset 0x5a530, 23,122 slots. Slot 17,466 reads "Mother's Powder Contain..." and slot 22,008 "These stones with runes on them are said to strengthen the magic power of the herbs growing her...". CAVEAT, MEASURED NOT GUESSED: the index arithmetic is ~2 bytes out (slot 1 renders as '\x1a\x00Seraph' where the text is 'Seraphim'), and the first u32 of each slot is NOT an id - it rises past 2 billion. The offset/length pair is right, the alignment needs finishing.

THE startcode TAG TABLE IS SOLVED TO 96.5%, AND funkcode.bin IS THE SAME FORMAT. Fourteen tags, read off the data by grouping records on (opcode, length) and marking the byte positions that are constant across the group - not guessed: 0x01/0x09/0x1e/0x29/0x41 are NUL-terminated strings, 0x02/0x0b/0x1f are u32, 0x03/0x28 are u16, 0x04/0x0c/0x0d/0x2a are TWELVE-byte payloads (almost certainly 3 x u32; the tool currently prints them as one 96-bit integer, which is ugly but not wrong), and 0x10 is a ZERO-LENGTH marker. That last one is why the first solver stalled - 0 was not among the candidate sizes it tried. 13,855 of 15,422 startcode records parse under this table. Opcode 40 (1,021 records, always 84 bytes) accounts for most of the rest and is NOT a tag stream at all but a FIXED 80-BYTE STRUCT beginning ffffffff with bytes 30..67 always zero. 13,855 + 1,021 = 96.5% of the file explained. | funkcode.bin USES THE IDENTICAL FRAMING: 3,962,707 bytes, framed 100.000% end to end with no desync, 125,055 records, 102 opcodes. THE TAG TABLE IS REBUILT FROM THE INTERPRETER AND startcode.bin NOW PARSES 100%. Width is advance minus one, the one byte being the tag itself. Paths are kept SEPARATE rather than merged, so a handler that copies a string on one branch and takes a fixed field on another is reported as the VARIANT it is instead of collapsing to STR - which is exactly what row 719's version did to 0x04. | THREE RULES COMPLETE IT, AND THE MISSING ONE WAS WHY THE ENGINE TABLE HAD SCORED WORSE THAN A FITTED ONE. Modelled as STR2, it accounts for the op-58 and op-66 failures (28 records). | SECOND, AND MORE INTERESTING: THE ENGINE TOLERATES A PAYLOAD THAT OVERRUNS THE RECORD, and my parser was treating that as failure. The interpreter's loop test at 0x0826af30 is `cmp DWORD PTR [esi], eax / jge end` where eax is the record LENGTH - it checks the cursor BEFORE reading a tag, never after reading a payload. So when opcode 41's 2-byte body holds `02 00`, the 0x02 handler reads a u32 that runs four bytes past the record end into the next record, stores the garbage, advances the cursor to 9, and the loop then exits because 9 >= 6.
