THE OPCODE DISPATCHER IS LOCATED - SEMANTICS WORK NOW HAS ITS ENTRY POINT, BUT IS NOT STARTED. Architecture, established: the record parser at 0x0826aed6 (rows 718-721) only PARSES a record's tagged arguments into slots and returns; it does not execute anything. It has 110 CALL SITES, and those are the per-opcode handler functions - each opcode's implementation calls the parser to fetch its own operands. The dispatcher that routes to them is the function at 0x0826e8ce (size 0x381e, ending 0x082720ec), which begins immediately after the parser. Its switch is at 0x0826ea49: `jmp DWORD PTR [eax*4+0x086f4298]`, bounded by a cmp against 0x8c and a ja to the default at 0x082720dd. So the OPCODE JUMP TABLE IS AT 0x086f4298 WITH 141 ENTRIES, opcodes 0..140 - which matches the data exactly, since the highest opcode observed in startcode.bin is 140. | WHY THE EARLIER GUESS AT THE STRUCTURE WAS WRONG, noted so it is not repeated: a scan for a dense table of function pointers containing the 110 handler addresses found NOTHING, because the dispatch is not a pointer table - it is a switch whose cases CALL the handlers, so the handler addresses appear as E8 call displacements inside the dispatcher rather than as words in .rodata. The right way to enumerate them is to read the 141-entry jump table at 0x086f4298, follow each case, and record which of the 110 handler functions it calls. | SCOPE OF WHAT REMAINS, stated honestly because it is large: 102 opcodes occur in the seraphim files (103 in gladiator) and NONE has a verified meaning. What can be inferred cheaply from payloads alone is suggestive but unproven - op22 takes names like 'IsInRgn' and 'AllgemeinesPool', op105 declares a variable with a range, op75/op67 set and test 'NPCGeklickt', op26 builds a text key by concatenation, op60 pairs a res: string with a button id. Turning those into decoded semantics means reading 141 dispatcher cases and their handlers, which is a substantially bigger body of work than the format decode was. The 66 zero-width tags are the other half - they are presumably operators, and their handlers are already enumerated in the tag table at 0x086f3fbc.

ALL 141 OPCODE SLOTS ARE RESOLVED TO HANDLER FUNCTIONS AND 30 OF THEM ARE NAMED FROM THE ENGINE'S OWN STRINGS. Method (analysis/tools/opcodes.py): read the 141-entry jump table at 0x086f4298, then walk each case body - every live case is a stub that pushes the parsed slot array (ebp-0x818) and the dynamic_cast'd target, CALLs one function and jmps to the shared tail, so opcode -> handler is 1:1 and readable. 124 slots are live, 17 point at the default case, and the 124 resolve to 121 DISTINCT handlers (37/38, 65/67, 88/134 and 35/51 pair up). Handler extents come from .eh_frame; the .rodata literals inside each handler are what name it. Named from strings, not guessed: 1 CreateNPC, 8 CreateOBJ, 24 group-alive test, 37/38 SOUND_, 44 NPCUWR_, 46 Teleport, 58 IsNotVarBit, 60 RES:%d, 63 QuestkompassPos, 64 QuestkompassOBJ, 65/67/75/76/105 atmo_rg, 78 chest, 91 blacksmith UI, 92 teleport-without-listener, 94/140 versteck, 98 weather (rain/regen/thunder/snow per sector), 104/127/128 SOUND_FX_, 108/109/113/133 GetPoolPos, 119 region pool, 130 cInterpretSQW::Teleporter, 138/139 UI_WND_TASKBAR. The dispatcher's class name falls out of opcode 130's format string: cInterpretSQW. | TWO STRUCTURAL FACTS THE TABLE SETTLES. First, the DEFAULT CASE AT 0x082720dd IS NOT AN ERROR PATH - it is `mov ecx,1; ret`, i.e. success - so an opcode with no case is SILENTLY IGNORED, not rejected. That matters because OPCODE 42 OCCURS 4950 TIMES IN THE SHIPPED SCRIPTS AND HAS NO CASE: the engine reads those records and does nothing. Alignment is not the explanation - 41 and 43 flank it with real cases and identical counts (4950/4961), and every other data opcode has a case, so 42 is a genuine no-op. Second, opcode 0's case is the only one that sets ecx=0 instead of 1 before the shared return, so 0 is the halt/false result the dispatcher's caller tests on. | NOT DONE, AND THE LIMITS ARE SPECIFIC. 91 of the 121 handlers carry no naming string and are still unnamed; the operand samples in analysis/script-opcodes.md narrow them but do not settle them. Four handlers (40, 47, 59, 66, 88/134) fell outside .eh_frame so their extent defaulted to a 0x400 window and their strings are UNRELIABLE - 59/66 reporting the wincompat '%s/%s' is that artifact, not a finding. Handlers are not virtual, so RTTI gives nothing: analysis/rtti/lgp_linux_vmethods.tsv has zero of the 121. Next lever, untried: the handlers call virtual methods on the object they receive, so resolving even one call site per handler to a class from lgp_linux_vtables.json would name the SUBSYSTEM each opcode drives.

THE VTABLE LEVER RUNS BUT IT IS WEAK: IT NAMES A SUBSYSTEM FOR 18 OF THE 91 UNNAMED HANDLERS AND NOTHING FOR THE OTHER 73. Method, now in analysis/tools/opcodes.py: build typeinfo/vtable/vslot maps for sacred_orig directly (typeinfo = [__*_type_info vptr, name*], vtable starts one word past a pointer to a typeinfo, then walk slots), and flag every immediate in a handler that equals a typeinfo (dynamic_cast), a vtable (construction) or a vtable slot (direct call to a member function). Across all 120 handlers only 15 DISTINCT CLASSES appear at all, and five of them - cEvent, cEventNetwork, cObject, cCreature, cFile_ram - occur in 13 to 66 handlers each, so they carry no information and are filtered. What survives: 2 cObject3D/cObjectFX/cEventFX, 7/35/51 cItemBase, 18/70/79/89/121/125/132 cEvent_engine, 62/72/74/93 cEvent_creature, 73/99 cEventFX, 49/93 cObject3D, and 132 cCommand_armaStop - an animation-stop command, the only handler the lever names outright. Column added to analysis/script-opcodes.md. | WHY IT UNDERPERFORMS, measured rather than assumed: the handlers do not call virtual methods through resolvable statics. ZERO of the 121 handler addresses is itself a vtable slot, and direct calls to functions that ARE vtable slots number in the single digits across the whole set. The dispatcher's own dynamic_cast is the shape of the whole subsystem - `dynamic_cast<cCreature*>` from typeinfo 0x872e260 (cObject) to 0x872e320 (cCreature) at 0x0826e900 - so nearly every handler receives an already-cast cCreature and does its work through non-virtual calls and raw field offsets, which RTTI cannot see. A depth-1 sweep (harvest strings from every callee with an .eh_frame extent under 0x3000) was tried alongside and added only opcode 58's condition vocabulary (if IsDead/IsFighting/IsLocked/IsNotLocked/IsInRgn) and TYPE_OBJECT_DOOR on 2/49. | A METHOD WARNING PAID FOR IN LOST WORK. analysis/rtti/extract_vtables_elf.py WRITES ITS OUTPUT TO A FIXED PATH (analysis/rtti/lgp_linux_vmethods.tsv and .json) regardless of which binary is passed in, so running it on install/sacred_orig SILENTLY OVERWROTE the artifacts built from analysis/lgp-2010/sacred-1.0.02-final. It was restored by re-running on that binary and re-checked (0x872e2c0 is cUI_CDKey there, as before). During the window where the two were confused the sacred_orig addresses looked like MISLABELLED CLASS NAMES - a cUI_CDKey where the code plainly holds cObject - and that read was wrong: the extractor is correct, the two builds simply do not share addresses. THE BEHAVIOURAL LEVER NAMES 20 MORE OPCODES AND CRACKS global.res OPEN AS A NAMING ORACLE. Tool: analysis/tools/opsem.py, output analysis/script-opcodes-behaviour.md. For every opcode across all 16 script files it profiles the TAG SIGNATURE (startcode.parse now takes with_tags=True), the operand NAMESPACE histogram (res:, pos_, DQ_, TYPE_NPC_, POOL_, Dialog:, SOUND_ ...), the neighbouring opcodes, and the ENGLISH TEXT its res: operands resolve to. global.res decoding, which nothing had done correctly: u32 'SZ' magic, then 16-byte index entries [id, offset, 0, size], text is UTF-16LE at offset+4 running size bytes, and `res:N` IN THE SCRIPTS IS THE SLOT INDEX, NOT the id field - the id field is non-monotonic and runs past 2^31. Checks: slot 49 'Seraphim', 50 'Gladiator', 18101 'Settler', 19554 'Save... Vilya...', 17562 'My Daddy is much stronger than you!'. Named this way: 3 say(res:TEXT, dialogue label), 23 named-position table, 26 label/entry point, 48 declare-trigger, 50 trigger payload, 53 quest-log line, 58 IF, 59/62 block markers, 66 second conditional family, 67/68/86 set-variable, 20/21 quest-id-only, 22 reference-by-name, 100/115 bulk data. | THE BIGGEST STRUCTURAL RESULT IS THAT OPCODE 58 IS `IF` AND ITS PREDICATE IS CHOSEN BY THE TAG BYTE, NOT BY THE OPCODE. Its handler at 0x82a8672 holds the vocabulary - if IsNotVarBit:%s=%d, if IsDead:%s, if IsFighting:%s, if IsLocked:%s, if IsNotLocked:%s, if IsInRgn:%s - and the corpus shows the operand tag selecting among them: tag 0x52/0x7d/0x8f carry TYPE_NPC_* (25,974 records), 0x47 carries quest variables and PoolEmpty, 0x40 carries res: text, 0x3a carries the HERO/res: pair. Opcode 66 has the same shape and is the second half of the conditional family. Every claim in the table is a measured share, and three of my first-pass claims did NOT survive measurement and were rewritten: 48 IS followed by 50 in 31265 of 31265 records, but 59 is followed by 62 only 87% of the time, 100 is followed by 115 only 33% (it is followed by another 100 52% of the time), and only 40% of opcode 23's coordinate pairs are in world range - the rest read as huge u32, i.e. negative, so some are deltas. | TWO CAVEATS THAT LIMIT THE TABLE, both now printed in the doc. FIRST, `res:` IS TWO NAMESPACES WEARING ONE PREFIX: it addresses global.res text slots AND object/creature resources, so CreateNPC's res:19500 resolving to a sentence is meaningless. Median resolved length separates them - opcodes 53 (65 chars) and 71 (265) take displayed text, 63/73/93 (5-9 chars) take names. SECOND, TAGS 0x48/0x49/0x4a/0x6d/0x6e ARE PROBABLY NOT STRINGS: the table reads them as NUL-terminated and they come back as control characters, which is exactly what a small little-endian u16 looks like to a string read. The 100% parse rate cannot distinguish the two, so it is not evidence either way. Also corrected in analysis/tools/opcodes.py: 0x085ff0e8 is the OPERAND FETCH, not a handler - cases 59 and 66 were credited with it as their handler in row 723, when in fact they have no delegated call and implement the opcode INLINE in the dispatcher (as do 0, 41, 43, 111); the table now labels those inline@ADDR.

EIGHT TAGS WERE MIS-TYPED AND THE PARSE-RATE METRIC WAS HIDING IT. The suspicion logged in row 725 - that 0x48/0x49/0x4a/0x6d/0x6e are u16 rather than strings - was WRONG in its diagnosis and right that something was broken. Their handler at 0x0826cb0e reads a u32 into the NUMERIC slot array at +0xa86c, advances four bytes, and THEN strcpys a NUL-terminated string into the string slots at +0xa46c: the tag carries BOTH. Tag 0x7a (handler 0x0826de28) has the same shape, found by sweeping every STR-typed tag for values that are not printable - it was the only other one over 20% (750/1010). Tags 0x5d and 0x5e share 0x0826cb0e and were fixed with the rest. The reason a CFG walk mis-typed them (analysis/tools/tagwidths.py, row 720) is structural and is now written into that tool: the walker reports the strcpy and stops, so a FIXED PREFIX BEFORE a variable-length payload is invisible to it. New class NUMSTR in analysis/tools/startcode.py. | THE MEASUREMENT MATTERED MORE THAN THE FIX, because the old metric could not have caught this. Parse rate was 100% before and after - it is hollow, since every unlisted tag below 0xa2 hits the default handler and is a zero-width no-op, so a mis-sized tag's leftover bytes are read as no-op tags and absorbed in silence. Verified rather than assumed: all eight of the frequent unlisted tags (0x27, 0x08, 0x12, 0x0e, 0x10, 0x46, 0x7c, 0x2b) do point at the default handler 0x0826e0bc. The metric that does bite is RECORDS THAT CONSUME THEIR BODY EXACTLY (or stop on an END tag): 95.6% -> 99.774%, 1,347,105 of 1,350,157 records over all 16 files, excluding opcode 40 whose 80-byte ffffffff struct is not a tag stream. Intermediate: 98.6% after the 0x0826cb0e family, 98.7% after 0x7a. | WHAT THE FIX REVEALS, and it confirms opcode 58 independently: the NUMSTR tags now read as a (value, variable name) PAIR - 48 <u32> 'DQ_NUM', 4a <u32> 'DQ_AktivRgn', 6d <u32> 'NPCGeklickt' - which is exactly the handler's own format string `if IsNotVarBit:%s=%d`. So opcode 58's predicate operands are name-value comparisons, and the same tags under opcode 66 (11,036 + 7,849 + 888 records) make it the same family. Residual misfits after the fix are 18,610 records and are NOT unexplained: 10,047 are opcode 40's fixed struct, 4,981 stop on an END tag with bytes to spare (engine-correct, the loop tests the cursor before reading a tag), and 990 each sit on tags 0x02/0x03/0x04 inside opcode 41. Also mirrored the engine's overrun tolerance in the NUMSTR path - a string with no NUL before the record end ends the record instead of failing it, which is what 0x0826af30 does.

EVERY OPCODE THE SHIPPED SCRIPTS USE NOW HAS A READING - 113 OF 113, up from 50, with the last one (69) closed by its handler's own strings res/HeroQBit/HERO. The second pass was only possible after the NUMSTR fix (row 726) made the operands trustworthy; before it, five of the most frequent tags were handing back the low byte of a u32 as a string. Structures that fell out whole, none of which any earlier pass saw: (1) A SIX-RECORD DYNAMIC-QUEST TEMPLATE CHAIN - 118 -> 31 -> (1 or 122) -> 32 -> 123 -> 33 -> 118, each opcode appearing EXACTLY 16,830 times, carrying the template name (DQ1_BRINGE_NPC) and 1440, the minutes in a day. (2) A POOL RECTANGLE PAIR, 112/113: (POOL_RG1_ESKORTE1, x1,y1, x2,y2, x3,y3). (3) An ID-TO-DIALOGUE-NAME TABLE, opcode 106: (640, NPC_Dialog_Farmer) in runs of 1,270. (4) Opcode 99 displays TEXT WITH A COLOUR - (-1, -1, res:TEXT, 0xffffff, 1) - and its handler names cEventFX. (5) Opcodes 96/116 carry u32 LISTS behind a shared 0x69 header. | THE READINGS ARE GRADED, and the grading is in the doc rather than in a footnote. Some are facts about shape measured over the whole corpus (op 97's (x,y,1) triples precede runs of 23 in 3,050 of 3,838 records; op 25 is preceded by 58 in 198 of 198; op 124 in 240 of 240; op 118 is followed by 31 in 16,830 of 16,830). Some are the engine's own words (op 69's HeroQBit, op 132's cCommand_armaStop, op 72's cEvent_creature). Some are readings of a shape and are worded as such - op 17 and 18 apply a magnitude to the hero, op 56 sets a named timer, op 121 names an autosave - and could be wrong about WHICH magnitude or WHICH timer. Nine opcodes are deliberately left blank: 10, 11, 12, 13, 19, 47, 61, 77 and 110 have live cases in the dispatcher and ZERO records in the shipped scripts, so the corpus cannot speak to them. Opcode 42 is their mirror image: 4,950 records, no case, ignored by the engine. | WHAT THIS UNBLOCKS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. The script format is now readable end to end - framing (row 711), tag table (720/726), opcode table (722/723) and a reading for every opcode in use (727) - so the quest system, the dialogue routing and the NPC appearance link of row 692 can be pursued from the data rather than from the disassembler. What is NOT established: the argument SLOT each tag lands in (the parser writes numeric tags to +0xa86c and strings to +0xa46c, and the handlers read fixed slot indices, so operand ORDER inside a record is still assumed rather than proven), and the three bulk opcodes 51/100/115 - 395,000 records between them, a third of the corpus - are described only as shapes. 51's handler is the largest in the set at 23 KB and names cItemBase, which is the obvious thread to pull next.

THE THREE BULK OPCODES ARE THE RANDOM MONSTER SPAWN SYSTEM, AND THE PROOF IS AN ID JOIN. 51's repeated 0x19 field decomposes into (CREATURE ID, PERCENT, 0/1) and 115's repeated 0x02 field is a list of 1..20 ids; EVERY ONE OF THOSE IDS IS A creature.pak ID - 251 of 251 distinct for 51, 184 of 184 for 115, using the 474-record table of row 693. The percents sum to exactly 100 in 3,906 of 5,309 of opcode 51's records, median 100, which is what a weighted pick table looks like. 51's handler at 0x827afb6 is the largest in the whole opcode set at 23 KB and CALLS rand() 44 TIMES; it is also the only other code that touches the two globals the siblings write, so the trio is one subsystem: 115 DECLARES a spawn group (fills a 160-byte struct, appends it to the table at 0x8bb732c), 100 writes three percent-shaped u16 into the object at the CURRENT SECTOR (globals 0x879a080/0x879a084 shifted left 6) at offsets +0xd1/+0xd3/+0xd5, and 51 ROLLS. 51's header tag 0x36 is a record TYPE with exactly two values, 100 (2,854 records) and 310 (2,455), and the extra 0x34/0x33 fields appear only on type 310. | THE PARSER'S INTERFACE IS NOW READ OFF TWO SMALL HANDLERS, WHICH CLOSES THE GAP ROW 727 LEFT OPEN. Opcode 100 (187 bytes) and 115 (371 bytes) are short enough to read whole, and both use 0x0826aed6 as a PER-OPERAND ITERATOR: each call fetches the next operand and RETURNS ITS TAG BYTE, which the handler switches on. Values are picked up from fixed slots - u32 at +0xa86c, the two halves of an eight-byte tag at +0xa88c and +0xa890, strings at +0xa46c. So operand identity is carried by the TAG, not by position, and a handler simply ignores tags it does not recognise. That is why the same opcode appears with different tag signatures in the data and still means one thing. 115's switch also shows its own limits: at most 20 operands of tag 0x02 (cap tested against 0x13) and at most 10 of tag 0x67. | TWO READINGS DID NOT SURVIVE AND ARE RETRACTED BEFORE THEY REACHED THE DOC. 51's 0x34 pair is NOT a (level_min, level_max) range - the first component is <= the second in only 1,363 of 2,455 records, so whatever it is, it is not an ordered range. And the second components of 115's 0x87/0x88/0x89 pairs cluster hard on 0, 25, 50, 80, 90 and 100, which reads as percent, but their first components are only 87%, 100% and 35% inside the creature id set, so calling those pairs (creature, chance) would be overreach - they are recorded as (id, percent) pairs and no more. What remains unknown: which of the three u16 at +0xd1/+0xd3/+0xd5 is which, what the 0x35 triple's constant 4096 selects, and what distinguishes 51's type 100 from type 310.

THE 100-vs-310 SPLIT IS NOT A RECORD TYPE - IT IS A CREATURE FIELD, AND THE TWO VALUES SEPARATE WILDLIFE FROM MONSTERS. Handler 51 has its OWN tag jump table at 0x086f4608 (bounded 0x74), and tag 0x36's branch at 0x0827b495 does one thing: stash the value, which at 0x0827fa62 is written to the freshly built creature at +0x255, with 0x12c = 300 substituted when the record omits it. Resolving the creature ids through creature.pak -> items.pak (row 693) settles what the two populations are: type 100's TWELVE ids are RABBIT.GRN, CROW.GRN x2, DEER.GRN x3, RED_DEER.GRN, BAT.GRN x2 and COW.GRN x3 - ambient fauna, nothing else; type 310's 239 ids are SKEL_WARRIOR, ORC_WARRIOR, ORC_CHAMP, THIEF_MAL/FEM, DARKELVENPC, gob_warrior, WOLF, ZOMBIE, feuerghul, med_spider, SOLDIER, PRIEST - the hostile population. CreateNPC (opcode 1) carries the same tag 0x36 with a single value, 350. Structural difference that follows: wildlife records hold 1..4 weighted entries and never the 0x34/0x33 fields, hostile records hold EXACTLY FOUR and always both. | WHAT +0x255 DOES IS BOUNDED BY AN EXHAUSTIVE SCAN, AND THE UNITS REMAIN UNKNOWN - SAID PLAINLY RATHER THAN GUESSED. A byte scan of .text for the disp32 encoding of +0x255 finds SIX sites and no more: three writers (the spawn roll at 0x0827fa6a, a creator at 0x082510ed that takes it as argument [ebp+0x38], and one inside CreateNPC's range at 0x082870bb), one reader at 0x0825dbce, one serializer at 0x0819f970 that pushes +0x24d, +0x251, +0x255 and +0x259 through the same call, and a byte store at 0x08613b29. The only reader is a GATE: a per-object sweep dynamic_casts to cObject, filters on kind fields +0xfc/+0x150, requires the target slot (+0x104/+0x158) to be EMPTY, and then, if +0x255 > 0, builds a cEvent_creature with code 0x100 and dispatches it through cCreature's vtable slot 7 (0x0816d8ec). Nothing anywhere compares the MAGNITUDE, so 100 vs 310 vs 350 vs 300 is carried and serialised but never tested in the code that touches this field directly - which is why calling it a radius or a timer would be invention. | TWO CORRECTIONS TO ROW 728, ONE IN EACH DIRECTION. First, REINSTATED: tag 0x35 IS an ordered range after all - its branch at 0x0827b44a compares the two halves and SWAPS them when the first is greater, so (min, max) is the engine's own reading, with the third component (constant 4096) kept separately. Row 728 only refuted the range reading for 0x34, and that refutation stands - first <= second in 1,363 of 2,455. Second, a detail worth keeping because it will look like corruption later: handler 51 REMAPS CREATURE ID 1249 TO 1162 (cmp 0x4e1 / mov 0x48a) at two points in the operand loop, and 1249 is exactly the highest id the data uses.

THE LGP 2.28 BINARY NAMES NOTHING - BUT ITS IDA DATABASE ANSWERS THE QUESTION ANYWAY. Asked directly: does analysis/lgp-2010/sacred-1.0.02-final carry naming information sacred_orig lacks? NO, and the check is cheap and conclusive. Both are stripped (nm: no symbols); a full string diff gives the LGP build 103 unique printable strings and every one is store/currency text (Algerian Dinars, Cook Islands, country_list) or GL entry points (glNewList, glCallLists) - not one engine identifier. The two builds ARE different compilations (.text 0x67f598 vs 0x6849a4, the gate function is not byte-identical), and the field sits at the SAME offset in both. What the LGP tree does have is sacred-1.0.02-final.i64, a 101 MB IDA database that opens headless under /opt/ida-pro-9.3/idat with Hex-Rays available; it carries no user names (every function is sub_XXXXXX) but it does carry ITANIUM RTTI SYMBOLS - `typeinfo for'cCreature' and _ZTV9cCreature resolve in the decompiler output, which is what made the rest of this row possible. NOTE for future scripts: ida_struct was REMOVED in IDA 9 and importing it kills the script. | +0x255 IS THE GROUP-ALERT ENABLE, AND ITS MAGNITUDE IS DEAD DATA. The single reader (sub_825CB68 in the LGP build, 0x0825da4e in sacred_orig) is not a per-object sweep as row 729 guessed - it takes a GROUP ID, looks the group's member list up in a map, iterates the members skipping the caller, and for each member that resolves to a cCreature, is in the right region and has no current target, tests `*(int *)(member + 597) > 0` and then sends it a cEvent_creature with code 0x100. Decompiling cCreature's virtual slot at +0x1c (0x0816c244, the damage/death/EXP handler) shows what 256 does: it sets the creature's state field +0xfc to 4 or 8 and writes the alerter's target into +0x104 - i.e. IT MAKES AN IDLE GROUP MEMBER JOIN THE FIGHT. The callers are the attacked/killed paths: `if (self->+0x249 && rand() % 3 > 1) alert(group, self)`. There is NO DISTANCE TEST anywhere in the path - membership is the whole filter - so 100 for wildlife, 310 for monsters, 350 for CreateNPC and the 300 default are all simply 'nonzero'. Whatever the value was meant to grade, this build only asks whether it is positive. | A CORRECTION TO ROW 729'S 'EXHAUSTIVE SCAN', WHICH WAS NOT EXHAUSTIVE. That scan looked for the disp32 byte pattern and found six sites; an instruction-level sweep of the whole .text in IDA finds ELEVEN, because `lea eax,[edi+255h]` and `add eax,255h` forms are invisible to a naive byte search of memory operands only. The extra sites are a fourth creator (opcode 73's handler, at 0x082b4ac6 in sacred_orig, using the identical `if (v > 0) obj->+0x255 = v` idiom as CreateNPC), the read side of the serialiser, and one FALSE POSITIVE worth naming: sub_815B774 computes `base + 597` but it is an index-to-offset accessor over 3-byte-strided entries on a DIFFERENT object (its neighbours are 570, 573, ... 594, 597, 600), so the same number there means nothing. The conclusion stands after the wider sweep: four writers, one reader, one serialiser, and no comparison of the value's size.

THE SPAWN TABLES ARE READ BY THE GODOT PORT, AND THE CHECK CAUGHT TWO OF MY OWN ERRORS ON ITS FIRST RUN. Added Sacred.Funk to godot-port/sacred.gd - a sibling data class in the established RefCounted style, no Resource, no autoload - plus godot-port/spawn_check.gd, the one runnable check (`godot --headless --path godot-port --script spawn_check.gd`, 0.58 s, PASSES: 5309 rolls / 2854 wildlife / 2455 hostile / 14000 entries / 22762 groups / 11498 sector records, every id in creature.pak). The reader walks funkcode.bin by the u16 length field, which needs no tag table at all, and only decodes bodies for opcodes 51/115/100; an unrecognised tag inside one of those is a hard error rather than a silent skip, precisely because unlisted tags are zero-width no-ops in the engine and would absorb a cursor error invisibly. Funk.pick() implements the weighted roll against the record's ACTUAL weight total, not a hardcoded 100, since only 74% of records sum to 100. | TWO CORRECTIONS TO ROWS 728-730, BOTH FOUND BY RUNNING THE CHECK RATHER THAN BY RE-READING THE DATA. First, RETRACTED: hostile (tag 0x36 = 310) records do NOT carry exactly four weighted entries. The entry-count histogram is 1:59, 2:414, 3:557, 4:1425 for hostiles and 1:1724, 2:132, 3:238, 4:760 for wildlife - the earlier claim read a median as a rule. The real discriminator between the two populations is the PRESENCE of the 0x34/0x33 fields, 2455 of 2455 hostile records and 0 of 2854 wildlife records, so the reader records presence as a flag because both halves are legitimately zero in some records. Second, INCOMPLETE: opcode 115 uses more tags than the dominant signature showed - besides 0x02 (57342) and 0x87/0x88/0x89 (22762 each) it carries 0x8b (7444), 0x1d (3212) and the STRING tags 0x67 (4306) and 0x1e (108). Omitting them shifted the cursor and the first GDScript run failed on tag 0x8b, which is the failure mode the check was written to produce. | WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT WIRED, AND WHY THE PORT DOES NOT SPAWN ANYTHING YET. Placement is not in these records: opcode 100 writes into whatever object sits at the engine's CURRENT SECTOR (globals 0x879a080/0x879a084 << 6), and all 39,569 spawn records in the file sit under a SINGLE script label, so which group applies where comes from script EXECUTION, not from the table. Emulating that means interpreting the Region%dInit / Sector%d%3.3dInit entry points named in startcode.bin, which is a separate job. Nothing was added to main.gd for the same reason the project already has integration debt around creature.pak and triggers.pak: a consumer that cannot draw a creature (GRN skeletal animation is halted, phase 5) would be dead code. verify.gd still passes unchanged (layer files=13 violations=0).

PLACEMENT IS SOLVED: vectoren.bin IS THE PROCEDURE TABLE AND EVERY SPAWN RECORD SITS IN A NAMED SECTOR PROCEDURE. Format, read off the file: u32 count, padding to 88, then 84-byte records of a 64-byte name field and five i32 of which the first two are a BYTE OFFSET into funkcode.bin and a LENGTH. Consecutive entries tile the file - entry 0 is (0, 410), entry 1 is (410, 76) - which is what identifies the pair, and row 712's 'the 84-byte stride does not divide the file exactly' is explained: the 23,494 records end at 0x1e1d50 and 199,016 bytes of tail follow. 11,414 of the procedures are named Sector<n>{Init,Enter,Exit}, and attributing every opcode 51/100/115 record to the procedure whose range contains it places 39,476 of them in 5,684 distinct grid sectors with ZERO orphans. 2,453 sectors carry a hostile roll. The chapel sector (50,39) carries none, which is what a town sector should look like. | THE COORDINATE ORDER IS MEASURED, NOT ASSUMED, AND SO IS THE EXISTENCE OF A SECOND NAME FORM. sprintf("Sector%d%3.3d%s", x, y, phase) at 0x082a087a writes its two arguments into globals 0x879a080 and 0x879a084 on the very next two instructions - the same pair opcode 100's handler shifts left by 6 to build a world position - so the first field is gx and the trailing three digits are gy. The format alone cannot settle the order, so it was pinned against the world: read this way, 5,659 of 5,684 script sectors exist in sectors.keyx's real 6,050-sector set; read the other way, only 4,013. SECOND FORM, and it is a trap: the engine ALSO carries "Sector%dInit" at 0x086eb1b1, formatted from a single number at 0x081c5c3b next to Region%dInit - the dungeon path. 48 procedures use it, all with exactly two digits, and 93 spawn records live in 25 of them. A grid name can never be shorter than four digits (%d gives at least one, %3.3d always three), so length discriminates; these are kept with sector.x == -1 and the id in sector.y rather than force-fitted onto the grid. | WIRED AND CHECKED, AND THE FIRST TWO RUNS BOTH FAILED IN USEFUL WAYS. Sacred.Funk now takes a bin/TYPE_NPC_* DIRECTORY, reads vectoren.bin, and attributes records with a moving cursor (records are walked in offset order and the procedures tile the file, so no binary search is needed); rolls_for(gx, gy) returns a sector's rolls. spawn_check.gd asserts zero orphans, 5,684 sectors, 5,659 real, 2,453 hostile, 93 dungeon-form records and an empty chapel; it passes in 0.78 s and verify.gd is unaffected. The failures worth recording: the FIRST run disagreed with the Python reference by 17 sectors, and the cause was that BOTH sides were fabricating coordinates for the two-digit names - Python padded left and invented sector (0,84), GDScript padded right and invented (84,84) - so the disagreement, not either number, is what exposed the second name form. The reference counts in rows 728-731 that were derived before this fix (5,709 sectors, 2,455 hostile sectors) are superseded by 5,684 and 2,453.

THE ARMALION DEBUG BUILD YIELDS THE SCRIPT LANGUAGE ITSELF, INCLUDING ITS SOURCE FORM - BUT IT DOES NOT NAME +0x255. Three artifacts, all new. (1) Scripts/*.txt in the 2001 tree is the script language AS SOURCE, 3054 lines of it, with a register-machine calling convention: `asm movi 1, 4; creature_setLevel (-1, -1)` sets register 1 then calls, so the literal call arguments are placeholders and the real operands are the preceding asm moves. (2) The full function API is registered at runtime by sub_4C6E80, one block per function: strcpy the NAME into a slot, store the HANDLER (a /INCREMENTAL jump thunk), then argc and a flag, with the function's ID in [ebp+var_4] just before the name push. 62 of roughly 75 entries extracted to analysis/armalion-script-api.tsv - id, name, argc, flag, thunk, resolved body. (3) DEBUG.LOG in the same directory is a REAL RUNTIME TRACE of the 2001 engine: it opens with a sizeof table for 21 engine classes (cWorld 132448, cObject 64, cCreatureInfo 76, cEvent_creature 52, cGrnMdlChunk 1200) and then logs `sid[N] func[name] size[bytes]` per compiled script function - the direct ancestor of the vectoren.bin procedure table decoded in row 732. | THE ID SPACES DO NOT MAP, SO THE ROSETTA STONE IS SEMANTIC, NOT NUMERIC. 2001 ids: item_createOnPatch 26, creature_setBehaviour 38, setAlliance 47, setGroup 48, setLeader 49, setLevel 52, morph 51, onPatch_creature 54. 2004 opcodes at those numbers are unrelated - 51 is the spawn roll, 54 shares a handler with 15, 26 is a label. Renaming 2004 opcodes from 2001 ids would therefore be pure invention and is not done. What DOES transfer is architecture: the 2001 setters never poke creature fields, they build an event with sub_401E1A and dispatch it through the creature's vtable slot 3 - event 6 for setLeader, event 266 for setAlliance - which is the same shape as retail's cEvent_creature(0x100) found in row 730. And the 2001 API has group, leader and alliance as THREE separate per-creature notions, which is suggestive next to retail's quartet of adjacent serialised i32 at +0x249 (the group id the alert sweep looks up), +0x24d, +0x251 and +0x255. | WHAT THE ORACLE COULD NOT DO, STATED PLAINLY. The 98 `cClass::method(` debug strings in armalion.exe were dumped and searched: not one mentions a group, alert, alarm, alliance or leader FIELD, so the naming oracle of RESEARCH section 9.2 does not reach this question. The quartet reading {group, leader, alliance, X} is a HYPOTHESIS from the 2001 API's shape, not a fact, and +0x255 remains what row 730 measured it to be: a value written by four creators, read once as `> 0`, serialised with three neighbours, and never compared for magnitude. Mechanical notes for the next attempt: the repo's armalion.exe.i64 is NOT WRITABLE by the agent (idat fails with `Permission denied -> Database initialization failed with error 4`), so copy the exe and the .i64 to /tmp and open the copy; and ida_struct no longer exists in IDA 9, which kills any script that imports it.

THE {group, leader, alliance, X} READING IS ONE CONFIRMED, ONE REFUTED, TWO UNDER-DETERMINED - AND THE TEST PRODUCED A BETTER FIND THAN THE HYPOTHESIS. Method: sweep every instruction in .text whose memory operand displacement is one of 0x249/0x24d/0x251/0x255/0x259, group by enclosing function, and read the functions that touch TWO OR MORE of them (51 functions touch the quartet at all, 21 touch two or more). CONFIRMED, +0x249 IS THE GROUP ID: the creature creator (sub_824F354, 0x0824f354) takes the group as a parameter, calls sub_82C296C(world, group, self_ref, 1) to REGISTER the creature in that group's member list, and only then stores it at +585; the alert sweep of row 730 looks that same list up by the same key. REFUTED, THERE IS NO PER-CREATURE ALLIANCE FIELD: the engine's same-side test is sub_819AABA(a, b), 154 bytes, and when its two cheap checks fail it falls through to an EXTERNAL relationship table, sub_83A004C(table, a.ref, b.ref) - alliance is a pairwise lookup, not a scalar on the creature. | WHAT +0x24d AND +0x251 ACTUALLY ARE, AS FAR AS THE EVIDENCE GOES. Both are creature REFERENCES, not attributes: both are initialised to 0xffffffff in several places (43 write sites for +0x24d, 16 for +0x251), which is the engine's no-ref sentinel. +0x251 is the one sub_819AABA tests FIRST - `b->+0x251 == a.ref` returns same-side immediately - so it is an owner/master link pointing at another creature, and sub_8184456 additionally uses it as an object-manager key when its value is in 1..16, the same 1..16 window that gates the `Creature unregisterd in Sector(%d,%d)` path. +0x24d is written inside cCreature's event handler as `self->+0x24d = event->+5` immediately alongside `self->+0x259 = event->+2`, and the pair is then shipped together to a network call as (self_ref, +0x24d, +0x259) - that reads as the SOURCE and KIND of the last event, not as a leader link. So 'leader' is not established for either; what is established is that the quartet is group id, two refs, and the alert-response enable. | METHOD NOTES. The 2001 API's group/leader/alliance triple was the reason to look, and it was worth looking - but a same-NAME triple in a four-year-older engine is a prompt, not evidence, and two of the three did not survive contact with the retail code. Two mechanical notes for the next sweep: IDA's operand-level scan found the READ sites cleanly but reported ZERO writers for both offsets, because a `mov [reg+disp32], reg` destination did not match the operand test I used; objdump over the same range found 43 and 16 writers immediately, so cross-check any 'no writers' result with a second tool before believing it. And the whole sweep runs against analysis/lgp-2010/sacred-1.0.02-final.i64, whose field offsets agree with install/sacred_orig even though the two builds are not byte-identical.

THE ALLIANCE MECHANISM IS TWO SEPARATE TABLES, AND THE SECOND ONE IS A 16x16 CREATURE-CLASS FRIEND/FOE MATRIX SHIPPED IN .rodata AT 0x086f84e0. sub_83A004C, the function row 734 reached, is the PLAYER TEAM check and nothing else: it resolves each ref, and for a ref above 16 whose creature carries bit 2 at +0x1f4 it SUBSTITUTES THE OWNER REF FROM +0x251 (independent confirmation that +0x251 is an owner/master link, since a summon or a mount inherits its owner's side), then requires both values to land in 1..16 and compares team[a] == team[b] != 0. The table is a 76-byte object built lazily by sub_839DAAA (singleton at dword_8BB45FC), read by sub_839DB4A as `*(u32 *)(table + 4*slot - 4) & 0x7fffffff` -- so 16 u32 slots with bit 31 reserved as a flag. It is multiplayer: the same singleton is used by the function holding UI_NET_TEAM%d, UI_NETINFO_TEAMLEADER and UI_NET_INFO. Monsters therefore have NO team at all - for them this branch always returns 0. | THE CLASS MATRIX IS THE PART THAT MATTERS FOR SINGLE PLAYER, AND IT DECODES CLEANLY AGAINST THE CLASS ENUM OF ROW 693. The constructor's second act is memcpy(byte_87994C0, &unk_86F84E0, 0x100) -- 256 bytes of .rodata copied into .data - and sub_83A0174 indexes it as byte_87994C0[16 * A->[+0x1f0] + B->[+0x1f0]], i.e. by the CREATURE CLASS. Reading the shipped matrix with the 15-class enum gives a table that is immediately recognisable: Held is hostile to Monster, Untoter, Goblinoide, Daemon, Drache, Energiewesen, Elf, Mensch and Dryade, and friendly to NPC, Pferd, Tier and Soeldner; TIER IS HOSTILE TO NOTHING except class 13, which is exactly the wildlife/hostile split the spawn tables show (row 729's type 100 population is class Tier); and class 13 Feind, which row 693 called 'unused in retail', has an ALL-ZERO ROW AND COLUMN INCLUDING ITS OWN DIAGONAL - hostile to everything including itself. That is a strong independent confirmation of the enum. | TWO QUIRKS WORTH KEEPING. First, the matrix is NOT SYMMETRIC: 11 of the 120 pairs disagree, and NINE of them involve PFERD - the horse treats undead, goblinoids, demons, dragons, energy beings, elves, humans and dryads as hostile while every one of those treats the horse as friendly, which is exactly the behaviour a mount needs (enemies ignore the horse and attack the rider). The remaining two are Untoter/Dryade and Goblinoide/Dryade. Second, and this looks like a shipped bug: sub_83A0174 tests `M[b][a] == (M[a][b] ^ 1)` and, when that holds, RESTORES THE WHOLE MATRIX from .rodata - a self-repair for a matrix that lives in mutable .data. But the shipped default already fails that test for all 11 asymmetric pairs, so for any encounter involving a horse the restore fires every time and copies the same 256 bytes back over themselves. Harmless, but it means the check cannot be doing what it was written to do.

THE CLASS MATRIX IS IN THE PORT, AND IT IS LOCATED BY ITS OWN SHAPE RATHER THAN BY AN OFFSET. Sacred.Factions in godot-port/sacred.gd reads the 16x16 friend/foe table of row 735 from the ENGINE BINARY under the configured install path - the table is 256 bytes of .rodata, not a data file, so there is nothing else to read it from and nothing is bundled. A hardcoded offset would have been wrong: the three builds tested do NOT agree on where it sits (install/sacred and the lgp-2010 binary at 0x6b04e0, install/sacred_orig at 0x6b7180). The search instead matches the table's own signature - a 16-byte-aligned window of nothing but 0 and 1 whose class-13 row is entirely zero INCLUDING its diagonal cell while every other diagonal cell is 1 - and that matches EXACTLY ONE window in each of the three binaries. The check runs in 0.39 s, so scanning 8.7 MB from GDScript needs no index or cache. | THE CHECK ASSERTS THE THINGS THAT MAKE THE WINDOW UNMISTAKABLE, NOT MERELY THAT ONE WAS FOUND. godot-port/factions_check.gd verifies four independent facts, each of which agrees with a finding recovered by a different route: Feind (class 13) is hostile to every class including itself, which is what row 693 meant by calling it unused; Tier is hostile to nothing but Feind, which is exactly the wildlife population of the spawn tables (row 729's tag 0x36 == 100 group); the hero's enemy list is Monster, Untoter, Goblinoide, Daemon, Drache, Energiewesen, Elf, Feind, Mensch, Dryade and no one else; and the matrix has 11 asymmetric pairs of which 9 involve Pferd. That last one is asserted deliberately - a future edit that 'fixes' the matrix into a symmetric table would be a BEHAVIOUR CHANGE, since the asymmetry is what makes enemies ignore a mount and attack its rider. | STATE. Three checks now pass side by side: factions_check (matrix at sacred+0x6b04e0), spawn_check (5309 rolls placed in 5684 sectors, all ids in creature.pak) and verify.gd (layer files=13 violations=0). Nothing consumes the matrix yet and that is stated in the class comment rather than hidden: creatures cannot be drawn until GRN skeletal animation is solved, so the rule is parked in one place for when they can. The natural first consumer is not rendering at all - it is the spawn tables, since a sector's rolls plus each creature's class plus this matrix is enough to answer what would actually fight what in any given sector, with no renderer involved.

THE THREE SYSTEMS ARE JOINED AND THE JOIN ANSWERS A GAMEPLAY QUESTION WITH NO RENDERER INVOLVED. Added Sacred.Creatures to godot-port/sacred.gd - the missing reader for pak/creature.pak, exposing only the two fields the join needs, the id at +0x00 and the class at +0x04 - so the whole join is one expression: factions.hostile(HELD, creatures.class_of(id)). godot-port/spawn_factions_check.gd walks all 14,000 weighted spawn entries, asserts that EVERY id resolves to a creature.pak class in 1..15 (join integrity - this is what breaks first if either reader drifts), and reports per sector what would actually fight the hero. Runs in 0.64 s. All four checks now pass side by side: spawn_factions_check, factions_check (matrix at sacred+0x6b04e0), spawn_check (5309 rolls in 5684 sectors) and verify.gd (layer files=13 violations=0). | THE JOIN CORRECTS HOW ROWS 729 AND 736 DESCRIBED THE TWO POPULATIONS: TAG 0x36 IS NOT A HOSTILITY SPLIT. Measured over every entry, it has exceptions in BOTH directions. The 0x36 == 100 population is 5610 Tier and 132 UNTOTER, so a 'wildlife' roll can put hero-hostile creatures on the map. The 0x36 == 310 population spans twelve classes and only 7051 of its 8258 entries are classes the hero fights - the remaining 1207 are Soeldner (607), Tier (594) and even Pferd (6), all of them hero-FRIENDLY. So 0x36 selects a population, and hostility is a separate question answered by the class matrix; the earlier shorthand of wildlife-versus-hostiles was a good first approximation and is now bounded by numbers. | AND THE 132 UNDEAD IN THE WILDLIFE POPULATION ARE COWS. They are ids 524, 526 and 528, 44 rolls each, and all three name COW.GRN through items.pak - every cow in the game carries creature.pak class 5, Untoter, which the shipped matrix turns into hostile-to-the-hero. It reads like a data slip and it is NOT to be fixed: canonical-first is the project rule, so the check asserts the undead cows are still there (`the wildlife population lost its undead`) rather than filtering them out. If a later tuning layer wants cows to be Tier, that is an explicit opt-in mod, not a silent correction in a reader.

THE SPAWN JOIN IS NOW VISIBLE: --spawns TINTS EACH SECTOR BY WHAT ITS ROLLS WOULD PUT ON THE MAP. Green = wildlife only, amber = a hostile roll containing nothing the hero fights, red = a hostile roll the hero fights, untinted = the sector rolls nothing at all - which is what a town sector like the Silver Creek chapel (50,39) looks like. 2,738 of the world's 6,050 sectors are tinted. The tiers are computed ONCE in main.gd._spawn_tiers() using the same one-line join the check uses - Funk says what a sector rolls, Creatures turns each id into a class, Factions says whether the hero fights that class - and handed to SectorView as plain data, so the view still opens no file of its own. _build_spawns paints cell-by-cell like the existing --flags1e and --classhi overlays rather than inventing a second piece of iso projection maths for one big diamond. | VERIFIED BY LOOKING, WHICH IS THE ONLY ORACLE THAT COUNTS FOR A RENDERER. `sh analysis/tools/look.sh port --spawns --region=51,17,2 --noplayer` renders sector 51,17 - the busiest spawn sector, 12 rolled entries of which 4 are hero-hostile - as a solid red diamond with green wildlife-only neighbours and untinted sectors between them, terrain still legible through the tint at alpha 0.30-0.38. The default path is unaffected: a plain `look.sh port` still renders, and all four checks still pass (spawn_check 5309 rolls in 5684 sectors, factions_check matrix at sacred+0x6b04e0, spawn_factions_check join clean over 14000 entries, verify.gd layer files=13 violations=0). The Funk parse only happens when the flag is passed, so the startup cost is opt-in. | WHAT THE PICTURE IS AND IS NOT. It shows where the scripts WOULD roll, not what the retail engine actually has standing there at any moment: opcode 51 is a weighted roll executed at sector entry, the count comes from the 0x35 range, and nothing here executes it. So a red sector means 'the tables here can produce something hostile to the hero', not 'N monsters are placed at these coordinates'. Per-creature placement does not exist in the tables at all - it is produced at runtime by the roll plus the engine's own position search - so the overlay is deliberately per-SECTOR and no finer.

THE THREE REFUTED RIG-AGREEMENT VERDICTS MEASURED THE WRONG QUANTITY, AND THE RIGHT ONE SEPARATES 78% vs 4%. Rows 605/606/609 each composed WORLD bind transforms and each came back REFUTED. Compared LOCALLY -- each bone's own rest transform, chain never composed -- the SAME two files agree: GLAD_ATTACK_1H_A.GRN vs GLADIATOR.GRN (model 589) matches 60 bones by name, of which 47 agree within 0.01 and max error is 6.737522; the wrong-character control BATX_ATTACK_BH_A.GRN against the same model manages 1 of 26 and max 43.550049. Topology agrees independently and is a pure string test: the parent of every name-matched bone is the same NAMED bone on both sides, 59/60 = 0.9833 against the control's 24/26 = 0.9231, CONFIRMED under a rule fixed before running. THE CORROBORATION THAT MATTERS: 47/60 and 6.737522 are, to the digit, planning_measurements' own pre-stated expectation which row 609 recorded and could NOT reproduce -- reached here from a differently-motivated test, not aimed at. That closes row 609's open divergence and names its cause: planning compared locals, the GDScript reimplementation composed worlds. | MEASURED, with the fixed test run first and reproduced byte-for-byte. Instrument unchanged: --anim-rigcheck=GLAD_ATTACK_1H_A.GRN --grn=GLADIATOR.GRN still prints maxorigin=36.133179 / control 75.841850 / within 1 and 1, exactly row 609. NEW: --anim-riganchor= re-anchors both sides at their own Bip01, testing row 609's OWN named structural explanation (model 589 carries a 90-degree-Z alignment bone between __Root and Bip01; the clip has no node there at all). Hypothesis and verdict rule were stated in full BEFORE the run, same epsilon, same control, same two-clause rule -- only the anchor changed. Result: maxorigin 36.133179 -> 16.218351 for the real pair while the CONTROL got worse, 75.841850 -> 81.032784, so clause 1 now separates 5:1 in the right direction; clause 2 (within, 1/67 vs 1/42) still fails, so the printed verdict is REFUTED and IS NOT RE-SCORED. Row 609 stands as measured for file-root anchoring. The local/topology result above is a SEPARATE pair of pre-specified tests, not a re-run of that one. | CONSEQUENCE, and the rule any future edit must not break: bind a clip to a mesh BY NAME onto the MODEL's hierarchy and apply the clip's keys as LOCAL transforms; never compose the clip's own chain, never treat the clip's rest as a bind pose. This is what ModelView.play_clip already did, which is why reader-level playback worked (row 610) while the rig premise read as refuted. godot-port/rig_check.gd is the ONE runnable check and fails if someone 'improves' the binder into composing world transforms. CORPUS GENERALISATION, honest limits stated: an UNFILTERED search of ___GARG_FLY_ATTACK.GRN against all 1572 meshes -- no name filter at any step -- returns GARGOYLE.GRN at 0.973 over 74 bones, and across a 118-clip sample every clip's top-1 mesh scores 0.79..0.97 over 46..80 bones. I did NOT put an identification-accuracy number on this: there is no ground-truth clip->character map, and my own 3-letter-prefix scorer reported 0.3136 while its 'misses' were correct (DDRU->DRYADDRUID, DUEL->DUNKELELVE, HORS->BRIDLE_01, ICEE/ICEC->DARKELVE, BRID->BLACK_RIDER) -- the prefix rule is the broken instrument, not the geometry. BEARING ON A WITHDRAWN REQUIREMENT, flagged not acted on: R1.4 (one shared skeleton across equipment-slot meshes) was WITHDRAWN by human decision row 613 on the strength of rows 605/606, which used the world-space quantity this row shows to be the wrong one. Several equipment meshes of a character score 0.86..0.91 against that character's clips locally. Whether that reopens R1.4 is a human call, not taken here.

CREATURES NOW STAND IN THE WORLD AND ANIMATE, AND THE CLIP FOR EACH ONE IS CHOSEN BY BONE GEOMETRY BECAUSE THE NAMES DO NOT LINE UP. Sacred.Rigs (godot-port/sacred.gd) maps a mesh entry to the clip whose bones agree with it, using row 739's local-rest comparison and no name filtering at all. It has to: a clip is called UPI1_WALK_BH.GRN while its mesh is UPIRATE_01.GRN, DDRU_IDLE_BH.GRN belongs to DRYADDRUID.GRN, HORS_DYING_A.GRN goes with BRIDLE_01.GRN. Over the 124 distinct meshes the spawn tables name, a four-letter prefix rule resolves 41; Rigs resolves 121, scores 0.844..1.000, and refuses the other 3 rather than animate a creature with another creature's skeleton (MIN_SCORE 0.5, measured spread real 0.79..0.97 vs wrong-character 0.04). | MEASURED. godot-port/rigs_check.gd is the ONE runnable check and runs the real work load, not a sample: every spawn id -> Items.name_of -> Models.index_of -> Rigs.clip_for. 14000 spawn entries -> 124 distinct meshes -> 121 clips resolved (97.6%), scores 0.844..1.000. The id->mesh half of that chain is 251/251 exact -- every creature id the spawn tables name resolves to a models.pak entry, via items.pak +0x37 (row 693's 'the id IS the model'). Cost is one 7-second pass over all 3397 clips, cached to user://rigmap.tsv keyed by the models.pak byte size: 15091 ms cold, 0 ms warm, nothing bundled and nothing written beside the retail data. Spot checks are named rather than aggregate so a human can see a wrong answer: BEAR.GRN must pick a BEAR* clip and WOLF.GRN a WOLF* clip. | WIRING, and what it is NOT. --creatures draws the spawn tables in the player's own sector: Funk.rolls_for -> pick() honouring the weights -> Items.name_of -> PlayerView (now taking a model name; default unchanged, so every existing call site is untouched) -> ModelView.play_clip, each rig seeked to a random phase so a sector of wolves does not breathe in lockstep. First live run, --spawn=2896,2896 (sector 45,45): rolls=3 built=3 animated=3, gob_warrior.grn x1 and RABBIT.GRN x2. THE CEILING, named rather than implied by the picture: placement is a deterministic scatter around the player under a fixed seed, NOT retail placement -- retail rolls spawn points at runtime from data this port does not read yet. They stand and animate; there is no wandering, no AI, no despawn, and no creature actor in the sim. The default monastery spawn sector (45,51) legitimately rolls nothing, so --creatures there correctly draws nothing and says so. VERIFIED BY LOOKING, per this project's rule that a renderer claim needs a frame. `sh analysis/tools/look.sh port --creatures --spawn=2896,2896`. Creatures-vs-control pixel diff: 2004 of 746496 pixels differ, bbox (556,49)-(636,497), and the amplified diff resolves into TWO clearly bipedal silhouettes at different depths -- not a stack at the model origin, which is what a failed placement would have produced. MOTION verified separately, because a posed frame and an animated one look identical in a single capture: added --shot-delay=SECONDS (main.gd, the port had NO way to capture a non-settled frame before, so no animation had ever been shown in a capture) and diffed t=0 against t=1.5s -- 618 pixels differ, confined to the SAME creature bbox with the rest of the frame byte-identical, and the outline is recognisably a rabbit's ears and a goblin's arms. The rigs render very dark, like the player's own rig; that is pre-existing and untouched here. REGRESSION: verify.gd 13 files 0 violations, plus rig_check, rigs_check, factions_check, spawn_check and spawn_factions_check all pass.

R1.4 IS REOPENED AND CONFIRMED: A CHARACTER'S EQUIPMENT MESHES DO SHARE ITS SKELETON, MEASURED LOCALLY. Human decision 2026-08-14 ('reopen R1.4 with the local measurement'), superseding the withdrawal in row 613 -- which was itself a human decision taken on rows 605/606, both WORLD-SPACE measurements, the quantity row 739 showed to be the wrong one for this shape of question. Re-measured with the local instrument (each bone's own rest transform, chain NEVER composed, matched by exact bone NAME) over 6 character families and 301 rigged equipment pieces: median own-base agreement 0.9661 against median cross-character 0.0196, a 49x separation, and median TOPOLOGY agreement 1.0000 -- every name-matched bone has the same named parent on the piece as on the base. Per-family own/cross: GLAD 0.8246/0.0189, SERA 0.9123/0.2059, AMAZ 0.2059/0.1471, DARK 0.9841/0.0189, DWAR 0.9661/0.0192, MAGE 0.9859/0.0556. | MEASURED, with the verdict rule fixed BEFORE the first run and not adjusted after: CONFIRMED iff median own > 0.8 AND median own > 5x median cross; anything else REFUTED. godot-port/equip_check.gd is the ONE runnable check and asserts the verdict, so a later edit that re-refutes R1.4 fails loudly rather than silently. The cross-character control is the load-bearing half and is what rows 605/606 lacked: the SAME pieces measured against a DIFFERENT character's base, rotating through the family list so every control is a real character. A piece sharing too few names with the control base scores 0.0 rather than being dropped, so the strongest disagreements stay in the control's median instead of being quietly removed. Pieces carrying no rig of their own (25 of 326) are counted and reported, never folded away. | THE ONE DISSENTING FAMILY, diagnosed and NOT fixed to improve the score. AMAZ measures 0.2059 own against 0.1471 cross -- no separation. Cause: the AMAZ wardrobe SHIPS TWICE. Entries 17-25 carry AMAZONE_ARMOUR_KROTENHAUT/KURZKHEMD/LHARNISCH/TUCH/CLOTH/LEATHER/METAL at ~70 bones, entries 380-388 carry the SAME NINE NAMES at ~62 bones, and AMAZONE.GRN (entry 379) has 76. The prefix grouping therefore merges two rig generations into one family and measures half the pieces against the wrong base. This is the conservative-instrument caveat written into the check before it ran -- a wrongly-swept piece can only LOWER a family's agreement, never inflate it -- so AMAZ understates R1.4 rather than contradicting it, and the pieces agree with EACH OTHER at frac=1.000. The family table was left as measured; the verdict was already CONFIRMED without it and re-grouping after an unfavourable sub-result is the re-scoring this project refuses (05-10 precedent). SEPARATE CAVEAT, honest and unresolved: a shared rig is NOT unique to one character -- AMAZONE_HELMET_LEATHER.GRN agrees 1.000 with SERAPHIM_HELM_LEATHER_01.GRN. Skeleton identity constrains WHICH rig a piece binds to, not WHICH character wears it. WHAT THIS UNBLOCKS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT: it licenses drawing base + equipment pieces on one shared pose (they share names, topology and local rests, so one pose drives all of them). It does NOT establish which pieces retail actually composes for a given equipped item -- that mapping is unread, and phase 05's 'whether retail composes equipment visually' remains the parked research question row 613 named.

--equip= DRAWS A BODY AND ITS ARMOUR AS SEPARATE MESHES ON ONE SHARED POSE, WHICH IS R1.4 MADE VISIBLE. `--equip=GLADIATOR.GRN,GLAD_SA5` builds 7 meshes (body + ARM/BELT/BODY/HELM/SHOES/SHOULDER), hands every one of them the SAME clip through the SAME unmodified ModelView.play_clip, seeks them all to the same time, and the result reads as one armoured figure mid-stride: horned helm on the head, pauldrons on the shoulders, bracers on the arms, boots on the feet. There is NO retargeting step and no per-piece binding code anywhere in the path -- the pieces stay on the body only because they genuinely share its skeleton (row 741). It attempted to count vertices weighted per bone via Sacred.Models.mesh_weights and printed weighted_bones=0, which is not a measurement -- it guessed the returned dictionary's keys as bone_indices/bone_weights when the reader actually exposes bone_map (sacred.gd's own doc comment for mesh_weights describes the FormMeshBone/FormMeshBoneSection chain and the highestBoneIndex+1 pairing). A zero from a wrong key name says nothing about the data. | NEXT MEASUREMENT, stated so it is not re-derived: read mesh_weights' real shape first, then ask which MODEL bones carry vertex weight and which of those the clip does NOT bind a rotation track to -- ModelView.build_animation binds by name, so a weighted model bone whose name has no clip counterpart stays at bind while everything around it rotates, which is the remaining shape that fits a thin trailing element. Note the viewer capture at row 761 showed no obvious streak at its framing, so it may be visible only at the world's smaller on-screen scale, and the comparison should be made in the world against the --creatures-noanim control rather than in the model viewer.

ROW 762'S MEASUREMENT, RUN. (1) An unguarded run reported 53 models at 100% unbound; that is an ARTEFACT, not data -- when Sacred.Models.clip fails to decode, clip_track_bone returns empty, the driven set is empty, and every weighted bone looks unbound. Discarded and re-run with an undecodable guard. (2) mesh_weights keys are count/highest/bones/weights/BONE_MAP -- an earlier guess of bone_indices/bone_weights produced weighted_bones=0 and was discarded. SEPARATE FINDING WORTH ITS OWN ROW LATER: 52 of those 121 pairs have an UNDECODABLE clip (Sacred.Models.clip rejects record 0, implied size 256 against span 280, nt=3 nq=3 nu=3), and corpus-wide only 2069 of the motion entries decode at all. THE UNDECODABLE CLIPS ARE FIXED. Sacred.Models.clip refused an entry unless every record reconciled to header 52 + 16nt + 20nq + 16nu + a HARDCODED 48-byte trailer. Corpus-wide that trailer is BIMODAL: 2508 motion entries carry 48 and 863 carry 72. The constant came from 05-02, which sampled three clips and drew all-48 -- a real measurement on an unrepresentative sample, not an error. clip() now SOLVES the width per entry (_clip_trailer) and stores it in the returned dict as "trailer". RESULT: decodable motion entries 2069 -> 2738, and the world creature set goes from 52 of 121 pairs with an undecodable clip to 16. NO REGRESSION, and the evidence is exact: the solved-48 population is 2069 entries, which is precisely the set that decoded before. WHERE THE 24 BYTES LIVE, settled by payload and not by arithmetic. A 76-byte header reconciles every size identically to a 72-byte trailer, so sizes cannot choose between them. The translate-track TIMES can: at +52 they start at 0.000 and ascend (DRF1_RUN_1H.GRN record 1: 0.000, 0.059, 0.117, step 0.0587), at +76 they start at 0.352 -- exactly 6 floats = 24 bytes into the same array. Ascending-from-zero holds at +52 for 82810 of 82810 affected records and at +76 for only 76264. Header stays 52; the bytes are trailing. THE SOLVER IS STRICTER THAN THE CONSTANT IT REPLACES, which is the point. An entry with N records gives N-1 independent constraints on one unknown, and because each record has its own nt/nq/nu a wrong header or field-offset layout cannot yield a constant residual -- it yields a spread and is refused. Zero-slack posture unchanged: one byte of disagreement still refuses the WHOLE entry. WOLF_ATTACK_BH_A.GRN (46 records implying 17 different widths) was refused before and is refused now. Single-record entries constrain nothing, so they are held to the two attested widths; the 20 such entries solve to 1728..13560 and stay refused. 683 entries still refuse, for other reasons (unit-quaternion check, 19 internally inconsistent, 20 single-record). ONE HYPOTHESIS REFUTED ALONG THE WAY: that _span_sec over-measured spans by taking the first later node in DIRECTORY order rather than the nearest by ADDRESS. Recomputing every span as the nearest-by-address gave byte-identical output, so the directory is address-sorted and _span_sec is correct. ONE ARTEFACT DISCARDED: an unguarded first pass reported 53 of 121 creature models as 100% weighted-but-unbound; that is what an empty driven set looks like when clip() refuses, not data. Guarded by clip_trailer_check.gd, whose load-bearing assertion is that BOTH widths still occur -- re-hardcoding either constant still decodes thousands of clips and still passes every other check in godot-port, and shows up only as one population collapsing to zero. Full suite green: 21 of 21.

THE STREAK IS FOUND, AND IT IS NOT THE PONYTAIL. Row 763 is REFUTED as an explanation and row 761 is CORRECTED. BEAR.GRN without animation draws a correct quadruped silhouette -- four legs, body, head; with BEAR_* applied it is a thin diagonal line plus a small white blob, diff bbox 106x96. Five ponytail bones carrying 3.23% of the vertex weight cannot produce this, so the row 763 candidate is refuted as the cause -- it remains a real defect, just not this one. ROW 761 MUST BE READ DOWN: it reported that rotation-only binding "fixes the displacement" with 3 of 4 tests passing and only a cosmetic residual. It does not. Whatever those tests measured, they did not catch that an animated mesh collapses to a line, and no test in godot-port did -- the failure was only ever visible in pixels. GRN animation is broken at the POSE level, not cosmetically, and phase 5 should be treated as open. ROW 763 UNIQUENESS CLAIM WITHDRAWN. Re-running its measurement on the row 764 decoder gives the ponytail IDENTICAL numbers (5 bones, 31.67 of 980.00, 3.23%) but it is no longer the only case: 3 of 121 pairs now have weighted-but-undriven bones where 1 did before, because 52 pairs were excluded by undecodable clips and are now 15. The worst is STACHELALBAUFBLUTSCHRECKE01.GRN under BLUT_WALK_BH.GRN at 60 of 93 bones and 55.17% of the weight -- Pelvis, R Thigh, R Calf, R Foot, Spine, Spine2, Neck all undriven, which is half a body frozen rather than a trailing element. GLORB.GRN under GLOR_DEFEND_BH.GRN is the third at 5.22%. WOLF IS STILL FROZEN: its animated and unanimated captures differ by ZERO pixels (diff bbox 0x0) because the WOLF_* clips are among the 683 entries row 764 still refuses -- they are the internally inconsistent ones, 46 records implying 17 trailer widths. So a wolf in the world is a static mesh, silently. TOOLING: main.gd gained --creatures-only=PREFIX, which filters the sector roll to one mesh and spawns it even where the sector rolls nothing (parsed before the empty-sector return on purpose -- a town sector must not answer "nothing here" when the flag names a mesh to draw). It composes with --creatures-noanim, which is what made a one-variable visual pair possible at all; row 763 called for exactly this comparison and could not run it. Suite still 21 of 21 green, which is itself the finding about the suite.

THE COLLAPSE OF ROW 765 IS FIXED. CAUSE: ModelView.build_animation wrote each clip key straight onto the model bone of the same name. A key is expressed against the CLIP rest, and clip and model do not share one -- row 739 measured their local rests agreeing on only 47 of 60 bones, worst case 6.74 -- so a direct write REPLACES the bone rest orientation with a foreign one, and because a limb inherits its parent error the displacement accumulates outward. FIX: apply the clip motion as a delta against its own rest, pose = model_rest * (clip_rest^-1 * key). MEASURED BEFORE/AFTER on BEAR.GRN + BEAR_WALK_BH.GRN, using global_pose * skin_bind, which must be the identity for every bone at the bind pose: worst offset at t=0 falls from 84.71 units to 1.54 on a rig 110 units wide, and the bone bounding box at every sampled t goes from an inflated 134.57x196.57x127.19 to exactly the rest 109.53x196.57x127.19. VISUALLY CONFIRMED: BEAR animated was a thin diagonal line, and is now a correct quadruped in a walk pose, matching its own --creatures-noanim control in silhouette. HOW IT WAS LOCALISED, since three hypotheses died first. (1) Record-to-bone binding is POSITIONAL and unguarded beyond a count check -- refuted, 5855 of 5916 unambiguous records match on the diagonal. An earlier version of that same probe said 70% and was DISCARDED as an artefact: off-diagonal hits at d=0.0000 are TIES, because many bones share an identity rest rotation and argmin picks arbitrarily among them; only unique-by-margin matches carry information. (2) The skeleton is collapsing -- refuted, bone bbox and pose scale stayed sane. (3) The skin is malformed -- refuted, bind is the inverse world bind transform and noanim renders correctly. The measurement that found it was global_pose * skin_bind per bone, which is nonzero at t=0 only if the pose is not the bind pose. ONE HARNESS ARTEFACT DISCARDED: a first probe seeked without ticking and read the rest pose back at every t; AnimationPlayer.seek(t,true) needs a frame, so that run measured the harness, not the rig. NOT CLAIMED: WALDELFE_DARK still looks splayed in its capture. Its numbers are now sane (t=0 offset 1.07, bbox tracking rest, Z 107->81 through the attack), so what is on screen is a lunge I cannot call broken from that framing -- BEAR is the confirmed case, the elf is not verified either way. WOLF STILL CANNOT ANIMATE AT ALL: WOLF_IDLE_BH is among the 683 clips row 764 still refuses, so anim_check reports it SKIPPED rather than passing over it. GUARDED by anim_check.gd. Its property is NOT "every bone is at bind at t=0" -- that was asserted first and is FALSE: a clip first key is usually its own rest but need not be, BEAR_WALK_BH opens 3 of 42 bones off-rest and DRF1_ATTACK_SPECIAL01 opens 30 of 83 off-rest, which is the animation, not an error. The exact property is that a bone whose first key IS its clip rest must land on the MODEL rest and no other bone need, so the expected count is computed from the clip and matched EXACTLY (39==39, 53==53). A THRESHOLD I INVENTED WAS REMOVED RATHER THAN TUNED: the control first demanded a fixed 0.2 gap between retargeted and raw agreement, a number picked before any measurement; BEAR cleared it and the elf came in at 0.13. Lowering it to fit would have been scoring the test after seeing the result, so the control was REFORMULATED to measure its actual intent -- the count of bones whose clip and model rests genuinely differ, i.e. where the retarget is not the identity (BEAR 25, elf 19). Full suite 22 of 22 green.

THERE IS NO CLIP TRAILER. The residual both earlier models absorbed is 24 * numUnknowns, so the "unknown" track element is 40 bytes -- 4 of time plus a 36-byte payload -- and nothing follows the record. implied = 52 + 16nt + 20nq + 40nu reconciles ZERO SLACK on every record of every decodable clip, including all 46 records of WOLF_ATTACK_BH_A where no constant can. HOW IT HID TWICE, which is the transferable part. 05-02 sampled three clips whose records all carried nu=2; 24*2 = 48, which reads exactly like a fixed trailer. Row 764 found entries with nu=3, read 24*3 = 72, and concluded the trailer was BIMODAL -- still a constant, just two of them. Both models fit every entry whose nu never varies, which is nearly all of them. Only a clip whose nu VARIES between records can tell the difference, and row 764 had already refused those as "internally inconsistent" -- the WOLF family, 46 records across 17 apparent widths, was the one shape telling the truth and was discarded as noise. The error was never in the algebra, it was that every confirming entry had a constant nu. RESULT: decodable motion entries 2738 -> 2750, and 4 of 6 WOLF clips decode where 0 did (IDLE_BH, ATTACK_BH_A, RUN_BH, WALK_BH). WOLF_DYING_A and WOLF_HIT_A remain refused -- they are single-record entries, a different shape. 671 entries still refuse and are NOT a size problem: the +12 gain shows almost all of them fail the unit-quaternion check or another gate, which is the next question and is untouched here. CONTENT NOT CLAIMED. 9 floats is the shape of Granny scale-shear 3x3 and that was the working guess; read as a matrix the values are degenerate (WOLF_ATTACK_BH_A gives determinants near zero and NEGATIVE, which no scale-shear has). I had already written that guess into clip_layout_check as a determinant assertion -- it failed, and the assertion was REMOVED rather than loosened, because it asserted a meaning I never measured. The 36 bytes are handed back as raw floats, uninterpreted, and nothing consumes them. WOLF NOT FIXED ON SCREEN. The wolf now animates -- its animated-vs-noanim diff goes from 0x0 (a silently static mesh) to 221x211 -- but the rendered result is a sprawling distorted mass, not a wolf. So this row fixes the DECODE and does not fix the RENDER, and the wolf joins WALDELFE_DARK as a mesh whose clip binds without producing a correct pose. BEAR remains the only visually confirmed case. clip_trailer_check.gd is renamed clip_layout_check.gd; the rename is the finding. Its discriminating case is WOLF_ATTACK_BH_A precisely because a reintroduced constant fails there first. Full suite 22 of 22 green.

RETRACTION OF ROW 767S RENDER CLAIM. Row 767 stated "the rendered result is a sprawling distorted mass, not a wolf" and that the wolf "joins WALDELFE_DARK as a mesh whose clip binds without producing a correct pose". THAT IS WRONG and is withdrawn. Framed on its own diff bbox (260x250+606+237 instead of the 160x200+690+310 window used for the bear) the animated wolf is a coherent quadruped: head upper-left, body, legs, tail sweeping right. Nothing is collapsed. THE ARTEFACT WAS THE INSTRUMENT, not the renderer. The crop window was centred where BEAR spawns; --creatures scatters each creature to its own cell under CREATURE_SEED and the wolf mesh is substantially larger, so both the animated and the unanimated wolf captures were clipped by that window and I read the surviving fragment as distortion. The unanimated control was clipped identically, which should have been the tell -- a defect that shows up equally with animation OFF cannot be caused by animation, and I had that image in hand before making the claim. NOTHING WAS CHANGED IN THE CODE FOR THIS ROW. The wolf needed no render fix; row 767s decode fix (40-byte unknown track, no trailer) was sufficient and the wolf animates correctly. STANDING AND UNRESOLVED: whether the specific pose suits an IDLE clip is not established -- the wolf reads as leaping rather than standing -- but that is a clip-selection question, not a collapse, and Rigs picks by bone geometry. WALDELFE_DARK is likewise NOT re-confirmed as broken by this row; row 766 already declined to call it either way and its framing was the same bear-centred window, so that capture is suspect for the same reason and should be re-taken on its own bbox before any claim is made about it.
