wpmod-blk2-is-a-hyphen-separated-min-max-range-and-blk4-blk5-are-positional-with-no-tag-name | wpmod.bin's blk[2] is not two independent u16 fields but one RANGE written min-max in the source: the parser strchr's a hyphen, strtol's the part before it into BOTH halves, and only then overwrites the high half from the part after, so a bare number yields min == max. The file bears it out with no exception - min <= max in 1010 of 1010 blocks, zero violations, and min == max in exactly the 242 bare-number cases. Ranges run min 0..60 and max 0..90 and are scaled per bonus: VW spans 3..60 / 9..90, PD physical damage 2..30 / 5..50, GS 2..9 / 5..19. blk[4] and blk[5] have NO tag name at all - they are positional, the number following the class-spell group in a Spell: line and the number following the skill name in a Skill: line, each falling back to its default when absent, which is why 942 and 896 blocks carry 20 and 10. Their observed values are blk[4] in {12,15,17,18,20,25,30} and blk[5] in {10,11,12,14,15,20,22,25,27,30}. What any of these magnitudes is DENOMINATED in stays unknown: no tag names a unit and scripts\waffenmod.txt is not shipped, so that question cannot be closed from this install.

wpmod-is-wired-into-the-engine-and-the-tagged-union-is-what-the-gate-pins | bin/wpmod.bin now has a production reader, engine/formats/wpmod.gd, exposed as Sacred.Wpmod and gated by engine/checks/wpmod_check.gd. The reader parses the 54 + 6*fixed[53] length rule and refuses to report found unless it consumes the file exactly, since a mis-parsed block count would eat the next record's fixed part and still yield a plausible table. Its public view is modifiers(record), which returns each block already resolved through the TAGGED UNION - kind, id, skill, chance, resist, conditioning attribute, group, magnitude and spread - so a caller cannot read the magnitude from the wrong slot; raw_blocks() exposes the undecoded slots for the gate alone. The gate asserts records=572, blocks=1010, 1508 distinct items of which 1508/1508 name a .GRN, resist=151 with every flagged id in 801..808, 68 Spell magnitude overrides, 114 Skill magnitude overrides, min<=max in 1010/1010, EWT -1..32, MinLev ceiling 90, and the three cosmetic records that grant nothing. Falsifiability demonstrated rather than asserted: swapping B_SPELL and B_SKILL fires 988 assertions and exits 1, which is the silent-rot failure the per-block union invariants exist to catch. All 28 gates re-run, 27 green; pax_check's exit 1 is the standing $SACRED_CHARS dependency and is unchanged. One correction to my own work: the Fernkampf spot check first flagged three BOW_LONG entries, which was the CHECK being wrong about what counts as a ranged weapon, not the data.

wea-bin-and-sets-bin-are-wired-into-the-engine-with-their-decodes-as-the-gates | Two more loose bin/ tables now have production readers. engine/formats/equipment.gd reads bin/wea.bin as Sacred.Equipment: 256 groups of u32 n followed by n items.pak record ids, laid end to end with NO header of any kind, and since there is no magic, version or count the exact consumption of 1162 of 1162 int32 IS the decode - a wrong reading desynchronises on the first group. 114 pools carry members, 142 are empty, 906 member slots span only 265 distinct records. That last figure is a semantic fact the gate pins deliberately: the repeats are a WEIGHTED draw, the same shape sndprofiles.pak uses when it pads a short bank, so a caller that deduplicates changes the odds and equipment_check asserts members > distinct to catch exactly that regression. The reader does not validate members against items.pak, so a 4.6 KB table does not cost every caller a 4.5 MB items.pak load; that corroboration - 906 of 906 naming a .GRN - lives in the gate instead. engine/formats/sets.gd reads bin/sets.bin as Sacred.Sets and keeps the file's own 1-based numbering, because field 11 encodes the index and a reader that renumbers must remember to shift it back on every comparison.

sets-bin-self-index-field-is-a-load-time-check-and-the-name-column-carries-its-own-control | sets.bin has two independent proofs of layout and the reader uses both. 4 + 66*112 is the file exactly, which fixes the stride; and field 11 equals (index << 8) | member_count for 65 of 65, which ties each record to its OWN POSITION. The second is the one that matters, because a stride slipped by a whole record still satisfies the first and would quietly return a neighbour's set - so Sacred.Sets asserts it on load and refuses to report found otherwise. Record 0 is recognised by its 0xCCCCCCCC filler pattern rather than skipped by index, so a future file that fills the slot is read instead of dropped. The name column is checked with a control built into the gate: field 10 is negative because it is ALREADY HASHED, all 65 resolve through Resources.by_id, and reading the same bits as a plain id must resolve strictly fewer - if both resolved 65 times the test would not discriminate. Mutating F_NAME from 10 to 11 makes the key non-negative on all 65 records and fires 65 failures, which is the demonstration rather than the claim. One honest limit recorded in the reader: only 114 of the 378 members name a .GRN, because many members sit on items.pak records with no name at all, so an empty name is a property of items.pak and not a bad member. All 30 gates re-run, 29 green; pax_check's exit 1 is its standing $SACRED_CHARS dependency.

vectoren.bin section 2 in the gladiator tree lists 603 quests whose five hook slots resolve into 475,345 bytes of funkcode.bin bytecode across 14,017 records, and an opcode histogram over exactly those records shows 53 distinct opcodes of which 21 cover 98.1% -- op 53 (26.3%), 67, 63, 3, 23, 76, 1, 86, 58, 22, 59, 66, 132, 62, 5, 46, 68, 64, 4, 75, 8. This resizes the quest question: the 141-entry dispatch table and its 96 unnamed opcodes are the FORMAT's open question, but a port that wants quest logic to run needs the 21-opcode head of this distribution, of which nine already carry names recovered from the handlers (CreateNPC 1, CreateOBJ 8, Teleport 46, IsNotVarBit 58, QuestkompassPos 63, QuestkompassOBJ 64, atmo_rg 67/75/76) and one more is known from startcode.bin (23, named position). The tail is long and cheap to ignore because an opcode with no case in retail's own dispatcher is silently skipped by its length field, so an unimplemented opcode is a no-op in the port exactly as it is in retail.

The quest every shipped questcode.bin seeds -- 1101, 'Sektenpriester opfern Jungfrauen' -- was walked end to end: OnEnter is 910 bytes and 19 records that spawn ten priests by name at pos_Priester1..10 with two alternating patrol symbols, create a ritual object, place a victim at pos_Steinkreis, set the quest compass to Res:17112, write three log lines (Res:R11aNQ01_Log_Title/_Header/_Qstart), start a timer Zeitum1101 and set flag auftrag11a1; OnExit is three records (speech res:17643, atmosphere atmos_rg11a, flag befriedet_rg110) and OnLose is one (speech res:17656). Trigger is zero bytes, so entry is driven from outside the quest. Nothing here is inferred from a fitted layout -- every operand is either a literal string in the record or a res: id resolving through global.res -- which makes this quest, not a synthetic one, the smallest honest target for a first end-to-end quest in the port.

script-opcode-names-come-from-the-compilers-own-keyword-tables-not-from-handler-strings | 120 of the 141 script opcodes now carry retail's own name for them. The binary ships two keyword tables -- 61 entries at file 0x69b240/0x69b334 and 60 at 0x69b750/0x69b840 -- each a run of name strings followed by a pointer array and then a PARALLEL u32 opcode array whose slot 0 is a zero sentinel, so pairing pointer i with number i+1 gives name->opcode directly. The control is that seven opcodes had already been named by unrelated routes (handler .rodata, and two reached within two calls) and all seven agree: 1 CreateNPC, 8 CreateObj, 17 AddExp, 46 Teleport, 63 QuestKompassPos, 64 QuestKompassObj, 121 AutoSave. It also REFUTES three earlier entries: opcodes 67, 75 and 76 were listed as atmo_rg from their operand payloads and are actually SetVar, IncVar and DecVar -- naming an opcode by a frequent operand string is the failure mode this table removes. 21 opcodes remain unnamed (0, 27-34, 39-44, 47, 101, 102, 111, 122, 123), two contiguous runs plus four strays, so the tables omit a group rather than scattering it. Artifact: research/formats/generated/script-opcode-names.tsv. A name is not a behaviour -- what each opcode does to the world is still unmeasured.

every-character-class-has-exactly-one-startposition-record-and-the-seraphim-starts-at-3236-2511 | Opcode 45 is StartPosition, and each bin/type_npc_*/startcode.bin carries exactly ONE such record -- the per-class new-game spawn, which is why the classes begin in different regions. Base trees: seraphim (3236,2511) layer 1 sector 50,39; magician (3292,2508) 51,39; darkelve (3442,2698) and elve (3440,2703) 53,42; zwerg (3470,2779) 54,43; vampirelady (3500,2477) layer 2 54,38; daemonin (352,1722) 5,26; gladiator and netscriptcamp (3790,349) 59,5. All ten addon/ trees instead share a single Underworld start at (6265,3864) sector 97,60, consistent with nine of ten addon trees being byte-identical. The seraphim cell was then driven through the port itself: godot --headless --spawn=3236,2511 --autoplay=120 spawns, streams and derives a breadth-first goal at (3227,2632) 121 cells away, so the cell sits on a large connected walkable component rather than in a pocket.

hero-body-meshes-are-whole-body-rigs-and-models-pak-carries-seven-of-the-eight-classes | models.pak names each playable class's body as a short underscore-free mesh entry -- SERAPHIM.GRN 661, GLADIATOR.GRN 589, MAGICIAN.GRN 639, WALDELFE.GRN 403, DUNKELELVE.GRN 402, DWARF.GRN 722, DAEMONIA.GRN 519 -- all kind 64, sitting beside long-named families like SERAPHIM_LEATHER_02.GRN and SERA_BLACK_BODY.GRN which are ARMOUR worn over one rather than alternative bodies. The eighth base class has NO rig under any spelling searched (VAMP, LADY, SUCCU, NOSFE, DRACUL, WEREW, plus a scan of every underscore-free mesh name): type_npc_vampirelady is an Underworld class and its mesh is evidently not in this pak, so main.gd's class->model map is left with a hole and warns rather than guessing, since a wrong guess draws the wrong body silently. SERAPHIM.GRN was then built through the port's own PlayerView at index 661, 1421 vertices and 2054 triangles, and it is the rig the default run now draws because START_CLASS selects both the spawn cell and the body from one constant.

armour-binds-by-bone-name-but-bone-names-do-not-discriminate-the-wearer | A skinned garment can be put on a body by remapping its skin's binds onto the wearer's skeleton by bone NAME, and for Uriel's Legacy that join is total: the seven pieces carry 75-77 bones against SERAPHIM.GRN's 72, but every extra one is an unweighted locator (Angel_armor_Breast, Bip01 Ponytail1, the two Spot*.Target light aims) and the count of bones that are WEIGHTED and absent from the body is zero across all seven. The name test nevertheless discriminates NOTHING, which the control showed: offered the same seven garments, GLADIATOR.GRN bound 5 and refused 2, exactly SERAPHIM.GRN's own score, because every humanoid shares the Bip01 biped names. The instrument that does separate is R1.4's local one -- a bind bone's own rest transform in the garment against the same-named bone's rest in the body, chain never composed: SERAPHIM agrees on 1/1, 1/15, 5/7, 3/5 and 2/7 bind bones while GLADIATOR and DWARF agree on ZERO of every piece. Admission is therefore 'at least one bind bone agrees', weak-looking and totally separating on what has been measured; the own-rates are low and uneven because a garment poses fingers and extremities freely, so a per-bone fit score would be a better rule and needs a wider measurement to set a cut on. This matters because rust.bin exists precisely to say which mesh an armour becomes for a different wearer, so binding one to the wrong body is a real error rather than a curiosity.

Of 1571 rigged models.pak entries, 971 declare vertex weights and 240 of those -- 24.72% -- fail to decode, so composition can dress a character in only part of an outfit. The failure is not in the weight stream, which parses and consumes its span exactly; it is in the PAIRING RULE that maps a mesh's local bone indices to global bones, which searches the FormMeshBone lists for one whose length equals highest+1 and refuses unless exactly one matches. Both failure modes appear in one item set: SERABOOTS01.GRN finds 0 lists of the needed length and SERASHOULDER01.GRN finds 2. The failures are concentrated in armour -- DAEMONIA_ARMOR01_BODY, _SHOES, _SHOULDER, DAEM_SA1_ARMS and so on -- and 9 are SERA*. Separately, two of the seven class body meshes do not build at all under the current mesh decoder, DUNKELELVE.GRN and MAGICIAN.GRN, which are correctly NAMED, so the map is right and the renderer is short. Since the length search is a heuristic rather than something read off the interpreter, the likely correct rule is positional -- the i-th mesh pairs with the i-th list, which the existing code already half-assumes by consuming lists as it goes -- but that needs evidence before it replaces a rule that at least refuses loudly.

formmeshbone-pairing-is-a-perfect-matching-under-fits-inside-not-an-equality-search | The rule mapping a mesh's local bone indices to global bones was searching the entry's FormMeshBone lists for one whose length EQUALS highest+1 and refusing unless exactly one matched, which failed 24.72% of the 971 weight-declaring models.pak entries. Two structural facts refute that rule. First, the sections are not children of the Mesh nodes and their order is not mesh order -- DWARF_BLACK_BODY's three meshes need 27, 3 and 12 bones while its sections run 12, 27, 3 -- so neither containment nor position answers the question and plain positional pairing, measured, gains 171 entries but LOSES 87. Second, equality is the wrong constraint: a mesh may use a PREFIX of its list, which is exactly what SERABOOTS01 does with two meshes needing 4 against two lists of 5. Replacing it with a perfect matching under `len(list) >= highest+1`, accepted only when every valid matching hands each mesh the same list, decodes 802 against the old 736; both rules succeed on 736 and AGREE on all 736 with zero disagreements and zero regressions, so it is a strict generalisation rather than a different answer. The residual 169 are genuinely ambiguous on counts alone and refusing them is correct rather than conservative: they are LEFT/RIGHT SYMMETRIC pieces whose two lists are the same size but different bones -- SERABOOTS01's sections are [6,7,8,5,12] and [10,11,12,9,8], one leg each, and SERASHOULDER01's are [6,8,7,9] and [6,10,7,11] -- so a coin-flip would bind one boot to the opposite leg. The next lever is geometric, scoring each candidate matching by the distance from a mesh's vertices to its assigned bones' rest positions, with the 736 already-decided entries as the control.

quest-74-is-the-smallest-real-quest-a-four-opcode-interpreter-can-run-end-to-end | Choosing a quest to run was done by measurement rather than taste: over all 601 quests in the Seraphim tree, counting how many opcodes each needs beyond a state-and-log core, ZERO need none and exactly two need only one -- 65 and 74. Quest 74 'Kampf gegen den Damon' is 178 bytes across two hooks and uses four opcodes, SetQuestInfo, QuestBook, SetVarBit and AutoSave; its OnEnter writes three quest-book lines and its OnExit writes a fourth, sets state 3 and requests an autosave. QuestBook's shape reads (i32 quest id, i32 kind, string res key) with kind 0 on the title line and 1 on every other, and SetVarBit reads (string name, i32 value) where the name is the quest id AS A DECIMAL STRING. Two facts that a single quest would have hidden: quest 74's OnEnter writes NO state variable at all -- only OnExit does -- while quest 65 writes 1 on entry and 3 on exit, so the corpus is not self-consistent and 'has this quest started' is not answerable from the bytecode; and every Trigger hook in the corpus is ZERO BYTES, so entry and exit are driven from outside the quest by something not yet identified. The four Res: keys the log lines name (HQ_7_4_1_Log_Title, _Header, _Qstart and HQ_Log_Qend) appear in funkcode.bin and in NO other file in the install, so 0 of 4 resolve through global.res -- the same gap as the 389 symbolic credits keys.

an-interpreter-must-refuse-unimplemented-opcodes-rather-than-skip-them-like-retail-does | Retail's script dispatcher default case is `mov ecx,1; ret`, so an opcode with no handler is skipped by its length field, and copying that behaviour into a port looks like the faithful choice. It is not, and the reason is opcode 58 IF: retail skipping an opcode it never implemented leaves behaviour it never had, whereas a port skipping IF runs the guarded body UNCONDITIONALLY, which is different behaviour rather than less. So ScriptVM refuses any hook containing an opcode outside its implemented set, before executing any of it, and the refusal is all-or-nothing. Measured over the Seraphim tree's OnEnter hooks with four opcodes implemented, 481 of 496 non-empty hooks are refused and 15 run; the gate asserts both that refused hooks execute nothing and that refused hooks write no quest-book lines, because an interpreter that silently skipped unknown records would pass a 'the quest ran' assertion identically. An empty hook is NOT a refusal: every Trigger in the corpus is zero bytes and must run vacuously or no quest could ever be entered.

every-piece-of-script-prose-is-in-a-symbolic-namespace-this-install-does-not-carry | Quest-log lines and NPC dialogue are both unreachable, and the measurement is total rather than partial. Across the Seraphim tree's funkcode.bin there are 3377 distinct `Res:` operands, 728 numeric and 2435 symbolic, and ZERO of the 2435 resolve through global.res under any rule tried -- bare, with the Res:/res: prefix retained, lowercased, or with underscores stripped. Opcode 53 QuestBook carries 3676 operands across all 601 quests of which NONE is numeric, and opcode 26 Text -- the actual dialogue line -- carries 3367 symbolic operands of which 0 resolve, plus 33 that are COMPUTED at runtime (`NOVIZIN_0+Var(Zufallsdialog)`, `STEIN_000+Var(SNr)`) and so could not be a static key even if the namespace existed. The control that makes this absence rather than a broken hash: the name namespace is real and populated, since 64 of the 728 numeric keys also resolve when read as names, and set names from sets.bin resolve 65 of 65 by the same pre-hashed route. The keys appear in funkcode.bin and in no other file in the install, the executable included. This is the 389-credits-key question at full size, and it means a port reading this install can show NPC names (numeric res:N, 1377 of 1521) and German quest titles (plain text in vectoren.bin) but cannot show a single quest-log line or line of dialogue.

a-dialogue-resolution-rate-of-3506-of-3506-was-hollow-it-counted-button-labels | A first pass reported that 3506 of 3506 numeric `Res:` operands inside `Dialog:` procedures resolve to English text and concluded dialogue was available. That was wrong and the error is worth keeping: the regex scraped every res: operand in the procedure body rather than the dialogue LINE, so it was counting `SetButton res:1024` -- a UI button -- and reporting its text as the dialogue. Decoding `Dialog:NPC_Dialog_Novizin` record by record instead shows the shape: RndVar picks a variant, IF/ELSE branches on `NPCgeklickt`, and the line itself is opcode 26 `Text` with the operand `NOVIZIN_0+Var(Zufallsdialog)`, while the only resolvable operand in the whole procedure is the OK button's label. Slot 1024 really does hold 'Burn, hellcat!' -- verified through the engine's own Resources reader, which also returns the documented slots 0 Seraphim, 1 Gladiator and 18101 Settler -- so the reader was right and the metric was measuring the wrong operand. The lesson is the one row 720 already recorded in another form: a rate is hollow until it names WHICH field it measured.

per-creature-combat-stats-are-not-in-balance-bin-and-creature-pak-has-80-unread-bytes | balance.bin was checked as the source of the AT, PA and level values the recovered to-hit formula needs and it does not carry them: its 361 keys are global tuning -- GoldProLevel, RunenProLevel_S, DropRuestung, LevelUpBoss, MinLevelFactor -- with nothing per-creature. creature.pak is the remaining candidate and is 86 bytes per record of which the engine reads six, the id at +0x00 and the class at +0x04. A column census over its 474 records finds structure in the other 80: +0x08 and +0x0a are a pair related by roughly a factor of two (exactly 2x in 202 of 397 nonzero records, within one in 267, i.e. 67.3%, against controls of 0.0% for +0x0c/+0x0e and 1.1% for +0x26/+0x28 under the same test), and +0x26/+0x28 are an ordered pair with +0x26 <= +0x28 in 472 of 474 whose values are round numbers drawn from 19 and 20 distinct levels. NEITHER IS DECODED and 67% is a lead rather than a rule; recorded so the next attempt starts from the columns that carry structure rather than from a fresh census.

All 86 bytes of a creature.pak record are now accounted for, transcribed from the function that writes SCRIPTS\CREATURE.TXT back out (sub_8150646) rather than fitted to the data. Its own header comments are the documentation: '// CLASS: 0=UNK 1=HERO 2=MONSTER 3=NPC', '// EXP: <a>, <b> exp = A+level*B', '// BASE: <STK>, <RES>, <GES>, <REPHY>, <REMAG>, <CHARISMA>'. Map: +0x00 u32 id (also the items.pak record naming the mesh), +0x04 u8 class, +0x06 u8 FLAGS (01 FLY, 02 BIG, 10 NOSHADOW, 20 GHOST, 40 BANANE, 80 KURVE), +0x08/+0x0a u16 EXP a and b, +0x0c six u8 BASE attributes, +0x14 two u8 SKILLS and +0x16 sixteen u8 SKILLSX indexing skill-families.tsv, +0x26/+0x28 u16 SPEED pair, +0x2a six {u8 kind, u8 target} BONUS pairs, +0x36 six u8 bonus values, +0x3c six u8 bonus CLASS FILTER, and +0x42 four five-byte Damping blocks named RP, RF, RM and RG -- 0x51+5 = 86 exactly. The structural proof is the FLAGS byte: across all 474 records ZERO bits are set outside the six the writer names, which a wrong offset does not produce, and mutation-testing the offset from 6 to 7 collapses it to 0 of 474 flagged records. An outside table (Creature.pak.txt, SacredModdingStuff1.zip) had described about 60 of the 86 bytes and this reproduces every field it names while accounting for the 26 it left blank, so the new part rides on independent agreement about the old. Ranges corroborate: STK 2..80, GES 5..70, REPHY 1..80, SPEED ordered a<=b in 472 of 474, damping present on only 11 to 13 records per block.

a-creature-mesh-name-is-not-a-key-two-ghoul-records-differ-in-every-stat | GHUL.GRN is named by TWO creature.pak records, ids 36 and 50, and they are not duplicates: base attributes 35,35,25,40,0,50 against 33,34,24,43,0,50, experience terms (25,50) against (52,48), speed (50,50) against (80,80). A reader that looks a creature up by its mesh silently gets whichever record it meets first, and which one is correct depends on what placed the creature -- the encounter at monster107 is body id 50, so reading the table by name would give it the wrong numbers. This is the same shape as rust.bin's filename ambiguity (109 of 284 names span several armour groups) and as the FormMeshBone left/right pairing: the human-readable label is not the identity. Sacred.Creatures is therefore addressed by id only, and checks/creature_check.gd pins both that two records name this mesh and that their attributes differ, so a future dedupe that collapsed them would fail rather than quietly pick one.

no-attribute-becomes-at-or-pa-both-ratings-accumulate-from-skill-levels | The question 'which base attribute becomes the attack rating and which the defence rating' has no answer because neither is built from an attribute. sub_81F596E, the creature stat builder, dispatches on skill TYPE through the jump table at 0x81F5A94 and for each skill the creature carries feeds that skill's LEVEL -- the u16 at +2 of the skill entry, the type being at +0 -- into one shared curve twice, once per balance.bin triplet belonging to the skill's family. Case 8 is Agility, family W, and computes AW from WoffAW/W__sAW/W__wAW and VW from WoffVW/W__sVW/W__wVW off the same level; case 3 is Long-handled Weapons, family STK, and computes AW then SP, so the second output's meaning is per-family rather than fixed. The shared curve is sub_81F55B0 verbatim: `if S < 1 return 0; v = (1 - 1/((S-1)/s + 1)) * (w - off); return off + 2v`, a saturating function of the skill level with f(1) = off, f(1+s) = off + (w-off), and a ceiling of off + 2(w-off) it never reaches. An untrained skill contributes ZERO rather than off, which is a floor and not a clamp. WHICH SKILLS: ten balance families carry an AW triplet -- STK Long-handled Weapons, SK Sword Lore, AK Axe Lore, KK Blade Combat, FK Unarmed Combat, BK Dual Wielding, FEK Ranged Combat, W Agility, HR Constitution, and WT which no skill maps to -- while EXACTLY TWO carry a VW triplet, W Agility and HP Constitution. So defence comes from Agility and Constitution and from nothing else. VWFakBoss 2.0 and VWFakChamp 1.5 multiply the defence rating; what marks a creature boss or champion is not recovered.

creature-pak-carries-skill-types-but-no-skill-levels-so-a-monsters-ratings-need-its-level | The rating curve consumes a skill LEVEL and creature.pak carries skill TYPES only -- two at +0x14 and sixteen more at +0x16, indexing the same enum as research/formats/generated/skill-families.tsv, with no level beside them. So a monster's attack and defence ratings cannot be computed from creature.pak alone: something must supply the level at which it knows its skills, and the obvious candidate is the creature's own level, which is set where it spawns rather than in this table. That is stated as the open link rather than assumed, because assuming skill level equals creature level would silently fix a number the file does not contain. What IS now computable without it: the ten AW and two VW families and their triplets are read from balance.bin at the offsets the key map names (W: AW 7/50/125, VW 13/50/225 -- verified against the key map and mutation-tested by shifting the offset one slot), and the curve itself is implemented and gated on its algebraic identities rather than on a rate.

creature-level-comes-from-a-per-sector-band-declared-by-opcode-100-spawnvalues | Opcode 100 is SpawnValues and carries three int32: the first is 50 in all 11,498 records of the Seraphim tree and is not a level, and the other two are an ORDERED BAND -- lo <= hi in 11,498 of 11,498, against a control of 0.00% for the same test on the first pair, so the ordering belongs to that pair rather than to the record. 49 distinct bands, lo in 1..45, hi in 4..80, spans 3..35. The band is GEOGRAPHIC, which is what makes it a LEVEL band rather than a percentage or a weight: every Sector<cx><cyyy>Init and ...Enter procedure in vectoren.bin owns a funkcode span and the SpawnValues records inside it belong to that sector, and reading them out puts the Seraphim's own StartPosition sector 50,39 on (1,4) -- the lowest band in the game -- along with the magician's 51,39, both elves' 53,42, the dwarf's 54,43 and the gladiator's 59,5. SEVEN OF NINE class starts land on the lowest band, which a number that was not a level would not do. The counter-example keeps it honest: the Daemoness starts at 5,26 on (45,80) and the Underworld start 97,60 is (30,50), so the claim is not 'every start is low' but 'each start sits where its class begins', and only 22% of banded sectors are (1,4) so five hits is not chance. 5666 sectors carry a band, of which 60 declare MORE THAN ONE and nothing says what chooses between them. What is still not recovered: how a level is drawn from the band, and whether that number is also the level at which the creature's skills are known -- both are needed before the ratings of row 951 can be computed.

global-res-symbolic-namespace-resolves-after-fixing-the-int32-wrap-in-the-name-hash | The standing finding that the symbolic Res: namespace 'is not in this install' -- 0 of 2435 keys resolving, so no quest-log line or line of dialogue could ever be shown -- is REFUTED, and the cause was our own arithmetic. The hash was transcribed correctly as h = (h*0x71 + toupper(c)) % 999999991 but reimplemented in 64-bit GDScript, while retail's sub_80ACC3E runs it in int32: 113*v passes 2^32 from the FIFTH character on and wraps, and the modulo is x86 idiv, whose remainder takes the dividend's sign so v goes negative between iterations. The two implementations agree for exactly four characters and diverge after, which is why every numeric key in the shipped files (3-5 digits) resolved and looked like proof while every symbolic key, all of them longer, silently missed -- and why the old gate, whose every hashed name was '9400'-shaped, was green throughout. With the wrap in place: UI_QUICKSAVE resolves to 'Quicksave', INVENTAR_RES_PHYSICAL to 'Physical Resistance', DQ_BAUER_BEGRUESSUNG_LOG to 'The peasants need my help.', and 319 of the 1242 static QuestBook keys across the eight class trees come back as English quest-log prose against 0 before. The 144 res:D1Dorf_01..18 NPC references previously written off as dangling references retail could not resolve either are a village roster -- Smith, Healer, Bartender, Witch and 14 Peasants -- so NPC name resolution goes from 1377 of 1521 to 1521 of 1521. The remaining QuestBook keys are runtime-composed (DQ_BRINGE_ITEM+Var(DQ_2604)+_LOG) and instantiate correctly once the variable is substituted: DQ_BRINGE_ITEM2_LOGTITLE is 'The Fathers Sword.'. Two further corrections fall out: the file has no SZ magic at all -- the first u32 is the ENTRY COUNT, and 23123 == 0x00005A53 by coincidence, so the old check only passed on a file of exactly this size -- and the index is exactly 4 + count*16 bytes, which is now asserted structurally. checks/resources_check.gd carries the mutation control: the naive 64-bit hash must AGREE with retail's at four characters and MISS the table at twelve, so removing the wrap fails the gate rather than silently reverting the finding.

templates-hero0n-ptx-are-retails-new-game-characters-and-charactertype-is-the-class-enum | install/templates/hero00.ptx..hero07.ptx are .pax hero saves in all but extension -- same AMH\x1b magic, same 16-slot section table -- and retail does not parse them: cUI_Character::executeAction copies the chosen one 512 bytes at a time straight into Save/HeroNN.pax (the fread/fwrite loop at 0x853FA45), so a template IS a savegame. Reading the 0xC7 character stream gives the character each class starts with, which the port had been inventing: every class begins at LEVEL 1 with 5000 gold, zero experience, exactly TWO skills at level 1, and six u16 base attributes at +0x3E5 in creature.pak's own STK/RES/GES/REPHY/REMAG/CHARISMA order, duplicated byte-identically at +0x41F. CharacterType at +0x3DD is a ONE-BASED index into the class-name list, established twice independently: global.res slot N-1 names it, and the executable's own GetTypeName table (sub_815B3A2 over 5624 68-byte records at 0x8735AC0) gives the same order -- 1 SERAPHIM, 2 GLADIATOR, 3 MAGICIAN, 4 DARKELVE, 5 ELVE, 6 VAMPIRELADY, 7 VAMPN_DO_NOT_USE, 8 ZWERG, 9 DAEMONIN -- and it is that table which supplies the bin/type_npc_* directory name at runtime, since no lowercase tree name exists as a string in the binary. Type 7 is absent from the templates because sub_8265BF6 opens with if (charType == 7) charType = 6. Each identification is corroborated by the character itself rather than by the ordering: the Vampiress is the only class with the Vampirism skill, the Gladiator has the highest STK and REMAG exactly 0, the Battle Mage the highest REMAG, the Wood Elf the highest GES and the Agility skill, the Dwarf the lowest CHARISMA. So the Seraphim is CharacterType 1, hero01.ptx, and the MVP's hero level is now read rather than chosen. This also retires a permanently-red gate: pax_check demanded $SACRED_CHARS, a third-party corpus absent from every machine without one, while the install shipped eight subjects of its own all along.

the-per-sector-level-band-clamps-the-heros-level-rather-than-being-sampled-from | Row 953 established that a creature's level comes from the per-sector band declared by opcode 100 SpawnValues(50, lo, hi). How the level is drawn from that band was left open, and the natural reading -- a uniform sample across lo..hi -- is WRONG. sub_81806DC, called once from the creature spawn path sub_8180B22, transcribes as: level = the hero's own level (in a party, the highest); then if both band bounds are non-zero, lo = DiffLo[difficulty] + band.lo and hi = DiffHi[difficulty] + band.hi, and level is clamped -- below lo it is lifted to lo, above hi it is held at hi, and INSIDE the band it tracks the hero with the only randomness in the whole rule being a single rand()%2 worth +0 or +1. So the band is a clamp on the player's level, not a range to sample, and Sacred's world is level-scaled by construction. The distinction is invisible to any range check -- a uniform draw produces levels inside the same interval -- but it changes the difficulty curve everywhere, so checks/spawnlevel_check.gd asserts each branch separately: a level-3 hero in a 10..20 sector meets exactly level 10 with no randomness, a level-90 hero exactly level 20, and a level-15 hero meets only 15 or 16 across 512 draws with both values actually occurring. A new Seraphim at her own start, band (1,4), therefore meets a level 1 or 2 monster. The two difficulty tables at 0x8B89BA8 and 0x8B89DAC live in the executable rather than in any shipped file and their values are not recovered, so level_for takes them as arguments defaulting to zero rather than silently assuming a difficulty.

Every playable body was built and left standing in its bind pose. ModelView.play_clip is a correct, gated implementation and PlayerView simply had no path to it -- the only call sites were the opt-in --crowd, --grn, --creatures, --npcs, --equip and --figure modes, so the hero of a normal run was a statue, which is the loudest way a screenshot says 'not Sacred'. PlayerView.animate now binds the clip Sacred.Rigs picks for the body and main.gd calls it at both construction sites, with --noanim as the one-variable control in the same shape as --creatures-noanim. Five of the seven mapped class bodies animate; DUNKELELVE.GRN and MAGICIAN.GRN build no rig at all, which is a separate and already-known hole in the model map rather than an animation failure. The new gate checks/hero_anim_check.gd nearly shipped a hollow metric and the correction is the point: its splay measure originally compared each bone's LOCAL posed position against its rest, which is identically zero on every rig because ModelView deliberately drops all translation tracks (BIND_POSITION_TRACKS = false) -- it would have reported a clean 0% for a rig collapsed into a streak. Measured in GLOBAL pose space, where rotation error accumulates down the hierarchy the way the row-765 collapse did, it reads 0-1% of rig extent against the 77% that failure measured, so the bound sits between two regimes that differ by a factor of ten rather than being tuned to pass. The t=0 bind-pose residual is REPORTED and not thresholded: with automatically-picked clips scoring 0.817..1.000 the residual runs 0.033..0.101 rad, and asserting a constant just above the observed range would be fitting the gate to the data it has to survive.

the-creature-level-clamps-two-difficulty-tables-are-balance-bin-keys-offlevel-and-levelkap | Row 956 left the two difficulty adjustments in the level clamp unrecovered, on the reading that they lived in the executable at 0x8B89BA8 and 0x8B89DAC and so were in no shipped file. They are in .bss because sub_812B3E6 slurps the WHOLE of bin/balance.bin into the block at flt_8B89420, and the mapping is mem = 0x8B89420 + (keymap_offset - 4), cross-checked at four independent points. They are the keys OffLevel (file offset 1932) and LevelKap (2448), and both are SIX-ELEMENT int32 ARRAYS whose key-map entries name only their first element -- the gap to the next named key is exactly 24 bytes in both cases (OffLevel to Respawn, LevelKap to ObereEXPAnteil), and the text parser sub_812BA04 splits a `key = a,b,c,d,e,f` line capped at six. Read straight from the file: OffLevel = [0, 35, 70, 128, 0, 0] and LevelKap = [50, 120, 190, 250, 250, 0], added to the band's low and high bounds respectively for Silver, Gold, Platinum and Niob; index 5 is the fallback and is zero-zero, index 4 is dead data no code path selects. They are int32 despite sitting in a float table -- the writers are fistp after strtod with rounding forced to truncate, and a plain store after strtol -- and read as floats they are denormals. The consequence is large and was previously invisible: LevelKap +50 on Silver puts the Seraphim start sector's high bound at 54 rather than 4, so the clamp TRACKS the player for most of a playthrough instead of capping her in the second sector. checks/spawnlevel_check.gd asserts a level-30 hero there meets a level-30 monster with the tables and a level-4 one without, so a build that ignores them fails rather than silently playing a different game.

the-base-attack-and-defence-ratings-are-half-str-plus-dex-and-one-fifth-str-plus-four-fifths-dex | The last invented numbers in the port's combat are recovered. sub_81FA5AA and sub_81FA622 are the attack and defence getters and they are byte-identical in structure: AT = f32[+0x5A] * f32[+0xE6] and PA = f32[+0x5E] * f32[+0xEA], over the stat block at creature+0x3A8. So the multipliers already transcribed are only half of each rating and the BASES at +0x5A and +0x5E are the other half. cCreatureHero::CalcResults (sub_820E04C) is the only writer of either: it zeroes both at 0x820E512 and at 0x8210331 accumulates `base_AT += 0.01*(A*C[0] + B*C[1])` and `base_PA += 0.01*(A*C[3] + B*C[4])` where A and B are the u16 at +0x10 and +0x14 and C is a 64-byte per-class coefficient record at flt_8793720; at 0x820EE2F it adds the equipment aggregate through C[2] and C[5]. EVERY CLASS RECORD IN RETAIL IS IDENTICAL, C = [50, 50, 100, 20, 80, 100], so the per-class table is a lever the shipped game does not pull and the coefficients reduce to base_AT = 0.5*(STR+DEX) + gear and base_PA = 0.2*STR + 0.8*DEX + gear. The two attributes are the FIRST and THIRD of the six u16 at +0x10..+0x1A, which in creature.pak's own order (STK, RES, GES, REPHY, REMAG, CHARISMA) are Strength and Dexterity; the 20/80 split favouring Dexterity on defence is the corroboration rather than the source. One balance.bin key sits on this path: ProzAW at offset 1812, another six-element array [1.0, 1.5, 2.5, 4.5, 1.04, 0.65] confirmed by the 24-byte gap to ProzHP, and the getters apply it only when the creature's type-id exceeds 0x10 -- so it multiplies a monster's ratings by difficulty and never touches the player. The MVP fight is therefore fully derived: a new Seraphim is STK 22 GES 25 so AT 23.5, the Ghoul at monster107 is STK 33 GES 24 so PA 25.8, and at levels 1 against 2 she hits 31 percent of the time. One thing did NOT reproduce: neither the 200x factor nor the 5..95 clamp exists anywhere in the Linux binary, whose display path computes 100*AT/(AT+PA) through the saturating primitive sub_815D44C with w=1.0 and off=0.5, which reduces to exactly AT/(AT+PA); the port keeps the two-binary Windows transcription for the roll and this is recorded as a discrepancy rather than resolved.

music-and-atmosphere-come-from-a-per-sector-environment-record-in-world-sectors-keyx | The standing question of what selects the music and atmosphere profile as the player moves -- open because it is in neither global.res nor bin/*.bin -- is answered, and it is in neither sndprofiles.pak nor a script opcode at runtime. world/sectors.keyx is a 256-byte header followed by 6050 records of 768 bytes, and 256 + 6050*768 = 4646656 is the file length EXACTLY while every record keys to a distinct sector coordinate; a wrong stride gives neither. Each record carries a climate byte at +0x1D8 and a 256-byte cSectorEnvironment at +0x1E9 whose +0xD7 is a region id, +0xEF a SOUND_FX_* music id and +0xF3 a secondary atmosphere id. sub_80DB27C reads them when the player's current sector changes and passes music, region and climate into cMSS::receive_event type 2; the chooser sub_84EADBA then combines music id, climate and the day/night phase into an SOUND_FX_ATMO_* id, which is why climate belongs with the audio fields rather than with terrain -- 32 is desert, 96 ice, 48/64/80 volcano, 16 and 240 dungeon, each with a distinct night variant. Measured over the file: twelve distinct climates, all multiples of 16, and 1892 of 6050 sectors declare music 0 and inherit whatever is playing, which is retail's own `if (env->music)` guard rather than a decode failure. The Seraphim's start sector is climate 64, region 1, music 6560, and its neighbour at the magician's start is identical, while the Underworld start differs in both. sndprofiles.pak is ruled out and is a different system entirely: its only reader picks `tbl[profile].group[slot][rand()%8]`, the per-creature combat sound variation sets. Script opcode 98 SecInfo writes the same fields at authoring time, so the opcode is the source of the data rather than the runtime selector. The gate asserts the gladiator's start STORES 6551, so that the hardcoded override to 6508 that sub_80DB27C applies there is demonstrably a real override rather than a restatement of the file.

The .pax section-to-subsystem map is closed, and one of its findings corrects the port's quest model. The dispatcher is cObjectManager::loadHero (sub_811FB5C) and the key that unlocks it is that types are REMAPPED ON COMPRESSION by an eight-entry pair table at dword_86DA940: 0xC0 becomes 0xC7, 0xC2 becomes 0xC8, 0xC1 becomes 0xCA, 0xC6 becomes 0xCB and 0xCC becomes 0xCD, so the eight observed types are five compressed forms plus three that are never compressed. 0xC7 is the hero cCreature object; 0xCA is the hero's inventory container and 0xCB the shared stash at the hard-coded container index 17, both 4444 bytes because 12+1024+3072+120+200+4+4 is exactly that; 0xC8 is the item objects; 0xC3 is the save-slot preview and 0xC4 a 64-byte statistics block whose declared size of 556 is why retail hard-codes the read length; 0xCD is the map exploration bitmap, and parsing a template confirms 16 + 6051*8 + 6050*128 = 822824 exactly, one 128-byte mask per region rather than a flat world bitmap. 0xCE, the 100-byte section, is THE QUEST VARIABLE BITS -- five difficulty tiers of 160 bits, memcpy'd from cStatsManager+0x5724, and the SetVarBit opcode body calls sub_83A43C2(stats, difficulty, bit, 1) when the variable is named HeroQBit. That is what corrects the port: SetVarBit's second argument is a BIT INDEX, not a value. Measured over the Seraphim tree, 1137 of 1138 records are (string, int) and Teleporter_WP is written 26 times with indices 0..12, one bit per waypoint -- the port's `_var[name] = value` kept only the last one. A quest's state is therefore a MASK: quest 65 sets bit 1 on entry and bit 3 on exit, so a finished quest reads active AND done, a distinction assignment silently discarded while still answering is_done correctly for a linear quest.

the-in-game-hud-layout-is-a-static-sub-rect-table-and-is-now-drawn-from-retails-own-art | The HUD was the largest single thing the port did not draw -- zero lines of Control code against roughly a quarter of a Sacred screenshot -- and the reason it looked unapproachable was the assumption that its layout was spread across hundreds of call sites. It is not. There is a STATIC TABLE of 1887 texture sub-rects at 0x880DC68, stride 84, each `{char name[32]; int handle; float u0,v0,u1,v1; int hx0,hy0,hx1,hy1; int W,H; int id; int type}`, and the loader sub_8501A40 turns the stored inclusive corner into a size, rebases the hot rect to the element's own top-left, and divides the uv by 256 -- every sheet is 256x256. The persistent bar is cUI_Taskbar2 and its layout function is sub_85E85EE. THE CANVAS IS FIXED AT 1024x768: cUI_Manager::createWindows (sub_84FA548) hard-codes every window rect, UI_WND_TASKBAR is {0, 676, 1024, 92}, and no division against a screen-width global appears anywhere on the HUD path, so the interface is authored in a virtual space and scaled rather than re-anchored. The vertical convention is `y = 80 - hy0`, an anchor line at window y 80. Transcribed and now drawn: the console (gfx 12, GUI_main_03 texels (0,169)-(230,255), placed at x = 512 - W/2 = 397), the four taskbar buttons, the collect toggle, the two flanking icons, the five combat-art slots forming an arc whose middle slot centres on x 512 exactly, and the two five-slot 63x63 skill and spell wings at screen y 691. SIZE IS u1-u0 AND NOT u1-u0+1, which is not a rounding preference: the console's placement resolves to its transcribed 397 only for W = 230, and writing every rect one texel too large put the middle art slot one pixel off centre and pushed the collect toggle one row off the bottom of the canvas -- checks/hud_check.gd caught both, which is what asserting the arithmetic relations rather than the literals is for. NOT DRAWN, and recorded as an open question rather than invented: the life and mana gauges. All 46 functions of cUI_Taskbar2 were enumerated and the class references no orb, globe or fill-bar art and computes no fraction or scissor rect; the two orb-looking 95x107 elements in GUI_main_02 belong to the mercenary window. Drawing the most recognisable part of the screen from a guess would be worse than leaving the gap visible.

a-clips-action-is-readable-from-its-name-even-though-its-character-is-not | Sacred.Rigs binds a clip to a mesh by BONE GEOMETRY because the character prefixes do not line up -- `UPI1_WALK_BH.GRN` belongs to `UPIRATE_01.GRN`. That established fact was quietly generalised into treating the whole name as unreliable, and the consequence was that every animated body played whichever clip scored highest, which for several of them is an ATTACK: the hero stood in a meadow swinging a sword on a loop. The ACTION half of the name is a different question and the corpus answers it plainly. Censused over all 3421 motion entries (probes/clipname_probe.gd), 370 distinct underscore-separated tokens are led by ATTACK 989, IDLE 379, RUN 250, WALK 245, DYING 236, DEFEND 234, SPECIAL 225, CAST 203, HIT 154 and FIDLE 133 -- an action vocabulary, not a character one. So the two halves are now decided by the instrument that can answer each: the character geometrically, the action by name. Rigs keeps a per-action best above the same 0.5 geometric threshold, so an action a character has no clip for returns -1 rather than borrowing another character's, and rest_clip() prefers IDLE then FIDLE then WALK. All five buildable class bodies have an IDLE and now play it. One threshold moved as a result and the reason is worth recording: hero_anim_check's `fraction of bones moved` floor was 0.25, taken from the best-scoring clips which measured 35..86%; a real IDLE moves 22..31%. The assertion exists to catch a binder that does NOTHING, and that regime is 0%, so the bound was rebased to 0.10 -- between the two regimes rather than just under the numbers it has to pass.

The port has never turned a character: PlayerView.set_yaw and rig_placement.yaw are built and every call site passes 0.0, because the cell-space-to-yaw convention was never established. Two routes to establish it without inventing a constant were measured and neither settles it, which is worth recording so the next attempt starts from here. FIRST, REFUTED: a locomotion clip's ROOT translation would give the forward axis with no convention assumed. Sacred's clips are IN PLACE. GLAD_WALK_BH's root carries three position keys and nets to EXACTLY zero over the cycle -- it bobs, it does not travel -- and every class body's WALK and RUN behaves the same; only 9 of 67 records net-move at all and those are limbs. The engine moves the body and the clip does not, which is also why ModelView's BIND_POSITION_TRACKS note about lunges playing in place costs less than it sounds. SECOND, INCONCLUSIVE: the rigs are standard 3ds Max Biped, so `Toe0 - Foot` in the model's own global rest space is a forward vector whose SIGN is fixed by anatomy rather than chosen -- the half that a hip-axis cross product cannot settle. Over the seven bodies that resolve the worst pairwise dot is 0.4587, and the results do not scatter, they fall into two families: GLADIATOR, SERAPHIM, WALDELFE and DAEMONIA put forward in XZ with Y near zero, while DUNKELELVE, MAGICIAN and DWARF put it in YZ with X near zero. A toe is both forward of and below its ankle, so a correct reading has a small negative Y and a large horizontal part on EVERY body; half of them put the whole magnitude in Y. That is two authoring frames rather than two facings, most likely the 90-degree-Z alignment bone rigs.gd already names -- 'a mesh carries a 90-degree-Z alignment bone above Bip01 that a clip has no node for at all' -- being present in some chains and not others. So facing stays open deliberately: a single convention picked from these numbers would be right for one family and 90 degrees wrong for the other, and averaging them would be wrong for both.

the-facing-alignment-bone-is-the-net-rotation-above-bip01-and-set-yaw-is-now-wired | Row 964 left facing open with the toe-minus-ankle route inconclusive: the seven class bodies split into two families 90 degrees apart. THE SPLIT IS THE CHAIN ABOVE BIP01, and it is quantised rather than continuous. GLADIATOR, SERAPHIM and WALDELFE run __Root -> Root -> Bip01 where Root spins +90 about the vertical and Bip01 spins -90, netting zero; MAGICIAN and DUNKELELVE have no Root bone at all and DWARF's Root spins 0, so all three net -90; DAEMONIA's Bip01 spins -0.8 and nets ~0. Re-measured in BIP01's own frame the same seven agree at worst pairwise dot 0.9556 against 0.4587 in mesh space, and every forward comes out +X. So they are ONE rig convention differing by one authoring rotation -- which is what licenses using the MESH-space angle as a per-model constant, because that angle already contains the alignment and nothing needs special-casing per family. Measured, the rest facings are exactly 0.0 for the first family and exactly -90.0 for the second: averaging both feet cancels the toe splay completely, so the corrected spread across all seven bodies is 0.0000 degrees against a raw spread of 90.0. THE SECOND HALF, wiring set_yaw, exposed a different error worth recording. The first implementation derived the target angle from the WORLD displacement of a cell step, the same route update() uses for position -- and the four cardinal directions collapsed onto two facings, east and south both reading 'screen right'. The cause is that this world is ALREADY PROJECTED: terrain is built at cell-to-screen coordinates with a depth that exists only to sort (pz = (x+y)*DEPTH_STEP), so a cell step maps to a displacement whose horizontal components are +-HW on screen and a few thousandths of depth, and normalising throws the depth away. The working derivation treats the cell grid as the square ground plane it is and recovers only how the rig's horizontal axes sit against the camera, both read off the node's basis at call time: the rig-horizontal angle whose world image points most directly at the viewer (cell direction 1,1 runs down the screen since screen_y = (cx+cy)*HH, so a character walking it must show its front) and the one pointing along world +X (cell direction 1,-1), whose relative sense fixes the handedness. No constant is chosen in the file. The four cardinals now read E 45, N 135, W -135, S -45 -- distinct, exactly 90 apart, stepping the same way round. checks/facing_check.gd asserts the alignment is quantised to 0 or -90, that it PREDICTS which family a body's facing falls in, that correcting by the rest facing collapses a 90-degree raw spread to 0.0000, and finally that the yaw REACHES THE MESH: driving rig_placement directly and composing the bone chain by hand, the left hand swings 13.06 units between opposite facings while the head -- which sits on the axis of rotation -- drifts 0.11, which is what separates turning from tipping over and is the failure a yaw about the wrong axis would produce. Composing by hand was necessary because Godot only refreshes get_bone_global_pose while the skeleton is processing, and a check has no rendered frame: setting bone 0 to a clean 90 degrees leaves every descendant's reported global pose unchanged even after force_update_all_bone_transforms.

A full audit of the Godot port against the research documents, run with the gate suite and the layer verifier as its floor: 39 of 39 checks pass and parity/verify.gd reports 19 files with 0 layer violations, so nothing the project already asserts is broken. What the assertions do NOT cover came out in five groups. Three defects each draw a WRONG PICTURE SILENTLY, which is the class this project is least able to detect: view/sector_view.gd set the shader's hidden_bucket_count to hidden.size() with no bound against the 64-slot uniform array, so a town with more than 64 registered regions made the fragment loop index past the end of its own array -- and because hidden.sort() favours the earliest-registered region while world/interior.gd never retires one, the roof that got dropped was the building the player had just entered; iso_camera.gd derives its orthographic size from viewport height once, so any window resize left follow_cell snapping to a pixel grid that was no longer the pixel grid, defeating the one thing that class exists to guarantee; and sector_view.gd's object_texture_decodes counter could never leave zero because _image() inserts into the cache before returning and the miss test was asked afterwards, so every swap-apply line in every run has reported a perfect cache that was never measured. Second, three readers had a passing gate and zero production callers -- formats/sectors.gd, formats/equipment.gd and formats/wpmod.gd -- while research/engine/game-wiring.md marked link 6c 'yes', a claim that was true of the reader and false of the running game. Third, five places where the code and the prose contradict each other outright: pak.gd's ALLOWED_MAGIC admits the exact three files (CIF, WPN, MHP) its own docstring exists to exclude; balance.gd calls difficulty index 5 'no adjustment' when ProzAW[5] is 0.65, and difficulty_index() returns 5 as its out-of-range fallback, so an unrecognised difficulty silently weakens monsters by 35 percent rather than leaving them alone; granny-grn.md puts the node-directory count at +16 where models.gd reads +0; hud.gd promises one rectangle set and uses another; and combat-formulas.md calls OffLevel and LevelKap unrecovered when both are in balance.gd and consumed. Fourth, the findings log itself carries four malformed rows (an embedded newline spilling one row into the next, a literal backslash-t collapsing another to one field, a blank line, and a row whose id repeats its predecessor's). Fifth, main.gd at 3473 lines has begun to CAUSE bugs rather than merely host them: two doc blocks 2,950 lines apart contradict each other about a determinism-gate input, a sector key is composed as 32*100+54 in one line and 54*100+32 two lines later, Models.new() is called five times in seventeen lines, and Sacred.find_install() is re-entered inside _build_hud where it writes user://openheilig.cfg as a side effect of drawing the HUD.

The three silent-wrong-picture defects from the port audit are fixed and the sector environment reader is wired into the running game. The shader bucket overflow is closed at both ends: view/sector_view.gd gains HIDDEN_BUCKET_SLOTS := 64 and shaders/object.gdshader a matching #define, because GLSL cannot read a GDScript const and the two can only agree by convention -- so the convention is now named and explained in both files rather than being an unwritten coincidence. The count is clamped with mini(), the uniform array is built once at exactly the slot count instead of per material, and exceeding the slots raises a push_error naming how many regions will draw their roofs, which converts a silent wrong picture into a loud one. iso_camera.gd now connects viewport.size_changed to a handler that re-derives size at the current zoom step; the connect is guarded because _ready runs again on re-parent, and the added set_zoom_index call is render-neutral since main.gd already made the same call during setup. The decode counter now samples the cache BEFORE calling _image() rather than after, and a headless run at sector 50,39 reports decodes climbing 223, 258, 306 across successive swap-apply lines where every prior run reported 0. For the wiring, formats/sectors.gd gains a static sector_of() using floori rather than integer division, because GDScript truncates towards zero and would map both cell -1 and cell +1 to sector 0 -- every in-world cell is positive so the wrong version passes any test built from real cells, which is precisely why checks/sectorenv_check.gd now asserts cell -1,-1 resolves to sector -1,-1 as the control arm that separates the two. main.gd constructs the reader at startup and, per frame, fires the environment lookup on a change of the PLAYER's sector rather than the camera's, since panning the view does not change retail's music; music id 0 inherits whatever is already playing, which is retail's own if (env->music) guard in sub_80DB27C and not a decode failure. The selection half is wired and the playback half deliberately is not, because this port has no audio layer to hand the result to, and that is stated in the code rather than left to be inferred from its absence. Verified after all four changes: 39 of 39 gates pass, parity/verify.gd reports 19 files with 0 layer violations, and the live run prints the start sector's environment with no shader errors.

The four malformed rows found by the port audit (row 966) are repaired, and the repair script's own verifier found a fifth thing the audit had missed. Row 633's paragraph carried an embedded NEWLINE, so its tail became a line of its own -- and that line was padded with three trailing tabs, which is why every field-count check ever run over this file counted 4 and passed it. That is the whole lesson of the row: a corruption that pads itself to the right shape is invisible to the check the schema asks for, so the repair script verifies ids as well as fields. The tail is rejoined with an 'Artifacts:' lead-in, the only words added anywhere in this change. Row 635 had been written with literal backslash-t in place of its three separators, collapsing it to one field; exactly three were present so the row was recoverable unaltered. The row after it carried id 634, smaller than its predecessor's and out of append order, and is renumbered to 636 -- the next free id, cited by no prose in the repo, checked before the edit. One blank line was deleted. Verified after: no duplicate ids, none out of order, no blank lines, and the 35 remaining literal backslash-t sequences are all INSIDE paragraphs quoting tab-separated tool output, which is the escaping the schema requires rather than more of the same bug. What the verifier turned up unasked: rows 661-762, a hundred and two of them, are SIX fields, and rows before 452 use a status tag (VERIFIED, FINDING, REFUTED) where the current schema has a date. The log has three eras, not one, and any tool that parses it as uniformly four-field silently drops or mis-splits a fifth of the file. Those rows are left alone: they are consistent within themselves and rewriting 102 rows of research history is a decision, not a repair. Alongside this, engine/run.sh gives the port a launcher that needs no arguments -- bare to play, --checks to run all 39 gates under a timeout because a failed assert() hangs rather than exits (PASS=39 FAIL=0 in 51s), --layers for parity/verify.gd, and --flags which greps main.gd for the flags it actually parses rather than restating them where they could rot.

The findings log now has ONE schema. It had five: an iteration/binary/metric/runs/status/description table, three tag-led shapes of three, five and six fields, the current id/date/slug/paragraph form, and three rows where raw tab-separated tool output leaked in and split the paragraph into 7, 9 and 10 fields. 492 rows are normalised into the contract and NO TEXT IS LOST -- verified by re-reading both files and asserting every original field's text still appears in its rewritten row, all 964 of them. Extra columns fold into the paragraph in original order joined with ' | '; the status tag leads the paragraph where it is not the slug; a row named only by its tag takes that tag lowercased as its slug, which is a poor slug but a true one where a slug guessed from the prose would be invention. THE DATES ARE THE PART THAT COULD NOT BE RECOVERED and the log says so in its own header: 492 rows never carried one, and the repo's first commit imported the whole file at once, so git blame dates every legacy line to the import rather than to the work -- an inference dressed as a measurement, which is the failure mode this project exists to avoid. Each undated row takes the date its own prose names where that date falls inside the window its neighbours allow, else the nearest dated row above it; 37 came from prose, 492 from a neighbour. The clamp earns its place twice: row 360 quotes Godot's build date, 2026-07-13, a month before anything around it, and two more rows had prose dates that ran backwards against append order. Legacy dates are ORDERING, sound because the file is append-only, not evidence of a day. tools/parity/log_check.py loses its ratchet as a result: it was pinned at 539 non-conforming rows with the contract enforced only from row 661, and now enforces every row from the first, with ids allowed an optional letter suffix because rows 0, 0b, 0c and 0d are a run and three re-runs of it. Gate passes 964 conforming 0 not, and fails on an injected five-field row. The two READMEs that documented the old state are corrected, including research/log/README.md's standing rule that nothing here is rewritten to match a later convention -- which held until a record nothing could parse stopped being much of a record.

Staleness audit of research/ and tools/, and the headline is that the mechanical rot everyone expects is NOT THERE: of 22 path references that fail to resolve, all 22 are deliberate -- retail install paths (world/sectors.keyx), private-workspace paths the log's own README says it cites on purpose (analysis/rtti/, analysis/symbols/), a build artefact (live/altest), and paths inside the Armalion source tree rather than ours. Zero of 84 tracked tools is an orphan: every one is named in a README. __pycache__ is untracked behind an allowlist .gitignore that denies by default. The 105 godot-port/ references in tools/ and engine/ resolve through a live symlink with a SACRED_PORT override, so they are workspace-relative rather than stale. research/builds/ is fully linked. What the audit DID find is in the documents that describe state. Both generated tables that row 970 called un-regeneratable now regenerate byte-for-byte, and one of the two never needed a generator written -- it needed finding. skill-families.tsv is produced verbatim by tools/binary/skillmap.py, which already accepted an output path and already self-checked; row 970 missed it because the search was for the OUTPUT FILENAME inside tools/, and skillmap.py never names the file it writes. Absence of a filename is not absence of a generator, which is the correction worth keeping. It did carry a real bug: ROOT came from abspath(__file__), so run through the private workspace's analysis/tools symlink the link stayed in the path and ROOT landed inside the workspace, making it read a balance-globals.tsv that is not there -- the tool worked from the repo and failed the documented way. realpath fixes it and both invocations now produce the identical file. The genuinely missing one is written: tools/binary/opcode_names.py extracts the script compiler's own keyword tables, two runs of name strings each followed by a pointer array and a parallel u32 opcode array with a zero sentinel, so pointer i pairs with number i+1. Its output is byte-identical to the committed script-opcode-names.tsv: 121 entries, 120 of 141 opcodes named, and the 21 unnamed are exactly the set the document already listed. THE OFFSETS IN script-bytecode.md WERE WRONG -- 0x69b240/0x69b334 and 0x69b750/0x69b840, each low by exactly 0x6d90, which in sacred_orig lands in texture-name strings and item log formats. The extracted table predates the write-up so nothing downstream moved, but the document could not be used to re-derive its own claim, which is what a format document is for. The tables were re-found by anchoring on a name the table itself claimed (MachVersteck is A[60]) and walking back: A is ptr 0x6a1ee0 / op 0x6a1fd4, B is ptr 0x6a23f0 / op 0x6a24e0. The generator is a gate, not a dumper: it asserts the sentinel, the zero terminator past the last entry, every pointer inside .rodata, every name printable, every opcode within the dispatcher's 0..140, and re-checks the seven opcodes named by unrelated routes BEFORE the keyword tables were read. Both arms measured -- correct offsets give exit 0 and 7 of 7 controls; table A shifted by one slot gives exit 1, 6 of 7 controls, and three structural failures. The control counter itself was fixed before trusting it: it first printed the CONSTANT 7 whether or not the controls agreed, the same shape as the dead decode counter of row 967. New finding along the way: opcode 55 carries TWO keywords, DelNPC at B[26] and DelOBJ at B[27], while creation uses two separate opcodes (CreateNPC 1, CreateObj 8) -- the compiler distinguishes an NPC from an object when making one and not when destroying it. That asymmetry is pinned in the generator, so any other double-named opcode fails the run.

The port now takes retail's own autopilot script grammar, so one step list drives both engines and the two can be captured at the same milliseconds. godot-port/drive.gd implements ms/verb/args (move, click, hold, release, wheel, key) against Input, and main.gd dispatches --drive=/--shots=/--drive-out= ahead of --shot= through the same _await_settled(). Two divergences from autopilot.c are deliberate: key takes an Input Map ACTION name and an optional hold duration, because IsoCamera pans through Input.get_vector which samples HELD state and a press-release inside one frame pans by nothing; and text is refused rather than ignored. Actions are driven by Input.action_press, NOT parse_input_event(InputEventAction) -- the latter propagates to _input handlers but never reaches the singleton's action state, measured as 0.25 percent of pixels moving over a 1200ms iso_right. Confirmed live: wheel 5 1 moves 93.64 percent, and iso_right under --noplayer moves 95.24 percent, while the same key under a default run moves 0.27 percent because the camera follow overwrites the pan every frame. tools/drive/session.sh runs one script against both engines at 1024x768 and nothing else -- retail's grab is hard-coded to that size in autopilot.c, drive.gd exits 1 on --shots= at any other, and each pair is re-measured with magick identify before png_delta sees it. It keeps the port's FULL stderr, which look.sh filters, and that alone surfaced the unexplained hero: Models.mesh_weights entries 654 and 664 have two meshes and two FormMeshBone lists that admit no unambiguous pairing, so ModelView draws bones with no readable weight blocks.

First retail-vs-port comparison of the same scene: menu.sh new drives retail to the Seraphim's campaign start (Silver Creek cathedral) and the port, left on its own defaults, spawns her at cell 3236,2511 (sector 50,39) and draws the same room. session.sh reported an 85.82% delta and it is an artefact: the port's frame is retail's translated by exactly one pixel up-left, and correcting that translation makes 69.47% of the whole frame BIT-IDENTICAL to retail, with a bare wall patch at 100.00% identical and a bare floor patch at 91.05%. --sector= does not survive the camera's follow, so both runs captured the same view whatever was passed. What is left after the 1px fix is localised and countable: the benches sit 7px too high (best shift +1,+8, residual 21.7), the altar table is off by (+14,+31) and still 63.5 apart so it is not merely displaced, the chest is absent and a candelabra stands where retail has none, the Seraphim's own model draws as a distorted rig because Models.mesh_weights refuses entries 654 and 664, the white-robed novice and her ?! marker are missing entirely, and the taskbar is half identical. The 1px offset is the highest-leverage fix in the list because it is what makes every pixel gate in parity/ read as a total mismatch.

Fixed: IsoCamera centred the view one world unit up-left of retail's, so every frame the port drew was retail's frame translated by one pixel and every pixel gate read it as total disagreement. Confirmed as a WORLD-space constant rather than a screen-pixel one because it doubles with the zoom step (shift 1,1 at the middle step, 2,2 at 2x, on settled frames 4 s apart), and localised to the camera rather than the follow path because it survives --noplayer --at= with no player and no pixel snap, where the y term differs from the follow case by exactly HH=24 (the hero stands at cell centre) and the x term does not move at all. It cannot live in cell_to_world: terrain, objects and camera all share that function, so a constant there cancels and changes no pixel. Fix is IsoCamera.VIEW_ORIGIN = (-1,+1) world, applied in look_at_cell and follow_cell. Verified against retail at both zoom steps: shift 0,0 at each, raw delta 85.68 to 29.35 percent at 1x and 81.25 to 37.73 at 2x, and 70.54 percent of the whole frame is now bit-identical to retail with a bare wall patch at 100 percent. follow_parity.sh still PASSes both gates. The Seraphim renders as a distorted rig because models.pak entries 654 SERABOOTS01.GRN and 664 SERASHOULDER01.GRN refuse to pair meshes with FormMeshBone lists, and the enriched diagnostic says why: needs=[4,4] against list sizes=[5,5] and [4,4]. Both assignments satisfy the size constraint and the two lists hold DIFFERENT bones, so mesh_weights' rule that every valid matching must yield the same list correctly refuses to guess. The comment in _pair_bone_lists naming SERABOOTS01 as the case its identical-contents rule rescues is therefore stale: a left and a right boot need a left and a right leg, which no size test can tell apart. Not fixed, because a geometric nearest-bone tiebreaker would be an invention. The next step is documentation rather than more bytes: real Granny meshes carry their own BoneBindings array as a property of the Mesh, so the premise that the pairing has to be solved at all may be the bug, and the Iris1 reader is where to check that.

Implemented the geometric lever granny-grn.md named for the 169 left/right symmetric pieces the size rule refuses: score each candidate matching by the mean distance from a mesh's sampled vertices to the rest positions of the bones it would bind to, take the cheapest, and refuse when the runner-up is within 15 percent. The control is what makes it evidence rather than a coin flip with a distance in it, and it is now a gate: checks/bonepair_check.gd runs both rules over every entry and requires the geometric one never to contradict the size rule where the size rule decides. Result over models.pak: 1349 entries decided by size, 139 ties broken by geometry, 79 still refused, and ZERO disagreements. SERABOOTS01 and SERASHOULDER01 both decode now, the Seraphim's dress line goes from worn=5 worn_refused=2 to worn=7 worn_refused=0, and her greaves and boots appear in the isolated render. All 40 checks in godot-port/checks pass, so the _pair_inputs extraction the change needed broke nothing.

The port draws the hero as a vertical smear with a huge flat sheet flying out of it, and the cause is her DISTANCE FROM THE WORLD ORIGIN, not her model. Same rig, same run, only --spawn moved: at world offsets 576, 60000 and 99984 the Seraphim renders as a correct standing figure; at 134400 outdoors and at 137952 in Silver Creek's cathedral she is destroyed. So the threshold sits between 99984 and 134400, which brackets 2^17, and both indoors and the interior layer are excluded as causes by the outdoor 134400 case. It is not the model (the same entry renders perfectly through --figure=), not the animation (--noanim is pixel-identical), not the facing yaw (--figure-yaw=1.5 renders a clean profile), not the pairing, and not a bone that failed to place (traced: all 72 bones land at the placed position, none left at the origin). The mechanism is PlayerView's own documented design, which bakes world placement into the skeleton's root-bone POSE rather than the node transform so that sorting_use_aabb_center=false keeps reading the node's identity global position as its sort key. That is a deliberate and well-argued choice, and it puts a translation of order 1e5 through the skinning path; Sacred's world reaches 6400 cells, i.e. about 307200 world units, so most of the map is past the point where the port cannot draw a character at all. Not fixed here: the repair is either a floating origin or a different sort-key scheme, both of which change an invariant three view classes are written around.

Separately from row 979 and independent of position, a large flat blade-shaped surface is drawn with the player rig in the WORLD path at every distance tested including the near-origin control where the body itself is correct. It is part of the rig and not the scene: --hideplayer removes it along with her. The same model through --figure= shows no such surface and draws its socketed SWORD.GRN at a plausible size, so the world path is where it goes wrong. Prime suspect is the socket-attached weapon drawn at roughly ten times its size, unconfirmed because --equip= is a separate viewer mode and there is no in-world switch to drop the weapon; identifying it needs one.

RETRACTED: row 979's claim that skinned rigs stop rendering past about 1e5 world units is WRONG, and so is the alarm that most of Sacred's map cannot draw a character. Measured on the shipped build with the same rig at three positions and nothing else changed, the figure is identical at 576, at 134400 outdoors and at 137952 in the cathedral. What produced the false finding: before rows 981 and 982 the hero was untextured AND lit by a key with no fill, so she was a dark silhouette everywhere, and a dark silhouette at a far position was read as geometrically destroyed while an equally silhouetted near one was read as correct. The --spawn variable I thought isolated distance isolated nothing. Three later experiments all pointed at the same retraction and were misread first: moving placement out of the bone pose onto the node transform changed the picture not at all, detaching the skin changed it not at all, and yaw is 0.0000 at both positions so facing was never the difference either. The node-transform rewrite of PlayerView's placement was reverted with this, since it fixed nothing and rewrote an invariant three view classes are written around.

With row 983 removing the confound, the fill light of row 982 could finally be measured against retail IN THE SAME ROOM rather than through a near-origin proxy, and it does better than that proxy suggested: over the same pixels of Silver Creek's cathedral retail reads brightness p50=87 p90=168 saturation 0.20, the key alone read 46/102 at saturation 0.35, and key plus fill reads 85/119 at 0.20. Root cause of row 980's blade: ModelView.attach_socket sets piece.transform = grip.affine_inverse() to land the hilt on the hand, and the inverse of a scaled transform also inverts its SCALE, which is not the attacher's to apply. Measured across the corpus the grips carry wildly different scales -- SWORD.GRN 1.0000, SeraWindslicer 0.1497, SeraWindweaver 2.1800 -- so the raw inverse magnified the Seraphim's own starting blade by 6.68x and would shrink the other to 0.46x. Her sword is 49.2 units in the file against a 74.3-unit body, so at the rig's 1.315 scale it should draw about 65 units and instead drew about 432 against her 98: the flat sheet lying across her in every world capture. Three investigations mistook that sheet for a wing, a shadow and a broken rig before the line was read, and two of them were only excluded by skipping SeraWings01 (unchanged) and then the equip (gone). The --figure= viewer never showed it because the viewer attaches SWORD.GRN, whose grip scale is exactly 1. Fix is to orthonormalize the grip basis before inverting: T still maps the grip origin to zero so the hilt lands identically, only the magnification goes.
